Usability testing evaluates whether people can complete representative tasks with a design under defined conditions. It is not a focus group and not a popularity contest.

Write tasks as goals, not UI instructions (“Find out whether this claim was paid” not “Click Claims then Search”). Define success criteria before the session. Observe behavior; ask think-aloud carefully so narration does not become a second task. Measure completion, errors, time-on-task where meaningful, and severity of blockers. Prefer moderated sessions when you need diagnosis; unmoderated when you need volume and geographic spread—know the tradeoff.

Test with the right fidelity for the question. Paper can validate information architecture; interactive prototypes validate flow and feedback; production builds validate performance and edge-state recovery. Do not “validate” a high-risk assumption with five friends who already know the product.

Assumption Mapping

Before you spend participant hours, write down what you believe. An assumption map lists claims about users, jobs, context, value, and feasibility, then ranks each by risk (how wrong would hurt) and ignorance (how little evidence you have). High-risk / high-ignorance items become research priorities.

Assumption mapping prevents research theater: studies that confirm what the team already wanted to ship. Revisit the map after each study; retire assumptions that crossed your evidence bar, and escalate those that failed.

Triangulation: Qualitative + Quantitative

Qualitative methods explain why and how; quantitative methods estimate how often and how large. Neither alone is sufficient for consequential decisions.

Triangulation patterns include: diary themes checked against analytics event rates; interview friction mapped to funnel drop-offs; usability severity scored against support ticket volume; survey scales interpreted through a few deep interviews that reveal what “satisfied” meant. When signals conflict, treat conflict as information—different segments, different contexts, or a measurement error—not as a vote to ignore the inconvenient method.

Recruiting Screeners: Assistive Technology and Low Connectivity

A screener is a filter that selects for the jobs and constraints you claim to design for. Weak screeners recruit “people with smartphones.” Strong screeners recruit people who do the job under the constraints that break the product.

For assistive technology (AT) participants, screen for actual AT use (screen readers, magnification, switch control, voice control, captions as primary channel)—not merely self-identified disability. Confirm platform and AT combination; schedule longer sessions; compensate fairly; test with their setups when possible. Do not treat one Blind VoiceOver user as representing all accessibility.

For low-connectivity participants, screen for real network conditions: prepaid data caps, shared Wi‑Fi, rural latency, intermittent offline work. Ask about last failure due to connectivity. If your product assumes always-on broadband, your “representative” urban fiber users will never find the bug that dominates elsewhere.

Also screen out professional testers when authenticity matters, and screen in edge roles (proxy users, caregivers, shared-device households) when the job includes them.

Evidence Bars

An evidence bar is a pre-committed standard: what quality and quantity of signal is required before a decision type is allowed. Examples: “We will not cut a primary navigation path without at least two independent methods showing the same failure mode,” or “We will not claim ‘users prefer X’ without behavioral task evidence plus a segment-sized sample.”

Evidence bars protect against HiPPO (highest-paid person’s opinion) and against endless research. Not every decision needs a diary study. Map decision risk to bar height.

Research Ops Repositories and Event Dictionaries

Insights die in slide decks. A research ops repository stores study plans, screeners, consent artifacts, raw notes (access-controlled), synthesis, clips, and decision logs linked to product tickets. Tag by job, segment, platform, and assumption ID so future teams can find prior art.

An event dictionary aligns qualitative language with quantitative instrumentation. If interviews say “abandoned checkout because of surprise fee,” analytics must name that event consistently (checkout_fee_shown, checkout_abandoned_after_fee). Without a dictionary, triangulation becomes folk etymology.

Diary vs Interview: A Decision Frame

Prefer diaries when… Prefer interviews when…
Timing, frequency, or interruption patterns are the unknown You need rich causal narrative of few episodes
Social desirability would distort live answers Participants cannot or will not log reliably
The job spans days/weeks You need rapid iteration within days
You need ecological validity of when things happen You need to probe contradictions in the moment

Often the best design is diary → interview: logs identify moments; interviews explain them.

Key Terms

Contextual inquiry — Apprenticeship-style observation and interview in the participant’s real environment.
Story-based interview — Interview structured around specific past episodes rather than general preferences.
Diary study — Longitudinal self-reporting of events across time.
Probe — Generative kit or prompt that elicits contextual artifacts.
Assumption map — Prioritized inventory of beliefs ranked by risk and ignorance.
Evidence bar — Pre-agreed standard of proof for a class of decisions.
Triangulation — Cross-checking claims with independent methods or data types.
Event dictionary — Shared definitions linking qualitative phenomena to analytics events.
Research ops repository — System of record for studies, artifacts, and decisions.

Principles

  1. Observe the job in context before optimizing the interface.
  2. Prefer stories and behavior over opinions.
  3. Match method to the temporal shape of the job.
  4. Recruit for constraints that break products, not for convenience samples.
  5. Set evidence bars before fieldwork; retire assumptions explicitly.
  6. Instrument language: qualitative codes and quantitative events must share a dictionary.

Exercises

  1. Assumption map sprint. For a product you know, list twelve assumptions. Score risk × ignorance. Design the cheapest study that would move the top three across a stated evidence bar.
  2. Screener rewrite. Take a weak screener (“ages 25–45, owns a phone”). Rewrite it for (a) screen-reader primary users and (b) prepaid low-data users doing the same job. Justify each question.
  3. Diary vs interview brief. Pick a time-distributed job (e.g., weekly payroll approval). Write a one-page decision: method choice, logging channel, entry criteria, follow-up interview triggers, and success metrics for the study itself.

Anti-Patterns

  • Interviewing for “what would you like” and calling it research.
  • Usability tests with leading tasks that narrate the UI.
  • One AT participant used as universal accessibility proof.
  • Diaries with twenty daily questions and three days of compliance.
  • Insights trapped in PDFs with no tags, no assumption IDs, no decision link.
  • Analytics and research using different names for the same failure.

Further Reading

  • Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design
  • Portigal, Interviewing Users
  • ResearchOps Community practices (and Kate Towsey / community ResearchOps guidance) on repositories, consent, and research infrastructure
  • Rubin & Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing
  • Mixed-methods triangulation overviews in Creswell & Plano Clark

Chapter 8 — Modern Contexts: Mobile, Multi-Modal, AI, and Constraints

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 8 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Design for mobile interruption and multi-modal continuity across devices and channels.
  2. Treat AI as an unreliable teammate: propose→confirm→apply, definition of done, streaming, provenance, and agent boundaries.
  3. Place generative UI inside a stable shell; plan offline-first and shared-device realities.
  4. Use performance latency bands and platform conventions as design constraints, not afterthoughts.

Modern UX is practiced under constraints that classical desktop form design barely contemplated: discontinuous attention, multiple modalities, probabilistic systems, intermittent networks, and devices that belong to households rather than individuals. This chapter reframes “context” from a persona footnote into a set of operating conditions that determine whether a design is usable at all.

Mobile Interruption

Mobile use is interruption-native. Notifications, calls, location changes, and one-handed grips fracture sessions. Design for pause and resume: durable drafts, visible recovery points, undo, and state that survives app death. Avoid multi-step wizards that punish a thirty-second glance away. Prefer progressive disclosure that can be re-entered mid-flow without cognitive restart taxes.

Interruptibility also means time-to-value under partial attention. Primary actions must be reachable without reading a novel. Confirmations for irreversible actions must survive hurried thumbs—clear labels, reversible defaults where possible, and friction proportional to blast radius.

Multi-Modal Continuity

Users start on a phone, continue on a laptop, finish via voice or SMS, and review on a TV-sized display. Continuity requires shared job state: identity, draft, cart, ticket, or conversation thread that is addressable across surfaces. Design the handoff, not only each surface: what is summarized on return? What requires re-authentication? What is safe to show on a lock screen or shared display?

Multi-modal does not mean every feature everywhere. It means the job can progress without forcing modality loyalty. Voice may capture intent; screen may confirm detail; notification may close the loop. Continuity fails when each channel invents its own object model.

AI as an Unreliable Teammate

Generative and agentic systems do not “know”; they sample. Treating AI as an authoritative oracle produces confident harm. Treat AI as a junior teammate: fast at drafts, weak at accountability. Humans own outcomes.

Propose → Confirm → Apply

For consequential actions, structure interaction as:

  1. Propose — The system suggests a change, answer, or plan, with visible uncertainty where possible.
  2. Confirm — The human reviews, edits, or rejects. Confirmation UI must show what will happen, not a vague “Looks good.”
  3. Apply — Only then mutate durable state; provide undo and an audit trail.

Skip confirm for low-blast-radius assists (grammar tweaks in a private draft). Never skip for payments, medical advice presented as fact, access control, deletion cascades, or messages sent as the user.

AI Definition of Done (DoD)

An AI feature is not done when the model demos well. A practical DoD includes: scoped job; failure modes listed; human confirm path for high risk; empty/error/refusal states; evaluation set with known hard cases; logging for provenance; escalation to human support; and latency targets under real load. “It answered in the happy path” is not done.

Streaming

Streaming tokens reduce perceived wait and support early abort. Design for partial output: users may interrupt, edit mid-stream, or reject. Do not lock the UI until the full essay arrives if the job is “scan and steer.” Conversely, do not stream irreversible side effects—stream the proposal, apply only after confirm.

Provenance

Show why the system claims what it claims when stakes are non-trivial: sources, retrieved documents, policy citations, or “no source—model inference.” Provenance is not decoration; it is how users calibrate trust. Absent provenance, users either over-trust or permanently discount the feature.

Agents

Agents chain tools: browse, write, purchase, message, configure. Bound them with allowlists, budgets (time, money, steps), and explicit scopes. Surface a plan before tool use when effects leave the local draft. Provide a kill switch and a readable activity log. Multi-agent orchestration without a stable human-facing status model becomes an un-debuggable haunted house.

Generative UI in a Stable Shell

Generative UI can rearrange layouts, synthesize controls, or invent workflows. Unbounded generation destroys learnability and accessibility. Prefer a stable shell: navigation, safety chrome, account, and critical wayfinding remain consistent; generative content fills designated regions (summaries, suggested actions, draft canvases). Announce dynamic regions to AT; do not generate unlabeled custom controls that break platform expectations.

Offline-First

Offline-first assumes disconnection is normal. Design local-first reads and writes with sync semantics: conflict resolution, queue visibility, and honest indicators (“Saved on device · Pending sync”). Never imply server success when you only wrote locally. For low-connectivity contexts, reduce payload, cache critical paths, and degrade to SMS or USSD-like simplicity where appropriate.

Shared Device

Phones and tablets are often shared among family, retail floor, clinic, or classroom. Design session hygiene: quick switch, PIN/biometrics at sensitivity thresholds, hidden notification content, and clear “who is acting” indicators. Avoid leaving another person’s medical, financial, or chat content one Back gesture away.

Performance Latency Bands

Users experience latency in heuristic bands, not as absolute physiology laws. Treat the following ranges as design heuristics for choosing progress, cancel, and async patterns—calibrate with your product’s measurements and user research:

  • Instant (~0–100 ms) — Direct manipulation feel.
  • Immediate (~100–300 ms) — Still conversational.
  • Polite wait (~300–1000 ms) — Needs subtle progress.
  • Break in flow (~1–5 s) — Needs determinate progress and cancel.
  • Out of band (>5–10 s) — Asynchronous job pattern: notify on completion.

AI inference often lands in later bands; design the wait as part of the interaction (streaming, skeletons, useful partials), not as a spinner apology.

Platform Conventions

Respect platform navigation, typography scaling, permission idioms, back/gesture behavior, and notification norms. “Consistent with our brand” does not excuse fighting iOS/Android/desktop conventions that users already trust. Custom chrome that breaks system Back or share sheets taxes every session forever.

Key Terms

Interruption-native design — Flows built to pause, survive, and resume.
Multi-modal continuity — Job state progressable across channels and devices.
Propose→confirm→apply — Safe pattern for AI-assisted consequential actions.
Provenance — Traceable basis for system claims.
Stable shell — Persistent chrome around generative regions.
Offline-first — Local capability with explicit sync semantics.
Latency band — Heuristic perceptual category of delay that guides progress/cancel/async UI patterns.

Principles

  1. Design for resume, not only for first completion.
  2. Continuity is a product object, not a visual theme.
  3. AI proposes; humans confirm; systems apply with undo.
  4. Generate inside a stable, accessible shell.
  5. Honesty about offline and latency beats optimistic lies.
  6. Platform conventions are part of the interface language.

Exercises

  1. Interruption script. Storyboard a checkout interrupted twice (call + tunnel). Specify draft durability, resume UI, and what is not re-asked.
  2. AI DoD checklist. Pick an AI feature (e.g., auto-refund suggestion). Write DoD items for confirm gates, provenance, evaluation cases, and agent tool bounds.
  3. Latency redesign. Map each step of a flow to latency bands. Redesign any step that sits above 1 s without progress, cancel, or async completion.

Anti-Patterns

  • Irreversible AI actions behind a single “Accept all.”
  • Generative menus that relocate primary navigation per session.
  • “Saved” indicators that only mean local write.
  • Ignoring shared-device notification leakage.
  • Custom gestures that override system Back.
  • Treating demo latency on office Wi‑Fi as production truth.

Further Reading

  • Mobile interruption and attention research in HCI (Oulasvirta et al. and successors)
  • Nielsen Norman Group guidance on mobile UX and progressive disclosure
  • Human–AI interaction guidelines (Amershi et al.; industry AI UX playbooks)
  • Offline-first and CRDT/sync design primers for product teams
  • Platform HIG: Apple Human Interface Guidelines; Material Design; accessibility specs (WCAG, platform AT docs)

Chapter 9 — Operating Practice: Cadence, Gates, and Critique

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 9 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Run a weekly “Monday loop,” maintain a living one-pager, and enforce midweek gates.
  2. Manage a priority stack and apply conflict playbooks when goals collide.
  3. Critique work with an anti-pattern table and explicit Definitions of Done across risk domains.
  4. Apply a worked case method that turns incidents into durable practice.
  5. Use a compact operating checklist to keep teams honest under schedule pressure.

Talent does not scale; operating practice does. Teams with similar craft skills diverge because some have cadence, gates, and critique rituals that make quality the default path of least resistance. This chapter is the shop-floor manual: how Modern UX runs week to week, how decisions get stacked, how conflicts get resolved, and how “done” is defined so shipping does not mean abandoning users.

The Monday Loop

Start the week by reconnecting intent, evidence, and capacity—not by re-litigating strategy from zero.

A practical Monday loop:

  1. Outcome pulse — What user/business outcome are we moving this week? One sentence.
  2. Evidence delta — What did we learn since last Monday (support, research, metrics, incidents)?
  3. Priority stack review — Top items only; demote or kill with a recorded reason. When bets collide, apply the book’s priority hierarchy: safety / irreversible harm → mental model & recovery → inclusion on the critical path → job progress / outcomes → systems consistency → delight / differentiation.
  4. Risk scan — Auth, privacy, interruption, content, activation, support—any DoD gaps in flight?
  5. Owner map — Named owners for each top item; no orphan work.
  6. Midweek gate calendar — When will we decide go/no-go on risky slices?

Keep the loop under thirty minutes. If it regularly exceeds that, the one-pager is rotten or the stack is too wide.

The One-Pager

The one-pager is the team’s external memory. It is not a branding brief. Minimum contents:

  • Problem / job statement
  • Target segment and critical constraints (AT, connectivity, shared device, etc.)
  • Non-goals
  • Success metrics and evidence bar
  • Current priority stack (ranked)
  • Open assumptions (from Chapter 7 maps)
  • Risks & DoD status
  • Links to research repo, event dictionary, prototypes, and decision log

Update it when reality changes—not only at kickoff. If two people disagree about “what we’re doing,” the one-pager failed before the design did.

Midweek Gates

Gates are scheduled decision points that prevent weekend heroics and Friday ambiguity. Examples: “Wednesday noon: confirm whether AI refund agent may send email without human confirm”; “Thursday: usability severity bar met for navigation change.”

A gate has: decision question, evidence required, decider, default if undecided (usually “no ship”). Defaults matter; without them, silence becomes accidental yes.

Priority Stack

A priority stack is an ordered list of bets, not a parallel wish festival. Rules of thumb:

  • Only one “P0” human-attention consumer at a time per squad.
  • Sequence by risk reduction and learning, not by stakeholder volume.
  • Every item has an exit: ship, kill, or park with revisit date.
  • Forced ranking: if everything is high, nothing is.

When new work arrives, it must displace something explicitly. Insertion without displacement is how stacks become fiction.

Conflict Playbooks

Conflicts are normal: growth vs. privacy, speed vs. accessibility, AI automation vs. control, sales demo vs. offline resilience. Playbooks beat improvisation.

Playbook pattern:

  1. Name the colliding goods (not the people).
  2. Restate user harm if either side “wins” absolutely.
  3. Consult evidence bars and DoDs—many conflicts dissolve when “done” is explicit.
  4. Choose a time-boxed experiment or a principled constraint (e.g., “propose→confirm→apply remains non-negotiable”).
  5. Record the decision and the revisit trigger.

Escalate only after the playbook; escalation without framing wastes executive attention and teaches the team that politics beats method.

Anti-Pattern Critique Table

Use this table in design crits. Critique the work, not the author.

Anti-pattern Symptom Critique question Remedy direction
Preference theater Opinions without tasks What behavior would falsify this? Task-based test / assumption map
Happy-path only No empty/error/offline What happens on tunnel Wi‑Fi / AT / denial? State matrix + DoD
AI oracle Auto-apply consequential acts Where is confirm + provenance? Propose→confirm→apply
Dashboard hero First viewport is a control panel What is the one job of this surface? Single-composition redesign
Metric theater Vanity KPIs Which decision does this metric change? Tie to evidence bar
Stack fiction Twelve P0s What did we demote? Forced rank + displacement
Accessibility as phase AT at the end Who is screened into research now? AT in screener + DoD
Dark pattern creep Confirm shaming, hidden opt-outs Would we defend this in support? Ethics + support DoD

Definitions of Done (DoDs)

DoDs convert values into ship gates. Adapt thresholds to risk, but do not skip categories.

Auth DoD — Clear session actor; recovery paths; shared-device logout; no secret leakage in URLs or notifications; step-up auth for sensitive actions.
Privacy DoD — Data minimization; purpose limitation stated; consent where required; retention known; third-party sharing diagrammed; user-visible controls work.
Interrupt DoD — Draft durability; resume points; irreversible actions protected under hurried use; notifications safe on lock screen.
Content DoD — Source/provenance for claims; localization plan; empty states; harmful/unsafe content handling; editable AI proposals.
Activation DoD — First-value path measurable; time-to-value target; dead ends instrumented; support escape hatch on first-run failure.
Support DoD — Failure modes diagnosable; logs/IDs users can cite; macros match UI language; known defects documented before launch.

Wire DoDs into midweek gates. “Design approved” without DoD review is theater.

Worked Case Method

Turn incidents into curriculum.

  1. Case brief — What happened (user harm, not only downtime).
  2. Timeline — Decisions and skipped gates.
  3. Evidence — What we knew vs. assumed.
  4. Principle failure — Which principle/DoD was missing or ignored.
  5. Repair — Product fix + process fix (screener, gate, dictionary, checklist).
  6. Teaching artifact — One paragraph added to the team’s living anti-pattern table or Monday loop.

Run a worked case monthly. Blameless framing is mandatory; learning dies under humiliation.

Compact Operating Checklist

Use before you call something “ready”:

  • [ ] One-pager current: outcome, non-goals, stack, assumptions, links
  • [ ] Monday loop owners named; midweek gates dated
  • [ ] Priority stack forced-rank; displacement recorded for new work
  • [ ] Research/evidence bar met for high-risk claims (or explicitly waived with owner)
  • [ ] Event dictionary updated for new user-visible failures
  • [ ] DoDs checked: auth · privacy · interrupt · content · activation · support
  • [ ] AI paths (if any): propose→confirm→apply; provenance; abort; eval set
  • [ ] Mobile/offline/shared-device states designed, not promised
  • [ ] Latency bands accounted for; cancel/async where needed
  • [ ] Crit used anti-pattern table; open issues ticketed
  • [ ] Support and analytics can see the same failure names
  • [ ] Launch default is no if gate evidence missing

Key Terms

Monday loop — Weekly ritual aligning outcome, evidence, stack, risk, and owners.
One-pager — Living brief for intent, constraints, metrics, and risks.
Midweek gate — Scheduled go/no-go with evidence and default.
Priority stack — Forced-rank list with displacement rules.
Conflict playbook — Structured resolution for colliding goods.
DoD — Ship criteria for a risk domain.
Worked case — Blameless post-incident learning artifact.

Principles

  1. Cadence beats inspiration; write it down or it did not happen.
  2. Gates need defaults—usually “do not ship.”
  3. New work displaces old work explicitly.
  4. Critique patterns, not people; use tables.
  5. DoDs are product requirements, not QA niceties.
  6. Every serious failure becomes a taught case.

Exercises

  1. Install a Monday loop. Draft a 30-minute agenda and a one-pager template for a real or fictional squad; run a dry rehearsal with invented evidence deltas.
  2. Conflict playbook drill. Growth wants one-tap AI email send; privacy wants confirm. Write the playbook steps and a time-boxed experiment with a clear revisit metric.
  3. Worked case write-up. Take a public product failure. Produce the six-part case; add one row to an anti-pattern critique table and one checklist amendment.

Anti-Patterns

  • Kickoff decks that are never updated.
  • “We’ll gate it later” that becomes launch day.
  • Parallel P0s as a culture of urgency cosplay.
  • Crits that debate taste without falsifiable questions.
  • DoDs owned by nobody, therefore optional.
  • Postmortems that assign blame and change nothing.

Further Reading

  • Team cadence and ritual design in product operations literature
  • Google SRE / blameless postmortem culture (adapted to UX incidents)
  • DoD and Definition of Ready practices from agile quality communities
  • Decision logs and architecture decision records (ADRs) as cousins to UX decision logs
  • Facilitation guides for design critique (e.g., Frolicker / critique practice essays)

Chapter 10 — Case Studies and Capstone Practice

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 10 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Analyze real product failures through HCD, IxD, Inclusive Design, and Strategy lenses in one pass.
  2. Propose redesign decisions that respect the book’s priority hierarchy and Definitions of Done.
  3. Select outcome metrics that measure recovery, inclusion, and trust—not vanity engagement.
  4. Facilitate discussion that turns cases into team process change.
  5. Plan and execute a two-week capstone that ships a gated, evidence-backed redesign.

Cases are where theory becomes judgment. Each study below follows the worked case method from Chapter 9: brief → lens analysis → redesign → metrics → discussion. Read them as teaching artifacts, not postmortems of named vendors. Apply the priority hierarchy (safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight) when trade-offs appear.

How to Work a Case (student method)

  1. Restate user harm in one sentence before debating UI.
  2. Name which DoDs failed (auth, privacy, interrupt, content, activation, support, AI).
  3. Redesign the critical path first; polish later.
  4. Pick two leading and one lagging metric.
  5. Write one process fix (gate, screener, checklist row) so the failure cannot silently recur.

Case A — Mobile Interrupted Delivery-Time Modification

Context. A grocery delivery app lets customers change delivery windows until the driver is en route. Maya opens “Change time” on a crowded bus, selects a later slot, then takes a call. The app backgrounds; when she returns, a spinner flashes and the confirmation screen is gone. She assumes the change saved. The driver arrives at the original window. Support sees a “session expired mid-POST” log; Maya sees betrayal.

Lens analysis.

  • HCD: Conceptual model failed—there is no durable “pending / saved / failed” story. Knowledge stayed in the head (“I tapped it”).
  • IxD: Gulf of evaluation after interruption; no draft durability or resume point (Interrupt DoD).
  • Inclusive: One-handed, noisy, low-attention context is the default mobile condition—not an edge case.
  • Strategy: Activation and retention KPIs hid a support cost; “change rate” rose while on-time satisfaction fell.

Redesign decisions. Persist the in-progress change as a local draft; show sticky status (“Not saved yet”). On resume, reopen the exact step with the last selection visible. Confirm success with durable confirmation (push + in-app receipt + order timeline event). If the network fails, queue with honest copy (“Waiting to send · Tap to retry”). Soft-lock irreversible driver dispatch behind an explicit confirm that survives app death.

Metrics. % of change flows resumed after ≥30s backgrounding without data loss; confirmation-receipt open rate; support tickets tagged “wrong window after edit”; CSAT on delivery-time accuracy.

Discussion. Where is forgiveness enough vs. hard confirm? How would you instrument “assumed success” failures that leave no angry click?

Case B — B2B Admin Invite with Screen Reader

Context. An admin invites a contractor via a modal: email field, role chips, “Send invite.” Visually it works. With VoiceOver/NVDA, focus lands in the backdrop; role chips are unlabeled toggle buttons; success is a toast that is not announced; the invitee list updates silently. A blind admin cannot complete the job without a sighted colleague—violating employment-access expectations and WCAG operable/understandable criteria.

Lens analysis.

  • HCD: The job (“grant access with the right role”) is invisible to AT users—exclusion as product failure, not niche bug.
  • IxD: Signifiers and feedback exist only visually; focus order breaks the execution path.
  • Inclusive: Critical-path AT was deferred (“phase 2 accessibility”). Modal semantics and live regions were missing.
  • Strategy: Enterprise procurement now asks for VPAT evidence; this path would fail an evidence bar.

Redesign decisions. Use a dialog with proper role, labelled-by title, and initial focus on the email field. Role controls as a radiogroup with accessible names. Announce errors and success via assertive/polite live regions tied to the same language as the visual toast. Provide a non-modal fallback page for the same flow. Add AT users to the research screener; make “invite with SR” a midweek gate item before ship.

Metrics. Task success rate with SR/keyboard-only on invite; time-on-task vs. mouse baseline within agreed band; WCAG issues on critical path = 0 Sev1; support macros for invite failure cite the same IDs as UI.

Discussion. Is a “VPAT later” acceptable for admin-only tools? What is the minimum inclusive DoD for any access-control flow?

Case C — AI CRM Follow-Up Agent with Send Side Effects

Context. A CRM ships an agent that “drafts and sends follow-ups.” In the demo, it proposes polite emails. In production, a salesperson clicks “Run for overdue deals”; the agent sends 40 messages, including one to a customer mid-legal dispute and one with a hallucinated discount. Undo is “ask support.” Trust collapses inside the sales org first.

Lens analysis.

  • HCD: Agent framed as oracle; meaning should have been “propose accountable drafts,” not “send as me.”
  • IxD: Side effects streamed past confirm; no plan surface, no per-recipient review, no kill switch (AI DoD).
  • Inclusive / trust: Recipients with cognitive load or language mismatch suffer opaque, uneditable blast.
  • Strategy: Activity metrics (emails sent) rewarded blast radius; conflict playbook (automation vs. control) was skipped.

Redesign decisions. Enforce propose → confirm → apply for any external send. Show a review queue: recipients, subject, body, data sources, confidence/provenance, and policy flags (legal hold, do-not-contact). Default to draft-only; require step-up confirm for bulk send; budget caps (max N/day). Activity log + one-click revoke where providers allow. Evaluation set includes dispute-tagged accounts and hallucinated-offer probes. Midweek gate: “May the agent send without human confirm?” Default = no.

Metrics. % of agent outputs human-edited before send; wrongful-send rate; time-to-revoke; salesperson trust pulse; escalation count to legal/support.

Discussion. When, if ever, is auto-send acceptable? How do you stop metric theater from selecting for harm?

Case D — Offline / Shared Handheld Field Inventory

Context. Warehouse associates share rugged handhelds. The inventory app assumes always-online and single-user sessions. During a Wi‑Fi dead zone, counts appear saved (optimistic UI) but vanish on sync conflict. The next associate picks up the device and sees the previous user’s open cycle count—plus customer SKUs in notifications on the lock screen.

Lens analysis.

  • HCD: “Saved” lied; conceptual model of local vs. server truth was absent.
  • IxD: No queue visibility, no conflict resolution UX, silent identity continuity on a shared device.
  • Inclusive: Gloves, glare, and intermittent connectivity are the operating environment.
  • Strategy: Throughput KPIs ignored shrinkage and audit risk; Privacy/Auth DoDs were paperwork.

Redesign decisions. Offline-first with explicit sync states (“On device · Pending · Synced · Conflict”). Conflict UI compares counts with timestamp, actor, and location; never auto-drop without visibility. Session actor always visible; quick lock + PIN on sensitivity; clear switch-user. Notification content minimized on lock screen. Support DoD: every failed sync has a citeable ID matching the handheld screen.

Metrics. Sync-success within SLA; conflict resolution time; inventory variance attributable to app loss; accidental cross-user exposure incidents; time-to-lock after idle.

Discussion. Optimistic UI vs. honest pending—where does warehouse trust break? How do shared-device patterns differ from personal phone patterns?

Case E — Voice → Screen Multi-Modal Repair Booking

Context. A home-repair service lets customers start booking by voice (“Furnace won’t ignite”), then continue on phone UI. Voice captures a transcript into a ticket the screen never shows; the screen wizard asks the same questions again. On return from a second device, the voice session is a different object ID. Customers abandon; agents re-ask everything on the call.

Lens analysis.

  • HCD: No shared job object across modalities—continuity theater.
  • IxD: Handoff summary missing; gulf of evaluation on “what did we hear?”
  • Inclusive: Voice-only users and deaf/hard-of-hearing users both need the same ticket model with captions and editable fields.
  • Strategy: Channel metrics were siloed (voice containment vs. app conversion) so ownership of the handoff was nobody’s P0.

Redesign decisions. One addressable booking draft across voice, SMS, and app. After voice, push a deep link that opens a summary: heard intent, proposed urgency, missing slots—editable, not locked. Screen confirms details voice cannot safely finalize (address unit, payment). Announce dynamic updates to AT. Priority stack: fund the handoff object before new channel acquisition.

Metrics. Cross-modal resume rate; re-ask rate on agent calls; time-to-book from first utterance; accessibility task success on summary edit; drop-off at handoff step.

Discussion. What must voice never finalize alone? How do you measure continuity without punishing modality switches?

Capstone Project Brief (2 Weeks)

Brief. Teams of 3–5 redesign one constrained product slice that fails under a modern context (choose one: interruption, AT-critical admin, AI side effects, offline/shared device, or multi-modal handoff). Deliver a gated, evidence-backed improvement—not a brand restyle.

Week 1 — Discovery & framing

  • Day 1–2: One-pager (problem, segment, constraints, non-goals, success metrics, open assumptions).
  • Day 2–3: Assumption map + light research (5 task-based sessions or equivalent diary/support-log synthesis); include at least one AT or constraint-matched participant.
  • Day 4: Priority stack (forced rank); midweek gate calendar; DoD checklist for your risk domains.
  • Day 5: Concept critique using Chapter 9 anti-pattern table; revise.

Week 2 — Design, evidence, ship decision

  • Day 6–8: Prototype the critical path including failure/empty/offline/interrupt states.
  • Day 8–9: Usability eval (task success, severity); for AI slices, run a mini eval set with known hard cases.
  • Day 10: Midweek-style gate: go/no-go with evidence; default no.
  • Day 11–12: Polish only if gate passed; instrumentation plan + support macros; final critique.
  • Day 13–14: Demo + teaching artifact (one worked-case paragraph and one checklist amendment your fictional team would adopt).

Required deliverables. Living one-pager; prototype; evidence summary; DoD sign-off sheet; metrics dashboard sketch; 5-minute demo; retrospective on which priority-hierarchy layer drove the hardest trade-off.

Grading emphasis. Harm reduction and recoverability > visual novelty. Process quality (gates, inclusion in research, honest metrics) weights equal to interaction craft.

Key Terms

Worked case — Structured teaching artifact from user harm to process repair.
Lens analysis — Reading a failure through HCD / IxD / Inclusive / Strategy frames.
Critical path — The minimum path to complete the user’s job under constraint.
Handoff object — Shared job state addressable across modalities or devices.
Side-effect boundary — The line where AI/agent proposals become external mutations.
Capstone gate — Scheduled go/no-go with evidence and a default of no-ship.
Teaching artifact — Durable change to checklist, screener, or anti-pattern table.

Principles

  1. Restate harm before redesigning pixels.
  2. One failure usually spans multiple DoDs—name them.
  3. Redesign resume, confirm, and conflict states, not only happy paths.
  4. Metrics must detect silent failure and wrongful automation.
  5. Every case ends in a process fix, or it will recur.
  6. Capstones practice operating cadence, not slide craft alone.

Exercises

  1. Blind lens pass. Cover the “Redesign” section of Case A or C; write your own before comparing.
  2. DoD audit. For Case D, produce Auth, Privacy, Interrupt, and Support DoD checklists with pass/fail against the broken experience.
  3. Metric adversarial review. Take Case C’s vanity metric (“emails sent”) and invent two gaming strategies; replace with anti-gaming measures.
  4. Capstone one-pager drill. In 45 minutes, draft a one-pager for a campus or workplace tool that fails offline or under interruption.

Further Reading

  • Chapter 9 worked case method and DoD catalog (this volume)
  • Don Norman, The Design of Everyday Things—error and conceptual models in situ
  • WCAG 2.2 and platform accessibility APIs—operable dialogs and live regions
  • Google PAIR / people+AI guidance—human control, uncertainty, and handoff
  • Offline-first and CRDT/sync UX case writing in field-service and retail systems literature
  • Multi-modal service blueprinting (Bitner et al.) adapted to voice↔screen product objects

Worked Examples — Companion Guide

This directory contains one worked-examples document per chapter of
../Modern-UX-Complete-Practice-Textbook.md.
Every teachable concept in each chapter — the core concept(s) of every numbered
section plus every Key Term — has a dedicated, concrete worked example with
realistic product scenarios, actual UI copy, named states, bad-vs-good
contrasts, and an explicit tie-back to the chapter principle.

How these were produced

The documents were produced by a team of independent specialist experts, one
per chapter, mirroring how the textbook itself was authored. To keep the work
unbiased, three separate roles were used, each performed by a different
isolated agent that could not see the others’ work:

  1. Expert author — a domain specialist for the chapter (e.g., an
    inclusive-design expert for Chapter 3, a design-systems expert for
    Chapter 5) wrote the examples document from the chapter text alone.
  2. Independent examiner — a separate agent that did not author anything
    audited coverage concept-by-concept (without trusting the document’s own
    coverage table) and scored the document against the rubric below.
  3. Independent reviser — where the examiner flagged defects, a fresh
    expert with no attachment to the original text applied targeted fixes,
    after which a new examiner re-scored the document.

The cycle (analyze → revise → re-evaluate) repeated until the document scored
above 90/100. All eleven documents passed their initial evaluation
(92–95), and a full polish round was still run to fix every residual defect
the examiners had flagged — 83 issues in total, including factual errors and
internal contradictions — followed by a fresh re-evaluation of every document.

Scoring rubric (100 points)

Dimension Points What it measures
Coverage & Fidelity 25 Every section concept and Key Term has a dedicated example that accurately reflects the chapter’s definitions
Concreteness & Realism 20 Specific plausible products with real detail — UI copy, states, flows, metrics — not abstract restatements
Pedagogical Value 20 Bad-vs-good contrasts, explicit principle tie-backs, applicability to new situations
Modern Practice Alignment 15 2024–2026 contexts (AI, mobile, offline/queued sync, privacy, accessibility) where the chapter calls for them
Craft & Structure 10 Consistent per-example format, scannable headings, accurate coverage table
Internal Consistency 10 Honors the book’s priority hierarchy and vocabulary; no contradictions with the chapter

Anchors: 95+ exemplary, publishable as-is · 91–94 passes (exceeds 90) ·
85–90 strong with real gaps · 70–84 incomplete or generic · <70 inadequate.

Chapter 01 Worked Examples — Foundations of Human-Centered Design

This companion document gives one fully worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 1: the core concept of each numbered section (§1.1–§1.6), the callout material (design model / system image / user’s conceptual model, and the seven stages of action), and every entry in the chapter’s Key Terms box. Key terms already carried by a section concept share a single dedicated example, per the chapter’s own framing. Products vary deliberately across domains — fintech, health, government services, e-commerce, media, developer tools, and collaboration software — so no single scenario carries the chapter. Every example ends by tying back to the chapter principle, and all trade-off calls honor the book’s priority hierarchy: safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.

Coverage Table

Chapter source Concept Example
§1.1 Meaning over features (features as hypotheses about meaning) 1
§1.2 + Key Term Conceptual model 2
§1.2 callout Design model, system image, user’s conceptual model (three-way alignment) 3
§1.2 callout Seven stages of action 4

§1.1 Meaning Over Features

Example 1 — Meaning Over Features

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A feature is a capability; meaning is the reason that capability matters in someone’s life. Features are hypotheses about meaning — if a feature cannot be tied to a clearer model, safer action, or better recovery, it is decoration.

Scenario. Lumen, a mobile-first fintech app for freelancers, sees a spike in support tickets: “Did my invoice payment go through?” Average of 214 tickets/week; 41% of users who file one check the app more than five times in the following hour.

BAD (feature-first). The team hears “users want notifications” and ships a toast: “Payment sent! 🎉” that auto-dismisses after 3 seconds. Tickets drop only 9%. Users who were mid-distraction (on a train, between client calls) never see the toast; the underlying anxiety — is my money in flight, arrived, or lost? — is untouched. A second sprint doubles down by stacking more features onto the same unexamined hypothesis: a six-toggle notification-settings panel, an activity-feed widget, and a CSV export of payment events. Tickets drop only another 4%, and no one on the team can narrate the accreted toolkit as a single story of what a freelancer now understands — the chapter’s feature-stacking anti-pattern. The features “work”; the meaning fails.

GOOD (meaning-first). The team rewrites the product story in the language of outcomes: “A freelancer needs certainty that money reached the client’s bank, and proof they can show if it didn’t.” From that meaning they derive:

  • A persistent payment record with three named, durable states: Sent — leaves your account today, In transit — typically arrives in 1–2 business days, Deposited — confirmed by recipient's bank, Feb 12, 3:41 PM.
  • A “Share receipt” action producing a timestamped PDF — the proof.
  • If a payment stalls past 3 business days, the app says what to do next: “This is taking longer than usual. We’ve flagged it — no action needed yet. If it hasn’t arrived by Friday, tap here and we’ll trace it.”

Tickets fall 63% in six weeks; repeat status-checking sessions drop by half. Note what was not built: no confetti, no richer notification settings panel — those failed the “clearer model, safer action, or better recovery” test.

Why this works: The team treated “I can’t tell if this payment went through” as a request for certainty, not a request for a toast — exactly the chapter’s claim that people pursue meaning, and features are only hypotheses about it.

§1.2 Conceptual Models

Example 2 — Conceptual Model

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The user’s mental story of how a system works and what actions mean; a good one is coherent, limited, and teachable, and when the interface lies or stays silent, users invent folklore.

Scenario. Draftline, a 2025 AI writing assistant embedded in a docs tool, must answer the exact question the chapter poses: is the assistant editing my document or suggesting a draft?

BAD (silent model → folklore). V1 lets the AI rewrite paragraphs in place with a brief shimmer animation. Within a month, user interviews surface folklore: “I keep a copy in another tab because the AI sometimes eats my version,” “If you type while it’s thinking, it breaks,” and — verbatim from a session recording — “the AI is smarter if I ask nicely.” 28% of active users paste their text into a separate app before invoking the assistant. V1 also has the modal-state failure the chapter says makes modal editors fail: while a rewrite is pending, the editor is silently in a different mode — keystrokes replace the AI’s target selection instead of inserting at the cursor — and nothing on screen answers “what is selected? what will my next keystroke act on?” Users discover the mode only by losing a sentence to it. The system’s silence has taught a superstitious model.

GOOD (one coherent, teachable model). V2 commits to a single story the team can state in one sentence: “The AI never touches your words; it proposes, you dispose.” Everything in the UI reinforces it:

  • AI output appears in a right-hand panel labeled “Suggested draft — not applied”, never inline.
  • The only ways in are two explicit verbs: “Insert below” and “Replace selection” — and Replace immediately shows “Replaced 2 paragraphs · Undo” for 30 days via version history.
  • There is no hidden mode: the editor always behaves like an editor, even while a suggestion is pending. The target selection stays visibly highlighted with a labeled chip — “Replace will act on these 2 paragraphs” — so “what is selected?” always has an on-screen answer.
  • A first-run teaching moment, one screen, twelve words: “Draftline suggests. You decide. Your original text is always in History.”
  • Offline behavior states the model too: “You’re offline — your request is queued locally and will run when you reconnect.” (Queued locally, not lost — the distinction the chapter says mobile and AI surfaces must make explicit.)

The “backup copy in another tab” behavior drops to 4%; support questions about “lost text” fall from 130/month to 11.

Why this works: A coherent, limited, teachable story (“proposes, you dispose”) replaced silence, and once the model held, folklore had nothing left to explain — the designer made the system think like people, consistently enough that learning transfers.

Example 3 — Design Model, System Image, and the User’s Conceptual Model

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The design model is what designers intend; the system image is what the product actually communicates through behavior and UI; the user’s conceptual model is what people infer — and misalignment among the three, not merely “bad labels,” is a primary source of folklore.

Scenario. Nightreel, a streaming app, offers offline downloads for flights.

  • Design model (what the team intends): Downloads are licensed copies that expire 30 days after download or 48 hours after first play, whichever comes first, because of studio contracts.
  • System image (what the product communicates): A download icon, a checkmark when done, and… nothing else. No expiry shown anywhere.
  • User’s conceptual model (what people infer): “It’s on my phone now, like a file. I own it until I delete it.”

BAD (the system image stays silent). The collision detonates at the worst moment: mid-flight, airplane mode, a user taps a downloaded film and gets “Playback error (E-4012).” The license expired silently. App-store reviews fill with folklore: “downloads only work if you open them once at home first,” “re-download everything the night before you fly.” One-star reviews mentioning downloads: 340/month.

GOOD (repair the system image — the bridge). The team cannot change the contracts (design model) and should not expect users to intuit licensing law. So they change what the product communicates:

  • Each download shows a countdown chip: “Available offline for 23 more days.”
  • Starting playback surfaces the second rule once: “Heads up — once you press play, you have 48 hours to finish. Plenty for a flight.”
  • 72 hours before expiry, a queued local notification: “3 downloads expire this week. Renew them on Wi-Fi before you travel.” with a one-tap “Renew all.”
  • The old E-4012 dead end becomes: “This download’s license expired. Reconnect to renew it free — takes about a minute on Wi-Fi.”

Download-related one-star reviews fall from 340/month to roughly 60 — and then plateau there. Honest measurement matters here: the residual complaints target the 48-hour playback window itself, a contractual constraint that a truthful system image can soften but not remove. The team reports that residue upstream to the licensing negotiation instead of claiming design closed the gap. Renewal-before-flight does become the observed norm.

Why this works: The failure was never “bad labels” but a three-way misalignment; the interface is the bridge between design model and user model, and the fix made the system image finally tell the truth about the design model instead of leaving users to infer a false one.

Example 4 — Seven Stages of Action

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Norman frames interaction as goal → plan → specify → perform → perceive → interpret → compare — a cycle that maps closely to the gulfs of execution (first half) and evaluation (second half).

Scenario. Priya, 34, uses her state’s mobile portal, GovID, to renew her driver’s license before it expires Friday.

BAD (the 2023 portal). The home screen led with the agency-org-chart label “DMV e-Services Portal,” the vision step demanded “Attach form DL-62” with no plain-language gloss, and everything after payment was a blank page reading “Transaction complete.” Stages 5–7 of the cycle had no support at all: 31% of renewers phoned the call center within 48 hours to ask whether they were legal to drive.

GOOD (the redesign, walked through all seven stages). Walk Priya’s interaction through the cycle, noting where the design now supports each stage:

  1. Goal: “Have a valid license by Friday.” (Formed outside the app — designers must meet it, not assume users arrive knowing the system’s vocabulary.)
  2. Plan: She decides to renew online rather than visit an office. The home screen supports plan formation with a task-named tile — “Renew driver’s license” — not the agency-org-chart label “DMV e-Services Portal” it had in 2023.
  3. Specify: She must translate the plan into concrete actions. The flow shows a four-step map up front: “1. Confirm identity · 2. Vision certification · 3. Pay $42 · 4. Done” — she can specify her whole action sequence before performing any of it.
  4. Perform: She taps, types, and pays with Apple Pay. One stumble: the vision-certification step’s “Attach form DL-62” assumed she knew the form’s number; a redesign renamed it “Attach the eye-exam form your optometrist gave you (also called DL-62).”
  5. Perceive: After paying, the screen changes to a full-state confirmation — not a 3-second toast: “Renewal submitted — confirmation #R-88231.”
  6. Interpret: She must understand what that state means for her goal. The screen answers it directly: “Your current license stays valid while we process this. Your new card arrives by mail in 7–10 days.”
  7. Compare: Did the outcome match the goal (“valid by Friday”)? The interface closes the loop rather than leaving her to guess: “You’re covered for Friday — this receipt in your GovID wallet serves as proof of renewal if you’re asked.”

After the redesign, the confused-about-status calls fell from 31% of renewers to 6%.

Why this works: Each screen is doing named work for a specific stage of the action cycle — the first half shrinking the gulf of execution, the second half the gulf of evaluation — which is exactly why the chapter says the seven stages map onto the two gulfs.

§1.3 Gulfs of Execution and Evaluation

Example 5 — Gulf of Execution

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The gap between what the user intends and what actions the system makes available or discoverable — wide when the path is buried, dangerous when a destructive action looks identical to a safe one.

Scenario. CrateKitchen, a meal-kit e-commerce app. Intention: “skip next week’s box because I’m traveling.”

BAD (wide and dangerous). The path is buried five levels deep: Account → Billing → Manage plan → Delivery schedule → (long-press a week) → Skip. Nothing on the home screen hints that weeks are skippable. Worse, on the “Manage plan” screen, “Pause deliveries” and “Cancel subscription” are visually identical gray text buttons two rows apart — a destructive action indistinguishable from a safe one. Metrics tell the story: 22% of users who start looking for “skip” end up in the cancel flow; support logs 90 chats/week that begin “I didn’t mean to cancel.”

GOOD (match controls to intentions). The team lists the top user intentions from support transcripts — skip a week (58%), change delivery day (17%), swap meals (11%) — and puts controls where the intentions form:

  • The home screen’s next-delivery card gets a “Skip this week” button directly on it. One tap, then “Week of Mar 3 skipped. You won’t be charged. Unskip anytime.”
  • “Cancel subscription” moves to its own screen, styled distinctly, and is reworded to expose the safer near-neighbors first: “Need a break? You can skip up to 6 weeks or pause your plan — both keep your meal preferences.”
  • Hidden steps are removed: skipping no longer requires a reason survey (it was optional data dressed up as a required step).

Time-to-skip drops from a median 84 seconds to 6. Accidental cancellations fall 87%.

Why this works: The redesign shrinks the gulf of execution the way the chapter prescribes — matching controls to intentions, offering clear paths, reducing hidden steps — and removes the danger of a destructive action masquerading as a safe one.

Example 6 — Gulf of Evaluation

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The gap between the system’s state and the user’s ability to perceive and interpret it — in 2020s products with async jobs and generative outputs, people click the right thing and still don’t know what happened.

Scenario. ShipRail, a developer tool that deploys web services. Deploys are async jobs taking 2–9 minutes.

BAD (silent success + uninterpretable state). The developer runs a deploy from the dashboard. The button briefly shows a spinner with no progress, then returns to normal. Is the deploy running? Done? Failed? The only truth lives in a logs page three clicks away, rendered as a raw ANSI stream. Internal telemetry shows the classic evaluation-gulf signature: developers re-click “Deploy” an average of 1.8 times per deploy (spawning duplicate jobs), and 40% keep a terminal open running curl in a loop against production — probing nervously, exactly the behavior the chapter predicts when feedback is absent.

GOOD (make state visible, feedback timely, outcomes interpretable). The deploy becomes a persistent, named-state object:

  • A status card walks through explicit states: Queued (position 2) → Building — step 3/5, ~2 min left → Rolling out — 40% of traffic on v214 → Live — v214 serving all traffic since 14:32 UTC.
  • Failure states interpret themselves instead of demanding forensics: “Build failed at step 4 (tests). 2 tests failing — view the 11-line diff since the last green build.”
  • The AI-assisted layer earns trust the chapter’s way — interpretable, not just generated: “Suggested cause: missing env var STRIPE_KEY (added to code in this commit, absent in production config). Confidence: high — based on the error at line 212.” The suggestion cites its evidence rather than asserting.
  • The “Deploy” button disables during an active job and reads “Deploying v214…” — the control itself now reports state.

Duplicate deploys drop 92%; median time-to-diagnose a failed deploy falls from 19 minutes to 4.

Why this works: Every change attacks the evaluation side of the loop — visible state, timely feedback, interpretable outcomes (including a source-and-confidence cue on the AI reply) — closing the gap the chapter says now fails as often as execution does.

§1.4 Affordances, Signifiers, Feedback, and Knowledge in the World

Example 7 — Affordance

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A relationship between an object’s properties and an actor’s capabilities — a possibility for action, not a decoration.

Scenario. Thriftly, a secondhand-fashion marketplace, designs its mobile order-history rows.

Consider what the row-as-object actually affords, given a thumb on a 6.1-inch phone screen: a full-width list row affords tapping (large target, ~60 pt tall) and affords horizontal swiping (it’s a pannable surface under a touch-capable finger). A tiny 12-pt “…” glyph in the corner technically affords tapping too — but only barely, and only for users with fine motor precision; the relationship between object properties and this actor’s capabilities is what makes the affordance real. For a user with hand tremor, the 12-pt target affords almost nothing.

BAD (action possibilities that don’t exist where users expect them). V1 rows are inert images: tapping the product photo does nothing (only the tiny title text is linked), and swiping does nothing. Session recordings show users tapping photos 3–4 times, then rage-tapping. The photo looks like the object but affords nothing.

GOOD (design the possibility itself, then reveal it). V2 makes the entire row a single tap target opening the order; a left swipe on the row affords quick actions (“Track”, “Return”), with targets sized ≥44 pt so the possibility exists for the widest range of hands and abilities. A first-use teaching moment reveals the swipe once (that reveal is a signifier’s job — see Example 8; the affordance is the swipe-ability itself, which exists whether or not it’s communicated).

Tap-through on order rows rises from 31% to 79%; “how do I start a return” contacts drop by a third.

Why this works: The team designed relationships between object properties and actor capabilities — real, reachable possibilities for action — rather than treating interactivity as decoration, and kept the affordance/signifier distinction clean as the chapter requires.

Example 8 — Signifier

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A cue that communicates where and how action is available; many modern interfaces fail not because they lack affordances but because they lack signifiers.

Scenario. BenefitsNow, a state benefits portal used to manage food and childcare assistance — high stakes, many first-time and low-digital-literacy users, heavy mobile use.

BAD (mystery meat navigation). The 2024 dashboard is a row of five flat, unlabeled line icons: a leaf, a circle-with-arrows, a shield, a person, a bell. All are rendered in the same flat teal whether interactive or inert — the exact failure the chapter names. The circle-with-arrows (renew benefits — the single most important action, with a hard legal deadline) gets discovered by only 44% of users in usability testing; testers describe asking relatives which icon does what — tribal knowledge substituting for signifiers. 19% of households in the test cohort had missed a renewal deadline at least once.

GOOD (signify where and how to act). Same affordances, new cues:

  • Every icon gains a persistent text label: “Renew”, “My documents”, “Privacy”, “Profile”, “Alerts”.
  • Interactive elements are visibly distinct from inert ones: buttons get a filled shape and pressed states; static status text stays flat. Nothing that isn’t tappable looks tappable.
  • The renewal card adds a time-bound cue in words, not just color (color alone excludes colorblind users): “Renewal due in 12 days — takes about 10 minutes. Start now →” with a chevron signifying forward navigation.
  • On first visit, a one-time teaching moment shows that the document list is pull-to-refresh: “Pull down to check for new letters” — the pattern the chapter cites as a signifier teaching moment.

Renewal-action discovery in testing rises from 44% to 96%; on-time renewals improve 11 points quarter over quarter.

Why this works: The affordances were always there — the interface failed at communicating where action was available, and adding honest signifiers (labels, distinct interactive states, chevrons, teaching moments) fixed discoverability without adding a single capability.

Example 9 — Feedback

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Information that the system registered an action and how state changed — visual, auditory, haptic, or linguistic; absence of feedback is not minimalism, it is silence that forces people to probe nervously.

Scenario. DoseMate, a medication-tracking app for managing a parent’s blood-pressure regimen. The core action: logging “Mom took her 8 AM lisinopril.”

BAD (silent success). Tapping the pill row gives no visible change — the log is written to the database, the UI shows nothing. Caregivers double-log constantly (12% of entries are duplicates), and duplicates matter here: a double-logged dose can mask a missed dose in the adherence report the cardiologist reviews. Silence isn’t just annoying; in a health context it corrupts the record that clinical decisions lean on.

GOOD (multi-channel, state-changing feedback). One tap now produces layered confirmation matched to context:

  • Visual: the row transforms to a distinct logged state — checkmark, timestamp, changed background: “Lisinopril 10 mg — logged 8:04 AM”. Not a vanishing toast; a durable state change she can perceive even if she looks back a minute later.
  • Haptic: a single light tap confirms registration without requiring eyes on screen — useful when she’s simultaneously helping her mother.
  • Linguistic, for the queued-offline case: at the care facility with poor signal, the row shows “Logged — will sync when you’re back online” (queued locally, not lost), then flips to “Synced ✓ 9:12 AM”.
  • Feedback also carries recovery: the logged row offers “Undo” for 15 seconds, so confirmation and forgiveness travel together.

Duplicate log entries fall from 12% to 0.8%; the nervous pattern of opening the history screen right after logging drops by 70%.

Why this works: Every channel answers the two questions feedback exists to answer — was my action received, and how did state change? — replacing the silence that made a careful caregiver probe nervously and pollute a clinically meaningful record.

Example 10 — Knowledge in the World (vs. Knowledge in the Head)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Externalized structure — labels, defaults, visible constraints, progress, history — that reduces memory load, because most people cannot and should not have to carry complex shortcuts mentally.

Scenario. Relay, a team collaboration tool (channels, docs, tasks) used by a 40-person nonprofit whose staff includes seasonal volunteers.

BAD (expert-only knowledge in the head). Power actions live behind memorized shortcuts documented only in a help-center article: ⌘⇧M assigns a task, ⌘E archives a thread, and moving a doc requires remembering the exact channel name to type it, spelled precisely, from memory. Long-tenured staff fly; every seasonal volunteer cohort spends weeks asking “how do you…?” in a #help channel (median 26 such questions per new hire). The design assumes distraction-free experts; the reality is interrupted people on phones — precisely the conditions the chapter says to assume.

GOOD (put the structure in the world).

  • A command palette (⌘K — one thing to remember) exposes every action as searchable text: typing “assign” surfaces “Assign task to…” with the shortcut displayed alongside, so the world teaches the head over time instead of the reverse.
  • Moving a doc shows a browsable, recently-used-first channel picker — recognition over recall; no exact names to remember.
  • Inline validation moves rules out of docs and into the moment: naming a channel with a space triggers “Channel names use dashes, like grant-2026 — we’ve suggested one below” as-you-type, not as a post-submit error.
  • Sign-in switches to passkeys — “Sign in with your fingerprint — no password to remember” — moving the most fragile piece of knowledge-in-the-head out of memory entirely, the passwordless pattern the chapter cites.
  • Breadcrumbs (Programs / Grants / 2026 Renewal) and a visible version history (“Edited by Sam, 2:14 PM — view previous”) externalize “where am I?” and “what changed?”

New-volunteer #help questions drop from a median 26 to 7; task-assignment usage spreads from 9 power users to 31 of 40 staff.

Why this works: Each change relocates fragile knowledge from memory into visible structure — labels, defaults, constraints, history, recognition-based pickers — so the product works for distracted, interrupted, imperfect-recall humans rather than only for experts, which the chapter says is where designing for error starts.

§1.5 Design for Error

Example 11 — Slips, Mistakes, and Constraints (Blame the System, Not the Person)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Error is a predictable outcome of complex tools used under pressure, not a character flaw; slips (wrong action, right intention) and mistakes (wrong intention, coherent action) are design inputs, addressed with constraints that prevent illegal states, non-destructive defaults, and messages that explain what happened, why it matters, and what to do next.

Scenario. InfusaLink, a tablet app nurses use to program home-infusion pumps. Two distinct error types show up in incident reports:

  • A slip (wrong action, right intention): A nurse intends 10.0 mL/hr but, interrupted mid-entry by a patient call, types 100 — the classic decimal-entry slip under pressure.
  • A mistake (wrong intention, coherent action): A float nurse covering an unfamiliar patient coherently and carefully programs the morning protocol… for a patient who was switched to the evening protocol last week. Every action was correct for the wrong plan.

BAD (blame the person). V1 accepts any numeric input, then logs incidents as “user error — retraining scheduled.” Retraining does not change the conditions (interruption, unfamiliarity, time pressure) that produce the errors, so they recur: 14 dosing near-misses across the fleet in one quarter.

GOOD (treat both error types as design inputs).

  • Against the slip — constraints that prevent illegal states: the rate field enforces drug-specific hard limits from the formulary; entering 100 for this drug is simply not accepted: “100 mL/hr is above the maximum for this medication (12 mL/hr). Did you mean 10.0?” The illegal state cannot be reached, and the message says what happened, why it matters, and what to do next. A soft-range check (“11.5 mL/hr is within this medication’s limit but unusually high for this patient’s weight — confirm with the order”) catches values that are legal but improbable.
  • Against the mistake — fix the intention-forming context: the programming screen leads with the current order, pulled fresh: “Active protocol changed 6 days ago: EVENING schedule”, with the changed field highlighted. The mistake was coherent action on a stale model; the design puts the current model in front of the coherent actor.
  • Non-destructive defaults: starting a new program never overwrites the last one; the prior program remains one tap away under “Previous program (ended Mar 2)”.
  • Confirmation is reserved for the genuinely hard-to-recover step — starting the infusion — and it is informative rather than theatrical: it restates drug, dose, rate, and schedule in words a tired human can compare against the paper order.

Dosing near-misses drop from 14 to 2 per quarter; none in the following two quarters involve decimal-entry slips.

Why this works: The redesign treats the slip and the mistake as different design problems — constraints and limits for the slip, a corrected conceptual model at the point of intention for the mistake — and retires “user error” as an explanation, exactly the chapter’s blame-the-system stance.

Example 12 — Forgiveness (and the Confirmation-Theater Anti-Pattern)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Reversibility and recovery after error — undo, trash, version history — preferred over confirmation when recovery cost is low, with hard gates reserved for irreversible, high-stakes actions.

Scenario. ClientVault, a CRM for small agencies, handles two very different destructive actions: deleting a client record, and initiating a wire-transfer refund from escrow.

BAD (confirmation theater everywhere). V1 treats both actions — and archiving, and unsubscribing from a digest — identically: “Are you sure? OK / Cancel.” Users see the dialog ~30 times a week on trivial actions and, as the chapter predicts, learn to click OK without reading. Instrumentation shows median dialog-dwell time of 400 ms — nobody is reading. So when the dialog guards something real, it protects nothing: “I accidentally deleted the wrong client” tickets run 25/month, and each recovery requires a support-engineer database restore (median 2 business days). The illusion of safety has destroyed the attention safety needs.

GOOD (forgiveness where recovery is cheap; hard gates where it isn’t).

  • Delete client loses its dialog entirely. The action executes immediately with layered forgiveness: a snackbar — “Acme Design moved to Trash. Undo” — then a Trash that retains records for 30 days (“Restore” rebuilds the record, its notes, and its file links intact), backed by version history. Recovery cost is now near zero, so no gate is needed.
  • Wire a refund — irreversible, high-stakes, the chapter’s own “wiring money” case — gets a real gate, engineered to demand attention rather than a reflexive OK. It verifies both dimensions of the action: the recipient, by displaying the destination against the client record it must match (“Account name on file: Acme Design LLC · First Meridian Bank ···4417 — confirm this matches the refund request”), and the amount, by requiring it to be typed (“Type 4,250.00 to authorize”). Transfers over $1,000 add a 30-second hold with visible countdown, and the stakes are stated plainly: “Wire transfers cannot be recalled once sent.”
  • Low-stakes actions (archive, unsubscribe) get no dialog and no undo bar — just clear feedback — so the remaining gate stays rare and therefore meaningful.

“Deleted the wrong client” support tickets fall from 25/month to under 2 (all self-served via Trash); zero wire-recovery incidents are logged in the following year — the gate can verify amount and recipient-record match, though no confirmation can make a wrong underlying request impossible.

Why this works: Matching the mechanism to recovery cost — forgiveness for the cheap-to-recover, one attention-demanding hard gate for the irreversible — follows the chapter’s rule “prefer forgiveness over confirmation theater” and restores the scarce attention that real confirmations require.

§1.6 The Priority Hierarchy

Example 13 — The Priority Hierarchy as a Decision Policy

Definition (as this chapter uses it): When goals collide, decide in explicit order — safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight — this book’s local decision policy (practice scaffolding, not a claim that Norman ranked it so), with critical-path accessibility failures that block essential tasks counting as Safety (#1).

Scenario. CareLoop, a telehealth app, is redesigning its “join your video appointment” flow for a spring release. Six proposals compete for the same two-sprint budget. The team resolves the collision by walking the hierarchy top-down and recording the calls in a decision log:

  1. Safety. Audit finds the “Join visit” button fails screen-reader labeling — it announces only “button” — so blind patients cannot join appointments at all. This is a critical-path accessibility failure blocking an essential action, so per the chapter it is Safety, not merely polish. Also at this layer: the “End visit for all” control sits one ambiguous tap from “Mute,” risking irreversible harm mid-consultation (a dropped clinical call). Both are fixed first, before anything below is even estimated. Fix: labeled controls (“Join your 2:30 PM visit with Dr. Osei”), and End-visit moved behind a distinct, described control.
  2. Model and recovery. Patients don’t understand pre-call state (“is it waiting for me or the doctor?”). The team ships named states — “Waiting room — Dr. Osei has been notified” vs. “Reconnecting — you’re still in your visit” — and makes call drops recoverable: rejoining within 10 minutes returns the patient to the same visit with the message “Welcome back — Dr. Osei is still here.”
  3. Inclusion. Real-time captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing patients; Spanish and Vietnamese localization (34% of the patient population); a low-bandwidth audio-only fallback that triggers automatically below ~250 kbps with the notice “Video paused to protect audio quality.” Devices tested down to a 2019 Android on 3G.
  4. Outcomes. With the layers above solid, the team streamlines the happy path: appointment reminders deep-link straight into the waiting room, cutting median time-from-notification-to-joined from 3 m 40 s to 55 s, and post-visit summaries arrive in the app within an hour.
  5. Systems. The flow adopts platform-native call UI conventions (CallKit/ConnectionService) so incoming visits behave like calls the OS understands, and the team holds a performance budget: waiting room interactive in under 2 s on the test floor device.
  6. Delight. Last and only now: a calming waiting-room animation and a gentle chime when the clinician joins. One proposed flourish — an AI-generated “your visit at a glance” splash card shown while connecting — is cut because it would delay feedback about connection state: the chapter’s line that delight must never obscure status.

The log’s ordering survives a real fight: marketing wanted the animated waiting room shipped first “for the app-store screenshots.” The hierarchy gave the team a shared, non-personal way to say no — delight without safety is marketing.

Why this works: Every trade-off was resolved by explicit precedence rather than taste or politics — safety and recovery before efficiency, inclusion before polish, delight strictly last — which is precisely the decision policy §1.6 exists to provide.

How to Use These Examples

For each concept, try the transfer test the chapter’s Practice Exercises encourage: take the BAD half of any example, find its analogue in a product you use this week, and write the GOOD half yourself — naming the states, drafting the actual UI copy, and checking your fix against the hierarchy (does it touch safety? model/recovery? inclusion?) before you polish anything.

Chapter 02 Worked Examples — Interaction Design: Behavior, Flows, and Feedback

This companion document gives one worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 2: the core concept(s) of each numbered section plus every entry in the Key Terms list (merged where a key term and a section concept coincide). Each example follows the same structure — a one-line definition anchored to the chapter’s usage, a concrete scenario from a plausible 2024–2026 product with real UI copy, named states, flows, and numbers, a BAD vs GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Every example honors the book’s priority ladder: safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.
