Key-term merges: Mismatch = Example 1; Persona Spectrum = Example 3; POUR and WCAG 2.2 = Example 4 (WCAG 2.2 is anchored there by two criteria new in 2.2 — SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) and SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — beyond the POUR framing, with SC 3.3.8 in Example 5); SC 3.3.8 = Example 5; COGA = Example 6; ECCD = Example 7; kyōyōhin = Example 10; ADA = Example 17; EAA = Example 18; AT testing ladder = Example 19. Separately, AA vs AAA — a §3.8 sub-concept, not a Key Term — is covered in Example 16.

§3.1 Disability as Mismatch

Example 1 — Mismatch

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Disability is not a medical property of a body but a mismatch between what a person can do and what a product demands — exclusion is designed in, and therefore can be designed out.

Scenario. Lumen, a 2025 mobile-first neobank, requires mobile check deposit via a live camera flow: hold the phone steady over the check for 4 seconds while the screen shows “Hold still… aligning edges.” Support data shows 31% of deposit attempts fail on the first try; failures cluster among three groups the team initially filed as “user error”: a customer with essential tremor, a customer photographing checks one-handed while using a rollator, and — the largest group by volume — parents holding infants. Same demand (“two steady hands for 4 seconds”), three different human stories, one shared mismatch.

BAD. The team’s first fix: an error toast — “Deposit failed. Please hold your device steady and try again.” — plus a help article titled “Tips for a successful deposit.” This treats the limitation as the user’s problem and optimizes for exceptions and charity.

GOOD. The team redesigns the environment, not the user: (1) auto-capture fires the instant edges align, needing ~0.3 seconds of stability instead of 4; (2) a “Place phone on table” mode uses the rear camera with a countdown and haptic confirmation; (3) a fallback “Deposit at a partner ATM” path stays one tap away. First-attempt success rises from 69% to 94% — for everyone, not only the three groups that surfaced the mismatch.

Why this works. Relocating the problem from “the user’s limitation” to “the product’s demand” is exactly the definitional shift §3.1 makes: the team redesigned the system, and the shared constraint became the design brief.

§3.2 Recognize → Learn → Solve

Example 2 — Recognize → Learn → Solve: One Extends to Many

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Holmes’s deliberate cycle — recognize where people are excluded, learn from people at the extremes of the Persona Spectrum, solve for that person first, then ask who else benefits.

Scenario. Threadline, a team-collaboration app, shipped async voice notes in 2024. By Q1 2025 the feature shows a defined adoption gap: in enterprise accounts where at least one member has platform-wide captions enabled, 23% of members send or open a voice note in a given week, versus 31% across all accounts — an 8-percentage-point gap that flags where exclusion is concentrating.

  • Recognize. The team mines signals rather than assumptions: 214 support tickets tagged “can’t use voice notes,” an analytics funnel showing users in one enterprise account (a design agency with three deaf employees) open voice notes and abandon within 2 seconds, and a public post from a deaf PM: “My team switched to voice notes. I now find out about decisions two days late.”
  • Learn. The team runs paid sessions with five deaf and hard-of-hearing users — extremes of the hearing spectrum, not averaged away into a “typical user” persona. One participant demonstrates her actual workaround: forwarding voice notes to a paid third-party transcription bot with a 4-hour turnaround.
  • Solve. They ship on-device transcription with an editable transcript pane, defaulting on: “Transcript · auto-generated · Edit.” They solve for the deaf PM first — then ask who else benefits. Sixty days post-launch: transcripts are opened by 41% of all voice-note recipients — non-native English speakers, people in open-plan offices, and anyone searching old messages (voice-note content is now indexed, lifting search success 12%).

Caution the chapter insists on. The transcript work cost a quarter and required saying no to a stakeholder’s animated-reactions request. The multiplier was a frequent outcome of genuine “solve for one” work — not a guaranteed convergence of ethics and revenue, and the team would have owed the fix even without the 41% number.

Why this works. It runs the full Recognize → Learn → Solve cycle on real exclusion signals and treats “one extends to many” as an observed result of solving for the extreme, not a marketing promise.

§3.3 Persona Spectrum

Example 3 — Persona Spectrum: Permanent, Temporary, Situational

Definition (as this chapter uses it): For each capability, consider permanent, temporary, and situational limitations as equal design constraints — a constraint generator, not a substitute for people.

Scenario. Kanbanly, a project-management tool, plans a 2025 mobile release. The flagship interaction is precise drag-and-drop of cards between columns, with a 24×24px drag handle. Instead of a persona named “Busy Product Manager Priya who loves productivity” (which forces no hard choices), the team builds a spectrum table for the move a card task:

Capability Permanent Temporary Situational
Mobility/dexterity Cerebral palsy; tremor Wrist fracture in a cast (6 weeks) Standing on a moving bus, one free hand
Vision Low vision (20/200) Post-cataract-surgery blur Bright sunlight on a matte phone screen
Attention/cognition ADHD Concussion recovery Interrupted every 90 seconds in a stand-up

The table exposes that precise drag-and-drop mismatches all three columns of the mobility row at once — exactly the failure mode the chapter names.

BAD. Ship drag-and-drop as the only mechanism and log the complaints as edge cases.

GOOD. Add a “Move to…” action on every card (long-press or the M key) opening a column picker with 48×48px targets; make the whole card the drag surface, not a 24px handle; support full keyboard operation (arrow keys + Enter). Post-launch, 27% of all card moves on mobile use “Move to…” — the situational column was, as the chapter predicts, never niche.

Why this works. The spectrum table generated a real constraint (“this task must not require sustained pointer precision”) instead of a fictional average user, and the redesign served permanent, temporary, and situational users simultaneously — spectrum-aware product quality, not accessibility afterthought.

§3.4 WCAG 2.2 POUR as Product Language

Example 4 — POUR (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) as Critique Vocabulary

Definition (as this chapter uses it): WCAG 2.2 organizes success criteria under POUR — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — and inclusive teams use POUR as a product vocabulary in critiques, not only an auditor’s checklist.

Scenario. A state government’s 2025 benefits-renewal portal redesign goes to design critique. The proposal: a motion-heavy stepper where each of six steps slides in with a parallax animation, progress shown only by a green-filling ring, and a custom <div>-based date picker. The design lead runs the critique with the chapter’s four questions instead of a compliance spreadsheet:

  • Perceivable? The progress ring conveys state by color fill alone; a user with low vision or a monochrome e-ink display cannot tell step 3 from step 5. Fix: add “Step 3 of 6 — Household income” as visible text and an aria-live region announcing step changes.
  • Operable? The date picker cannot be reached by keyboard; the session times out at 10 minutes with no warning — renewers pausing to find a Social Security card lose everything. Fix: native <input type="date"> fallback, plus “Your session expires in 5 minutes. Extend time” (enough time is an Operable requirement, not a courtesy). Two criteria new in WCAG 2.2 surface in the same review: the stepper’s “Back” chevron is a 16×16px target, below the 24×24 CSS-pixel floor of SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — enlarged to 44×44; and the sticky “Chat with us” bar covers each field as keyboard focus reaches the bottom of the form, failing SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — the layout now reserves space so the focused control is never hidden.
  • Understandable? “Recertification adjudication window” appears in step 1. Fix: “When we’ll review your renewal (usually 10 business days).” Behavior is made predictable: the “Continue” button is in the same position on every step.
  • Robust? The <div> date picker exposes no name/role/value to assistive technologies; NVDA announces it as “blank.” Fix: semantic HTML first, ARIA only where semantics fall short.

Result: the critique produced 11 concrete WCAG 2.2 fixes before engineering handoff. The previous release had skipped this step: an external audit logged 43 violations post-launch, and the agency’s own remediation post-mortem estimated that fixing them after launch — rework, re-audit, and emergency releases — cost roughly six times what catching them in critique would have. That 6× figure is the agency’s internal estimate, not a universal constant, but it matches the familiar pattern that defects get more expensive the later they are found.

Why this works. POUR functioned as a shared product language during design — the conformance shipping bar applied as craft in the room, exactly as §3.4 prescribes — rather than an auditor’s checklist applied after the exclusion was already built.

Example 5 — SC 3.3.8: Accessible Authentication

Definition (as this chapter uses it): WCAG 2.2’s SC 3.3.8 limits cognitive function tests (puzzles, memorizing/transcribing, object recognition) as authentication barriers unless an alternative exists.

Scenario. CareBridge, a telehealth app, sees 22% of users over 65 abandon login before reaching their appointment — a safety-relevant failure, since missed logins mean missed consultations.

BAD (the 2024 flow). (1) Password field with paste disabled “for security,” breaking password managers; (2) a distorted-text CAPTCHA (“Type the characters you see”) — an object-recognition and transcription test; (3) a security question (“What was your first pet’s name?”) — a memory test. Three stacked cognitive function tests with no alternative: a direct SC 3.3.8 failure, and a mismatch for users with dementia, brain injury, dyslexia — and anyone logging in from a hospital bed.

GOOD (the 2025 flow). (1) Passkey as the primary path: “Sign in with Face ID or your device PIN”; (2) fallback email magic link: “We’ll email you a sign-in link — no password needed”; (3) where passwords remain, paste is enabled and password managers can autofill; (4) bot defense moves to invisible risk-based signals server-side instead of user-facing puzzles, with an “I can’t complete this — verify me another way” escape hatch if a challenge ever appears. Login abandonment for the 65+ cohort drops from 22% to 7%, and support calls titled “locked out before my appointment” fall 60%.

Why this works. Passkeys, paste-friendly fields, and non-puzzle verification are accessibility features that also reduce login abandonment — the chapter’s point that SC 3.3.8 remedies are product wins, not “nice-to-haves.”

§3.5 COGA Patterns as Ship Craft

Example 6 — COGA: Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Guidance

Definition (as this chapter uses it): COGA is W3C guidance (Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities) that operationalizes cognitive inclusion alongside POUR — complementary craft, not a set of WCAG success criteria and not a substitute for WCAG conformance claims.

Scenario. Voltly, an energy utility’s app, redesigns its “switch to a time-of-use tariff” flow in 2025. The old flow passed an automated WCAG scan (contrast: all green) yet had a 64% drop-off — the chapter’s exact warning that a page can pass contrast ratios and still fail cognitive usability.

BAD. One 14-field page titled “Tariff Migration Portal”; a row of ten unlabeled icons for plan features; jargon (“Your TOU delta will be reconciled at the next billing epoch”); a 5-minute hard timeout; a mistake in the meter-number field wipes the whole form.

GOOD — each fix named to a COGA pattern:
- Clear purpose on each page; no surprise navigation: new title “Switch your electricity plan — takes about 4 minutes,” and the flow never redirects unexpectedly.
- Chunked tasks with save-and-resume: three steps (“Your usage,” “Compare plans,” “Confirm switch”) with “Save and finish later — we’ll email you a link.”
- Plain language; define jargon: “Time-of-use plan: electricity costs less at night (11pm–7am) and more at dinner time (5–9pm),” with an inline “What’s a kWh?” expander.
- Consistent layout; reduced working-memory load: the plan you’re comparing stays pinned at the top of every step so nothing must be memorized across screens.
- Help in context; undo and error recovery that does not punish: a meter-number typo produces “That meter number doesn’t match this address — check the 10-digit number on your meter or bill” next to the field, with everything else preserved; after switching, “You can undo this switch within 14 days” appears on the confirmation.
- Control over timeouts and minimal distractions: the timeout is removed for the flow; no upsell interstitials interrupt it.

Completion rises to 71%, and calls to the support line about the switch drop 44%.

Why this works. COGA is where “Understandable” stops being abstract: the team reviewed the flow for cognitive cost the way they review for visual polish, shipping cognitive-inclusion craft alongside — not instead of — WCAG conformance, and honoring model/recovery (undo, non-punishing errors) right after safety.

§3.6 ECCD

Example 7 — Equity-Centered Community Design: Co-Decision, Not Token Consultation

Definition (as this chapter uses it): ECCD insists that communities most affected by exclusion participate in decision-making — shared framing, compensation and credit, power to change scope, and post-launch feedback loops — not interviews that validate a frozen roadmap.

Scenario. A metro transit agency builds a 2025 trip-planning app with real-time elevator-outage data.

BAD (extractive research). The agency runs six one-hour interviews with wheelchair users, pays nothing (“participation is its own reward”), drops three quotes into a slide deck (“Riders want reliability!”), and ships the roadmap exactly as frozen the previous quarter — elevator status buried three taps deep because the growth team wanted the home screen for a fare-promotion banner. The chapter names this pattern precisely: learning from disabled people, then optimizing for stakeholders who never feel the mismatch.

GOOD (ECCD in practice).
- Shared problem framing and success criteria: a working group of eight riders (wheelchair users, blind riders, a rider with an intellectual disability) co-writes the definition of done: “A rider using a wheelchair can determine, before leaving home, whether every station on their route has a working elevator — in under 30 seconds.”
- Compensation and credit: members are paid $95/session and credited by name in the app’s About screen and the launch post.
- Power to change scope: the group reviews the beta and votes to cut the animated route “fly-through” and reallocate that engineering time to push alerts — “Elevator at Jackson St is out. Accessible reroute adds 12 min. See reroute.” The cut sticks, over the marketing team’s objection.
- Feedback loops after launch: a quarterly review where the group triages accessibility issues with the product team; elevator-data accuracy becomes a tracked SLO (target: outage reflected in-app within 5 minutes), because accessibility is maintained, not “shipped once.”

Why this works. The community held decision power — scope, success criteria, and post-launch priorities were co-owned — which is the chapter’s line between ECCD and consult-and-discard research.

§3.7 Contexts Beyond the Desktop Ideal

Example 8 — Offline and Unreliable Networks

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Progressive enhancement, local drafts, clear sync states, and non-blocking queues matter for rural users, travelers, and crisis contexts — an “always online” assumption is a socioeconomic and geographic exclusion.

Scenario. FieldNote, a 2025 app for community health workers logging home visits in rural areas where connectivity drops for hours.

BAD. Tapping “Submit visit record” on a dead connection shows an infinite spinner, then “Error: network unavailable,” and the 20-minute intake form is gone. Workers respond rationally: they stop using the app and revert to paper, and the program’s data pipeline collapses.

GOOD. Every record saves locally first. The UI names its states explicitly: “Saved on this device” → “Queued — will sync when you’re back online (3 records waiting)” → “Synced ✓ 14:32.” Sync is a non-blocking background queue — workers continue to the next visit while records wait. Conflicts surface gently on reconnect: “This record was also edited on the clinic tablet. Compare versions.” Photos queue at reduced resolution with “Full quality will upload on Wi-Fi.” After the redesign, records lost per month drop from ~120 to 0, and average records per worker per day rise from 4.1 to 6.3.

Why this works. The design treats connectivity as a spectrum rather than an assumption — local drafts, named sync states, and a non-blocking queue — so geography and income no longer determine who gets to complete the core task, and recovery (nothing is ever lost) is designed in ahead of any polish.

Example 9 — Shared Devices

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Family tablets, library computers, and workplace kiosks require careful session design, privacy for sensitive content, easy sign-out, and avoidance of “remember me forever” defaults that expose personal data.

Scenario. WorkLink, a state employment-services site, learns from a 2024 survey that 38% of its job-seeking users apply from library computers or a family member’s phone.

BAD. “Keep me signed in” is checked by default; the dashboard greets the next library patron with the previous user’s full name, home address, and unemployment-claim status; uploaded résumés persist in the browser’s download history; session cookies last 30 days.

GOOD. On shared-context sign-in the site asks: “Is this a public or shared computer? We’ll sign you out automatically and won’t save your info.” Choosing “Shared” sets a 10-minute idle timeout with a visible warning (“Signing out in 2 minutes — I’m still here”), disables persistent login, masks the claim amount behind a “Show” toggle, and the prominent “Sign out” button confirms: “You’re signed out. It’s safe to leave this computer.” Sensitive documents preview in-page instead of forcing downloads onto a public machine.

The honest measurement. This fix did not pay for itself on any dashboard: 30-day active users fell about 5% (persistent logins had been inflating the count with phantom sessions), and sign-in friction complaints ticked up in the first month. The team shipped anyway and wrote the rationale into the decision log: exposing a stranger’s name, address, and unemployment-claim status on a library computer is a harm, full stop. As §3.2 warns, ethics and revenue do not automatically converge — this was the right fix even though no growth metric rewarded it.

Why this works. The session model matches how people actually access the service — a private-personal-device assumption is exactly the anti-pattern the chapter lists — and it puts the safety of exposed personal data ahead of the engagement metrics a “remember me forever” default would juice.

Example 10 — Kyōyōhin (共用品)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Japanese inclusive practice emphasizing products good for everyone in ordinary use — not segregated “special” goods; the ramp that is also a stroller path.

Scenario. Simmer, a 2025 recipe app, must decide how to serve blind cooks and cooks with motor disabilities.

BAD (the segregated “special mode”). An “Accessibility Cooking Mode” buried in Settings, with its own stripped-down screens, maintained by one engineer, three releases behind the main app. New features (AI ingredient substitutions) never reach it. This is the chapter’s anti-pattern of a special mode that diverges forever from the main product.

GOOD (kyōyōhin thinking). One default experience, good for everyone with messy hands: full voice navigation — “Say ‘next step’ or ‘read that again’” — designed with blind users and equally valuable to any cook whose hands are covered in dough; step timers announced aloud and shown as large text; a “keep screen on while cooking” default. There is no separate mode to fall behind, and telemetry shows 22% of all active cooks use voice commands at least once per session — far beyond the population the feature was designed with.

Why this works. The voice interaction is a ramp-that-is-also-a-stroller-path: one shared design serves disabled users and the hands-busy majority in ordinary use, so inclusion is the main product rather than a segregated special good.

Example 11 — Literacy

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Forms, errors, and legal copy must be readable — icons alone are not universal; support scanning, examples, and multilingual plain language.

Scenario. Prosper Micro, a microloan app serving small-scale vendors, sees 47% of applicants abandon at the terms-acceptance screen.

BAD. A 1,900-word terms block at grade-16 reading level (“The obligor shall remit installments notwithstanding force majeure…”), a bare warning-triangle icon with no text when a field fails, and a form asking for “Annualized gross revenue” with no example.

GOOD. Terms open with a scannable plain-language summary in the reader’s choice of three languages: “What you’re agreeing to: You borrow $500. You pay back $530 over 10 weeks — $53 each week, starting June 2. If you pay late, we add $5 per late week. No other fees.” The full legal text remains one tap below (“Read the complete agreement”). Field labels carry worked examples: “How much do you sell in a typical week? For example: $250.” Errors pair icon with words: “⚠ We need your ID number to check this — it’s the 9 digits on the front of your card.” An optional “Read this aloud” button speaks each section. Abandonment at the terms screen falls from 47% to 19%, and — the metric the team watches hardest — first-payment surprise complaints (“I didn’t know about the late fee”) fall 71%.

Why this works. Readable terms, examples, and multimodal access treat literacy variation as a design constraint rather than assuming high literacy — and in a lending product, comprehension is a user-safety issue before it is a conversion issue.

Example 12 — Internationalization Beyond RTL

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Locale is more than flipping layout for Arabic or Hebrew — handle locale-aware dates, currencies, address formats, name order and length, pluralization, sorting, and culturally meaningful imagery.

Scenario. Cartlane, an e-commerce platform, expands from the US to Japan, Brazil, and Egypt in 2025 and declares i18n “done” after translating strings and adding RTL layout for Egypt — the chapter’s anti-pattern of treating i18n as string translation only.

BAD (what broke in the first month). Checkout requires “First name” and “Last name,” mangling Japanese family-name-first order and rejecting single-name Brazilian customers (“Last name is required”); the address form demands a “State” and a 5-digit ZIP, making Japanese addresses (postal code 100-0001, prefecture, no state) unenterable; “Delivery on 04/05” reads as April 5 in São Paulo and May 4 in support’s US office, generating 300+ where-is-my-order tickets; the cart shows “1 items” in Portuguese because plural rules were hardcoded; prices render as “¥1,980.00” (yen has no decimal subunits).

GOOD. One “Full name” field (optional structured fields per locale, family name first where customary); address forms driven by locale metadata — postal-code format, region label, and field order per country; dates rendered unambiguously per locale (“5 de abril” / “4月5日”) and stored as ISO 8601; ICU pluralization (“1 item” / “2 itens”, including languages with more than two plural forms); currency formatting from locale data (¥1,980); imagery reviewed per market by local staff. Checkout completion in Japan rises 23% within a quarter of the address-form fix alone.

Why this works. Each fix removes a mismatch between the product’s embedded Western assumptions and how real locales express names, places, time, and money — internationalization as inclusion, not translation.

Example 13 — Motion/Vestibular Safety vs. Photosensitive Seizure Risk

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Two distinct harms — large motion (parallax, autoplaying zooms, infinite carousels) can trigger vestibular symptoms like nausea and dizziness, while flashing/strobing content can trigger photosensitive seizures; design for both, with pause and non-motion alternatives.

Scenario. Pulsewave, a music-streaming app, plans a 2025 “Year in Sound” recap: full-screen parallax zooms between stat cards, an auto-advancing carousel, and a finale where album art strobes to the beat at ~8 flashes per second.

BAD. Motion is mandatory brand expression: no pause control, prefers-reduced-motion ignored, strobe finale shipped as-is. The 8-flash-per-second sequence sits squarely in the seizure-risk band WCAG’s guidance exists to prevent — a physical-safety defect, not an aesthetic choice — and the parallax zooms leave vestibular-sensitive users dizzy and nauseated three cards in.

GOOD. The team separates the two risks and handles each, safety first:
- Photosensitive seizure risk: the strobe finale is redesigned outright — album art now cross-fades between covers at a rate capped at one transition per second regardless of tempo (a 180+ BPM track would otherwise push per-beat changes toward the 3 Hz danger band), keeping the sequence well below WCAG’s three-flashes-per-second general threshold; the soft cross-fade also avoids the abrupt luminance shifts that register as flashes in the first place. No user setting required; unsafe content is not shipped behind a toggle.
- Vestibular safety: the app respects prefers-reduced-motion from the OS — parallax zooms become simple cross-fades, the carousel stops auto-advancing. An in-app control mirrors it: “Reduce motion in this recap.” Every screen has visible “Pause” and “Next” buttons, and a “View as a list” non-motion alternative presents the same stats as static cards.

Recap completion among users with reduced-motion enabled matches the general population (81% vs 83%) — the brand moment survived, minus the harm.

Why this works. The design distinguishes vestibular triggers from photosensitive seizure triggers and mitigates both, honoring the priority hierarchy: seizure safety is non-negotiable and fixed at the source, motion comfort is respected via prefers-reduced-motion and pause controls, and delight (the recap’s flair) is preserved only after both.

Example 14 — Media Captions and Transcripts

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Captions serve deaf and hard-of-hearing users and anyone who cannot play sound; include speaker identification and non-speech information when meaningful; audio descriptions matter for visual-only content.

Scenario. LectureLoop, a university’s video-learning platform, audits its recorded-lecture experience in 2025.

BAD. Auto-captions only, unreviewed: “the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell” renders as “the might of Andrea is the power house of the sell”; no speaker labels in a two-professor debate, so a deaf student cannot tell who is arguing which side; a chemistry demo where the flask changes color is captioned only “[music]”; no transcript, so nothing is searchable.

GOOD. Captions are human-reviewed for STEM vocabulary (error rate cut from ~11% of words to under 2%); speaker identification is explicit — “PROF. OKAFOR: The evidence says otherwise.” — and meaningful non-speech information is captioned: “[flask turns from clear to deep blue]” plus “[class laughs]” where it carries social meaning. Visual-only moments get audio description: “The instructor points to the second term in the equation.” A full interactive transcript sits beside the player; clicking any sentence jumps the video there. Usage data mirrors the chapter’s point that captions are never only for deaf users: 63% of caption users in a semester survey are hearing students — watching on muted phones in shared dorm rooms, on buses, or replaying dense passages as text. Median time-to-find-a-concept in a 50-minute lecture drops from 7 minutes of scrubbing to 40 seconds of transcript search.

Why this works. Speaker IDs, non-speech information, audio description, and searchable transcripts serve the users the feature exists for and everyone who cannot or prefers not to play sound — captions as core media infrastructure, not an add-on.

Example 15 — Socioeconomic and Metered Data

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Compress media, avoid autoplay video, offer low-data modes, and do not force app downloads when a light web flow would suffice — data cost is an accessibility and equity issue.

Scenario. The Daily Ledger, a news publisher, finds that readers on prepaid mobile plans in several markets bounce at 3× the rate of readers on unlimited plans.

BAD. The homepage weighs 9.4 MB: autoplay video hero, uncompressed images, four ad trackers. On a $10/GB prepaid plan, one homepage visit costs about nine cents — a real tax on reading the news — and any article link redirects to “Get the full experience — download our app (48 MB).”

GOOD. (1) A “Data Saver” mode, offered proactively on metered connections — “You’re on mobile data. Switch to Data Saver? Pages will load faster and use about 90% less data.” — serving text-first pages at ~380 KB with images as tap-to-load placeholders labeled with their size (“Photo · 210 KB · tap to load”); (2) autoplay video removed globally, replaced by a poster frame with a play button and a duration + size label (“2:14 · about 18 MB”); (3) the full reading experience works on the mobile web — the app is an option, never a gate; (4) images move to AVIF at ~60% smaller than the old JPEGs for everyone. Bounce rate on prepaid-heavy networks drops 34%, and pages-per-visit in Data Saver mode exceeds the site average.

Why this works. Treating megabytes as money makes data cost a first-class design constraint, removing a socioeconomic exclusion the “always online, unlimited data” desktop ideal renders invisible.

§3.8 Color, Contrast, and Process

Example 16 — Color Accessibility as a Process (and AA vs AAA)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Color accessibility is a process, not a palette — redundant cues, early contrast checks, grayscale and color-vision-simulation testing, documented tokens, and rechecks after brand refreshes; Level AA is the usual product and legal baseline, AAA adopted selectively where it clearly reduces harm.

Scenario. DeployDeck, a developer-tools dashboard, undergoes a 2025 brand refresh introducing a lime-to-teal gradient and a lighter gray text ramp.

BAD. Marketing hands off the new palette at the end of the quarter; build status is a colored dot only (green = passing, red = failing — indistinguishable for the roughly 8% of males with red-green color vision deficiency (deuteranomaly alone accounts for about 5%)); the new gray-400 body text on white measures 2.9:1, failing the AA threshold of 4.5:1 for normal text; engineers, lacking documented tokens, hand-pick “close enough” hex values and invent inaccessible variants; nobody rechecks until a customer files a ticket titled “Can’t tell if my deploy failed.”

GOOD — the five-step process from the chapter, applied:
1. Redundant cues, never color alone: status becomes color + icon + text — “✓ Passing,” “✕ Failed,” “● Running” — legible even in grayscale.
2. Check contrast early, not at handoff: the design tool’s contrast lint runs on every frame; the proposed gray-400 body text fails immediately and is corrected to a 4.6:1 gray before any engineering time is spent. Meaningful non-text UI (input borders, focus rings, status icons) is checked against the 3:1 non-text threshold.
3. Grayscale and color-vision simulations: the dashboard is reviewed in grayscale plus deuteranopia and protanopia simulations as a standing design-review step.
4. Document tokens: the design system publishes --text-primary, --status-danger-fg, etc., each annotated “AA on --surface-default,” so engineers compose from verified pairs instead of inventing variants — a systems fix that prevents the whole class of regression.
5. Recheck after brand refreshes: the lime gradient behind white headline text measured 1.8:1 and was darkened at the gradient’s text zones; the check is now a release-gate item for every brand update.

Contrast is necessary but not sufficient. The same audit closes the rest of §3.8’s picture: every interactive control gets a visible focus state (the focus ring itself verified at 3:1 against adjacent colors); the log-filter chips are enlarged from 20×20px to a 24×24px minimum hit target (44×44 for primary actions); and the dashboard is verified at 200% text resizing without loss of content — at 200%, the deploy table reflows to stacked cards instead of clipping the status column off-screen.

AA vs AAA in practice. The team sets AA as the bar on the critical path (deploy status, logs, auth) and adopts AAA selectively where it clearly reduces harm: 7:1 contrast for the incident-alert banner people read at 3 a.m., without chasing AAA across the entire marketing site where it would break the brand for little user benefit.

Why this works. Every step treats color accessibility as an ongoing process embedded in tools, tokens, and release gates — not a one-time palette choice — and the AA/AAA split follows the chapter’s guidance to aim for AA on the critical path and adopt AAA where it clearly reduces harm.

§3.9 Legal Baselines

Example 17 — ADA as a Risk Floor, Not a Quality Bar

Definition (as this chapter uses it): In the US, treat ADA digital accessibility as a risk floor — case law and settlements often push toward WCAG-referenced remediation, but doctrine for websites and apps remains unsettled; “ADA = WCAG AA everywhere” is not settled statute.

Scenario. Hearthware, a US home-goods e-commerce retailer, receives a demand letter in 2025 alleging its checkout is unusable with a screen reader.

BAD (fear-based compliance). Legal hires a vendor to “make us ADA compliant”; the vendor installs a one-line JavaScript accessibility overlay and issues a certificate. The team declares victory. Six months later a second demand letter arrives — overlays are themselves a frequent subject of complaints — and blind customers still cannot complete checkout, because lawsuit avoidance did not produce a usable experience for AT users. The brittle checklist satisfied nobody: not the law, not the users.

GOOD (floor + quality bar). Counsel advises accurately: “Courts and DOJ settlements commonly reference WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA as the remediation target, but don’t treat ‘ADA = WCAG AA everywhere’ as settled statute — treat it as our risk floor.” The product org then sets the quality bar above the floor: WCAG 2.2 AA on the purchase path within two quarters, verified by the AT testing ladder (Example 19) including paid sessions with blind shoppers; accessibility acceptance criteria added to the definition of done so the floor is maintained, not re-litigated; the overlay removed in favor of semantic fixes to the actual checkout code. The settlement closes, and screen-reader checkout completion — previously 0% — reaches parity within 8% of the sighted baseline.

Why this works. The team used law as the minimum bar and inclusive design as the quality bar, exactly the chapter’s framing — because a settlement can be satisfied while AT users still can’t buy a lamp.

Example 18 — EAA as a Release Gate

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The European Accessibility Act expands accessibility obligations for many products and services sold into the EU, with enforcement timelines that make accessibility a release-gate concern.

Scenario. Ledgerly, a US-based SaaS invoicing platform, plans its 2025 EU market entry. The EAA’s June 2025 enforcement milestone means e-commerce and consumer banking-adjacent services sold into the EU carry accessibility obligations — for Ledgerly this is a launch prerequisite, not a post-launch cleanup ticket.

BAD. Treat the EAA as a compliance memo: launch first, put “a11y remediation” in the Q4 backlog, and assume the legal team will “handle Europe.” Result in this scenario: a blocked enterprise deal — the customer’s procurement checklist requires an accessibility conformance report — plus exposure to member-state enforcement, and a rushed retrofit priced at roughly 5× the cost of building it in.

GOOD. Accessibility becomes a literal release gate in the EU launch plan: the go/no-go checklist includes “WCAG 2.2 AA verified on signup, invoice creation, and payment flows (AT ladder steps 1–4),” an accessibility statement page, an accessibility conformance report (EN 301 549-aligned) that sales can hand procurement, and a support channel for accessibility issues with a named owner. The launch slips three weeks to fix keyboard traps in the invoice editor — a decision the VP defends in writing: “We don’t ship into the EU market with known launch-blocking accessibility defects.” First-quarter EU pipeline includes two enterprise deals won partly on the conformance report competitors couldn’t produce.

Why this works. Enforcement timelines turned accessibility into a strategic release-gate concern handled before launch — law as the floor, with the conformance work doubling as a sales asset, illustrating the chapter’s point that legal baselines are product strategy, not only compliance tickets.

§3.10 Assistive Technology Testing Ladder

Example 19 — AT Testing Ladder

Definition (as this chapter uses it): An escalating verification ladder — automated scans, keyboard-only, screen reader smoke tests, zoom and reflow, speech and switch where relevant, and compensated disabled user testing for high-stakes flows — because automation without human AT testing is theater.

Scenario. Bloomly, a flower-delivery retailer, applies the full ladder to its checkout (a high-stakes flow: it takes money) before Mother’s Day 2025 peak. The checkout is a single responsive web flow, served in mobile browsers and embedded via WebView inside Bloomly’s iOS and Android apps — so web tooling (axe-core) scans the code in CI, while VoiceOver and TalkBack test the flow as app customers actually experience it.

  1. Automated scans. axe-core in CI flags 14 issues: 9 images missing alt text, 3 unlabeled form fields, 2 contrast failures. All fixed — and the team explicitly does not treat the resulting green score as done.
  2. Keyboard-only. A tester unplugs the mouse. Findings the scanner scored green: the delivery-date calendar is a keyboard trap (Tab cycles inside it forever, Esc does nothing), and focus visibility is missing on the tip-selection chips, so a keyboard user can’t tell where they are. Both fixed.
  3. Screen reader smoke tests. VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) against the WebView-embedded checkout on the critical path: the “Add gift message” toggle announces as “button” with no name, and after tapping “Place order” the confirmation renders visually but nothing is announced — a blind user sits in silence wondering if they paid. Fixes: proper name/role/value; an aria-live="assertive" region announcing “Order confirmed. Your peonies arrive Thursday, May 8.”
  4. Zoom and reflow. At 400% zoom the “Place order” button falls outside the viewport with no way to scroll to it; at 200% the price column truncates to “$4…”. Layout reflowed to a single column under zoom; both orientations verified on mobile.
  5. Speech and switch. Via Voice Control, “Tap Place order” fails because the visible label (“Place order”) didn’t match the accessible name (“submit-btn-final”); names aligned so speech users can target what they see.
  6. Disabled user testing. Five compensated participants ($120/session): two screen reader users, one switch user, one low-vision user, one participant with a cognitive disability. The switch user surfaces what no prior rung could: the 90-second checkout timeout is unreachable for scanning-based input; the timeout becomes user-extendable. Preferred — as the chapter says — for exactly this kind of high-stakes flow.

Each rung caught defects every rung below it missed — 14, then 2, then 2, then 2, then 1, then 1. In parallel, recurring offenders (unlabeled toggles, missing focus styles) are fixed once in the design system’s components, because human testing without fixing systemic design system issues is endless whack-a-mole.

Why this works. The ladder escalates from cheap automation to compensated human expertise instead of stopping at a green scan — testing with AT and people, not only scanners — and routes recurring fixes into the design system so the same defect cannot ship twice.

§3.11 AI Exclusion Risks

Example 20 — AI Exclusion Risks

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Generative AI introduces new mismatches — biased training data, assumed fluent typed English, voice agents failing non-native accents, moderation flagging assistive communication, AI summaries omitting accessibility content, bot checks blocking AT — requiring human override, accessible AI controls, transparent confidence, and evaluation with diverse users.

Scenario. Wayfarer, a travel-booking platform, ships an AI trip assistant in 2025 (“Ask me anything about your trip”) and audits it for the chapter’s exclusion modes.

BAD (as first shipped).
- The voice interface fails non-native English accents: task-completion for speakers with strong Vietnamese or Nigerian accents is 54%, versus 91% for US-accent speakers — measured only after launch, because the evaluation suite was an accuracy benchmark on a majority-accent dataset.
- Automated moderation flags a user’s AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) app output as “bot-like, repetitive input” and locks the account behind a slide-the-puzzle-piece bot check that their motor disability makes impossible — a captcha-like gate blocking AT.
- The “AI summary” of a 40-review hotel page omits the one review reporting “the advertised roll-in shower doesn’t exist” — critical accessibility content summarized away.
- The AI chat panel is a <div> soup: responses stream without announcements, so NVDA users hear nothing; there is no way to reach “Regenerate” by keyboard. The AI feature cannot be operated or understood via AT.
- Answers are stated with uniform confidence: “This hotel is wheelchair accessible” — whether grounded in verified data or a guess.

GOOD (governed inclusively).
- Evaluation with diverse users: the accent gap becomes a tracked eval with per-accent-cohort dashboards; typed input is offered as an equal path everywhere voice exists (“Prefer to type? Tap here”), and accent task-completion reaches 87% before the next release.
- Human override: every AI decision has an escape hatch — the moderation flag now routes to “Verify me another way (a human will review within 2 hours),” never a puzzle-only gate; a standing rule exempts recognized AT input patterns from “bot-like” heuristics.
- Accessibility content protected in summaries: reviews mentioning accessibility features are pinned, never summarized away: “♿ 3 reviews mention accessibility — read them in full.”
- Accessible controls for AI features: the chat is rebuilt on semantic markup — streamed responses announced via aria-live="polite", “Stop generating” and “Regenerate” reachable by keyboard with visible focus, and the whole assistant operable at 400% zoom.
- Transparent confidence: claims carry their grounding — “Wheelchair accessible: confirmed by the property (March 2025)” versus “Mentioned in 1 guest review — not verified. Ask the property.”

Why this works. Each fix pairs an AI capability with the inclusive governance the chapter demands — human override, accessible controls, transparent confidence, and diverse-user evaluation — so the AI scales access instead of scaling exclusion.

Chapter 04 Worked Examples — Product UX Strategy and Continuous Discovery

This companion document gives one concrete, worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 4: each numbered section’s core concept(s) plus every entry in the Key Terms list (duplicates merged). Examples span fintech, health, government services, collaboration tools, e-commerce, media, and developer tools, in modern (2024–2026) contexts: mobile-first, AI-assisted, offline-capable, privacy-conscious, and accessible. Every example honors the book’s priority hierarchy — safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight — and uses the chapter’s vocabulary exactly.
