Section 4.1 — Strategy Starts With Jobs, Not Roadmaps

Example 1 — Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)

Definition (per this chapter): People “hire” products to make progress in a circumstance; a JTBD is a stable intent under constraints — not a demographic, not a feature request.

Scenario — “Ledgerly,” a mobile banking app for gig workers (fintech). Ledgerly’s roadmap draft for 2025 lists features: “crypto wallet, savings round-ups, dark mode.” A strategist runs twelve switch interviews with couriers and rideshare drivers and finds the job they actually hire a second bank account for:

“When my week’s payouts land at unpredictable times across three platforms, I want to know today what is safe to spend and what must be held for quarterly taxes, so I don’t get a $900 surprise from the IRS in April.”

Competing hires include: a spreadsheet updated on Sunday nights, a shoebox of receipts, and inertia (“my old bank is fine, switching is scary”). Anxieties blocking switching: “Will direct deposit break mid-week?” and “Can I get my money out fast if this startup dies?”

  • BAD (feature catalog): Ship the crypto wallet because a competitor has one. Q3 review: 40,000 downloads, 3% of users touched the wallet, tax-season churn unchanged at 22%.
  • GOOD (job-anchored): Ship “Safe to Spend,” a home-screen number that auto-holds an estimated tax percentage per deposit, with the copy “Held for taxes: $184 this week — you set the rate, you can release it anytime.” Address the switching anxiety directly in onboarding: “Your money is FDIC-insured through our partner bank. Withdraw to any account in minutes.” Tax-season churn drops to 11% in the pilot cohort.

Why this works: Strategy targeted the progress customers seek (predictable spending under irregular income) instead of cataloging screens, so shipped volume shrank while customer progress — and retention — rose.

Example 2 — Job Story (writing format)

Definition (per this chapter): The “When… I want to… so I can…” format is a useful way to write opportunities and stories; it is not identical to the full JTBD research method.

Scenario — a state government digital service for renewing an accessible-parking permit. The team must brief engineers and a policy reviewer in one artifact. They avoid both the persona-flavored user story and the raw feature request:

  • BAD (feature request masquerading as a story): “As a user, I want a Renew button on the dashboard.” (No circumstance, no motivation, no way to evaluate alternatives — it pre-commits to one UI.)
  • GOOD (job story): “When my permit expires in 30 days and I can’t easily travel to a DMV office, I want to renew from my phone with the documents I already gave the state, so I can keep my parking access without a caregiver taking a day off work.”

That one sentence generated three candidate solutions in the OST (pre-filled renewal form, SMS renewal link, automatic renewal with opt-out) instead of locking in a dashboard button. Note what the team didn’t claim: writing job stories is not the same as having done discovery — the story was written after six interviews, in the spirit of Torres’s discovery operating system, not as a substitute for it.

Why this works: The format captures stable intent under constraints (mobility, caregiver dependence) and keeps inclusion ahead of solution preference — exactly the chapter’s warning that a job story is a writing format, not the research method itself.

Section 4.2 — Outcome Over Output

Example 3 — Outcome vs Output

Definition (per this chapter): Outputs are artifacts (a redesign, three experiments); outcomes are meaningful changes in customer or business behavior (time-to-value drops, support contacts fall, retention rises).

Scenario — “Hemline,” a mid-size fashion e-commerce app, reworking returns.

  • BAD (output celebration): The quarterly review slide reads “Shipped: redesigned returns portal, 14 new screens, 2 A/B tests run, design system v3 adopted.” Applause. Meanwhile, “Where is my refund?” remains the #1 support contact at 31% of tickets, and 90-day repeat purchase rate among customers who returned an item sits at 18%.
  • GOOD (outcome management): The team’s stated outcome: “Customers who return an item repurchase within 90 days at ≥30%, and refund-status contacts fall below 15% of tickets.” They ship less UI — a single “Your refund: $42.50, arriving by Fri Mar 14” status card with push updates and an offline-readable QR drop-off code — and kill a planned “returns hub” when a prototype test shows it adds steps. One experiment fails (instant store credit didn’t move repurchase); the team writes up the learning in the experiment log instead of burying it in a changelog. Six months later: refund contacts 12% (target met), returner repurchase 29% — a near-miss against the team’s own ≥30% bar, and they report it as one. The quarterly slide reads “Outcome partially met: contacts target hit; repurchase 29% vs ≥30% goal, trajectory positive — persevere,” not “Success.” Managing to outcomes includes reporting honestly against the threshold you set, even when the number is one point shy.

Why this works: The team owned a problem, not a backlog of predetermined solutions — Cagan’s empowered-team stance — treated the failed experiment as learning, and held itself to its stated success criterion instead of quietly redefining a 29% as a win: the chapter’s definition of managing to outcomes rather than rewarding busyness.

Example 4 — North Star Metric and Input Metrics (vs Vanity Metrics)

Definition (per this chapter): A north star metric reflects delivered value; input metrics are leading indicators the team can influence; vanity metrics (raw downloads, pageviews, logins) inflate egos and starve strategy.

Scenario — “Boardwalk,” a collaborative whiteboard tool with AI diagram generation.

  • BAD (vanity north star): Leadership tracks “monthly logins” and “AI generations per day.” Both spike after a launch-week press cycle (logins +64%), then strategy meetings argue about a chart that measures curiosity, not value. Nobody notices that most AI-generated diagrams are deleted within two minutes.
  • GOOD (value-anchored north star): North star: weekly boards shared with ≥2 collaborators and edited again within 7 days — a proxy for “a real working session happened,” not merely a login. Input metrics the team can influence:
  • Activation rate: % of new workspaces creating a first shared board within 3 days (currently 34%).
  • Time-to-first-success: median 11 minutes from signup to first co-edit.
  • Invite acceptance rate: 41%.
  • AI-assist keep rate: % of AI-generated diagrams still present after 24 hours (currently 22% — a trust signal, not a usage signal).

Each squad owns one input metric; the dashboard shows the inputs leading the north star, so when invite acceptance climbs to 52% after rewriting the invite email (“Priya asked you to sketch the onboarding flow with her — open the board”), the north star follows five weeks later.

Why this works: The metric tree operationalizes outcome-over-output — every input is something UX can move, and the north star counts delivered collaboration value, not the login-counting anti-pattern the chapter names.

Section 4.3 — Continuous Discovery

Example 5 — Continuous Discovery

Definition (per this chapter): Weekly touchpoints with customers, conducted by the team that builds the product — a parallel cadence, not a phase before delivery and not a remote research guild throwing insights over a wall.

Scenario — “Relay,” a developer API platform for payment webhooks.

  • BAD (dual-track theater): Discovery is a quarterly “voice of customer” workshop run by a central insights team; findings arrive as a 60-slide deck eight weeks later. Meanwhile delivery ships the VP’s pet feature — a webhook “AI summarizer” — because the HiPPO saw one at a conference. Usage after launch: 4% of accounts.
  • GOOD (weekly cadence by the product trio): The PM, designer, and tech lead hold two 30-minute customer calls every Tuesday, recruited by an automated in-product intercept: “Building with our webhooks this week? Chat with the team for 30 min — $75 credit.” The cadence follows the chapter’s elements:
    1. Interviewing to understand opportunities, not to validate pet solutions — “Walk me through the last webhook failure you debugged,” never “Would you use an AI summarizer?”
    2. Mapping visually — every Tuesday afternoon, new opportunities land on the OST (“I can’t tell if a missed event was our bug or yours” appears in 7 of 9 interviews).
    3. Testing assumptions with the smallest honest experiment — a Figma prototype of a replay-with-diff view tested with 5 developers that Thursday.
    4. Feeding evidence into delivery priorities continuously — the replay view displaces the summarizer in the very next sprint.

Why this works: Decisions are informed by weekly customer contact from the people who build, which is exactly what the chapter says prevents “discovery” from collapsing into stakeholder workshops that ship the HiPPO’s preference.

Section 4.4 — Opportunity Solution Trees (OST)

Example 6 — Opportunity Solution Tree

Definition (per this chapter): A visual tree connecting a measurable outcome → opportunity spaces uncovered in research → solutions under each opportunity → experiments that test assumption risk.

Scenario — “Auricle,” a podcast app fighting drop-off among commuting listeners.

OUTCOME: Raise week-4 retention of new listeners from 23% → 32%
├── OPPORTUNITY A: "I lose my place when my commute has dead zones"        (14/20 interviews)
│   ├── Solution A1: Auto-download next 3 episodes of followed shows (offline queue)
│   │   └── Experiment: riskiest assumption = "users will grant background
│   │       download on cellular" → settings-sheet prototype test, n=8;
│   │       threshold: ≥6 of 8 enable it when copy says
│   │       "Downloads pause automatically when you're low on data"
│   └── Solution A2: Resume-across-devices with offline position sync
│       └── Experiment: riskiest assumption = "sync is trusted even after
│           offline listening" → 2-week diary study, n=6; threshold:
│           ≤1 report of "it lost my place"
├── OPPORTUNITY B: "I finish my shows and don't know what to try next"     (9/20)
│   └── Solution B1: AI 'because you finished…' shelf with human-readable
│       reasons ("Same host, shorter episodes")
│       └── Experiment: riskiest assumption = "listeners tap recommendations
│           that explain themselves" → shelf prototype, reasons vs. no
│           reasons, n=12; threshold: reasons variant ≥2× tap-through
└── OPPORTUNITY C: "Episode pages are unreadable with my screen reader"    (3/20, severity high)
    └── Solution C1: Semantic heading rework + labeled playback controls
        └── Experiment: riskiest assumption = "heading rework alone restores
            navigability" → moderated VoiceOver/TalkBack sessions, n=3;
            threshold: all 3 complete a find-and-queue task unassisted

The tree fights both failure modes the chapter names. Solution-first roadmap: an exec’s demand to “add AI chapter summaries” is parked because it maps to no researched opportunity. Opportunity sprawl: twenty insights were compared and pruned to three, using compare-and-choose: Opportunity A affects the most listeners and directly explains week-2 drop-off in cohort data — but Opportunity C is sequenced first despite lower frequency, because inclusion outranks outcome optimization in the book’s hierarchy. The tension with the retention outcome is smaller than it looks: C1 is a two-sprint fix that ships while Opportunity A’s download experiment runs in parallel, so honoring the hierarchy costs the outcome nothing — compare-and-choose still directs the big bet at A. In critique, the strategist asks the chapter’s question verbatim: “Show me the opportunity this prototype addresses, and the riskiest assumption it carries.”

Why this works: The OST makes trade-offs visible — which opportunity most moves the outcome, and which assumption, if wrong, kills the solution — instead of jumping to UI.

Section 4.5 — Dual-Track and the RAF Loop

Example 7 — Dual-Track Agile

Definition (per this chapter): Discovery and delivery run in parallel; discovery reduces uncertainty about value and usability, delivery builds production-quality increments, and the tracks inform each other.

Scenario — “Carewise,” a telehealth app adding asynchronous messaging with clinicians.

Week by week, the two tracks run side by side:

Week Discovery track Delivery track
1 3 patient interviews: “I don’t message because I don’t know if it’s urgent-safe” Ships message threading (already validated)
2 Tests prototype of triage copy: “For symptoms that need care today, call — messages are answered within 1 business day” Reveals operational constraint: nurse team can only staff 1-business-day SLA, not the 4-hour SLA discovery was about to test
3 Reprioritizes: tests expectation-setting UI against the real SLA Ships read receipts with the validated copy

The information flows both ways, as the chapter requires: delivery’s staffing constraint stopped discovery from validating a promise the product couldn’t keep (a safety issue — patients might wait on an urgent symptom); discovery’s triage insight stopped delivery from building a slick composer that patients were afraid to use.

  • BAD contrast: The tracks never talk. Discovery, running solo, prototypes the composer with the promise “A clinician replies within 4 hours” and validates it beautifully — 9 of 10 patients say they’d message instead of calling. Delivery ships that copy without anyone checking nurse staffing, which supports only a 1-business-day turnaround. In the first month the 4-hour SLA is missed 38% of the time; one patient with a worsening infection waits 26 hours on a message she believed was urgent-safe instead of calling, and the incident review traces the harm directly to a promise the product could never keep. Building the wrong thing faster, with safety consequences.

Why this works: Discovery reduced value-and-usability uncertainty while delivery exposed operational reality — the mutual information flow that keeps dual-track from being two teams shipping past each other, with safety honored above all.

Example 8 — The RAF Loop (Research → Assumptions → Feedback)

Definition (per this chapter): A practical loop — Research (interviews, observation, support mining, analytics), Assumptions (explicit bets across desirability, viability, feasibility, usability, ethics), Feedback (gather signal against the outcome, update the OST, decide persevere / pivot / kill).

Scenario — “SiteHand,” a tablet app for building-safety inspectors working in basements and remote sites with no connectivity.

  • Research: Support mining shows 19% of tickets mention “lost my inspection”; ride-along observation shows inspectors photographing paper forms “as backup” because they don’t trust sync; analytics show a spike in app force-quits in low-signal zip codes.
  • Assumptions (explicit bets):
  • Desirability: Inspectors want a visible queued-sync state more than faster sync.
  • Usability: A “Saved on this device — 3 reports waiting to sync” banner will be understood without training.
  • Feasibility: Conflict-free sync of photo-heavy reports is buildable in one quarter.
  • Viability: Reduced data-loss tickets cut support cost enough to fund it.
  • Ethics: No silent data expiry — a queued report must never be deleted without explicit user action.
  • Feedback: A two-week pilot with 40 inspectors measures against the outcome (data-loss tickets, force-quits). Banner comprehension passes (9/10 in usability sessions correctly predicted what happens in a dead zone); force-quits drop 61% in the pilot cohort. Decision recorded on the OST: persevere on queued sync; kill the “faster sync” workstream; pivot the banner copy from “Pending upload” to “Saved on this device” after two inspectors read “pending” as “at risk.”

Why this works: Every step of the loop fed the next — evidence became explicit bets, bets became measured signal, and signal became a persevere/pivot/kill decision on the OST — with the model/recovery concern (users must trust that saved means saved) driving the whole cycle.

Example 9 — Experiments as the Mechanism Inside Feedback (the honest fake door)

Definition (per this chapter): Experiments (prototypes, concierge tests, A/B tests, carefully honest fake doors) are the primary mechanism inside Feedback/testing — not a fourth letter of RAF — and every test needs a learning goal, a success/failure threshold, and an owner.

Scenario — “Cartful,” a grocery e-commerce app, testing demand for a “Reorder my usual week” AI-assisted basket.

  • BAD (fake door that punishes users): A prominent “Build my week ✨” button that, when tapped, shows “Coming soon!” with no follow-through. 12,000 taps, a wave of 1-star reviews (“the main button is a lie”), and — per the chapter — user distrust that outlives the test.
  • GOOD (carefully honest fake door + concierge):
  • Learning goal: “Do weekly shoppers want an auto-built basket enough to start one?”
  • Threshold: ≥8% of weekly-cohort shoppers tap within 14 days = build; <4% = kill; between = interview.
  • Owner: Growth-pod PM, logged in the experiment registry with an end date.
  • The door itself is honest: tapping “Build my week — early access” opens: “We’re testing this with a small group. Want in? We’ll hand-build your first basket from your history within 24 hours.” A concierge test fulfills the promise manually for the first 200 opt-ins; a $5 credit thanks everyone if capacity fills.
  • Result: 11% tap-through, 74% of concierge baskets accepted with ≤2 edits. Build decision made with evidence, not opinion — and no one was punished for their curiosity.

Why this works: The experiment was governed in miniature — goal, threshold, owner — and honesty preserved user trust, avoiding the chapter’s anti-pattern of “fake-door tests that punish users without follow-through.”

Section 4.6 — Lifecycle Metrics

Example 10 — Activation

Definition (per this chapter): Users reach a first moment of value; UX owns onboarding clarity, empty states that teach, and time-to-value — premature paywalls and tour tooltips are not activation strategy.

Scenario — “Minuteman,” an AI meeting-notes tool.

  • BAD: The paid-ad landing page is gorgeous and promises “Perfect notes, zero setup — AI joins your next meeting in one click.” The first run then opens with a 6-step tooltip tour (“This is your sidebar!”), then a paywall: “Start your Pro trial to unlock summaries” — and the “one click” calendar connection actually requires a workspace admin’s approval for most corporate signups. Activation (first useful summary within 3 days) is 19%; the tour is skipped by 83% of users; 62% of ad-driven signups never return after day 1. This is the chapter’s strategy bug in full: acquisition without activation — a beautiful marketing site feeding a confusing first-run experience — burning both trust and CAC.
  • GOOD: The marketing promise is rewritten to match what the first run can actually deliver (“Hear your first AI summary in 90 seconds — no calendar access needed to try it”). First run asks one question — “Connect your calendar so we can join your next meeting, or try it now with a 2-minute sample recording” — and the empty state teaches: “No notes yet. Your first summary will appear here about 5 minutes after your meeting ends. You’ll approve who it’s shared with — nothing is sent without you.” A privacy note sits inline, not buried: “Recordings are processed, then deleted within 24 hours unless you save them.” The sample-recording path delivers a real summary in 90 seconds. Activation rises to 44%; median time-to-first-success falls from 2 days to 31 minutes.

Why this works: Activation was earned by shortening time-to-value and teaching through the empty state — not coerced with tours and premature paywalls — the acquisition message was brought back inside what the first run truly delivers, and the privacy commitment (safety and consent first) removed the anxiety blocking the first “aha.”

Example 11 — Retention

Definition (per this chapter): Users return and succeed repeatedly; habit loops must be earned through reliable value, not notification spam.

Scenario — “Stridewell,” a physical-therapy exercise app prescribed after knee surgery.

  • BAD (notification spam): Streak guilt at 8 p.m. daily: “Don’t break your 6-day streak! 😢” plus three re-engagement pushes a week. Day-30 retention ticks up 2 points for two weeks, then notification opt-out hits 58% and day-60 retention falls below baseline — the chapter’s growth-hack pattern: spike now, destroy trust later.
  • GOOD (earned habit loop): The loop is anchored to the user’s real recovery job. One notification, timed to the slot the user chose (“When do you usually do your exercises?”), with content worth returning for: “Week 3, day 2: your knee-bend range improved 8° since last week — today’s set adjusts for that.” Missed sessions get recovery-first copy, not guilt: “Missed yesterday? That’s normal in week 3. Today’s session is rebalanced — no doubling up.” Day-60 retention rises from 27% to 41%, and the input metric that leads it — sessions completed per active week — climbs from 2.1 to 3.4.

Why this works: Return visits were earned through reliable, personally meaningful value (visible recovery progress), matching the chapter’s rule that habit loops are earned, never coerced.

Example 12 — Churn

Definition (per this chapter): Users leave; exit surveys and cohort analysis reveal whether churn is product failure, sales mismatch, or lifecycle completion — designing win-back without fixing the job is cosmetic.

Scenario — “Suppora,” a meal-kit subscription. Monthly churn is 9%. Instead of jumping to a win-back discount, the team runs cohort analysis plus a one-question exit survey (“What’s the main reason you’re canceling?” with a free-text option), then codes 400 responses:

  • Product failure (38%): “Recipes repeat too often” — cohorts show churn spikes exactly at week 10, when the recipe rotation loops. This becomes an OST opportunity with an owner.
  • Sales mismatch (24%): “I thought this was for one person; portions are for two” — acquired via an influencer campaign that showed solo cooking. Fix is upstream in marketing claims, not in the product.

  • Lifecycle completion (21%): “I learned to cook the basics — that’s what I wanted.” These users succeeded. They get a warm goodbye: “Glad we helped. Your recipe library stays free forever,” which later drives referrals.

  • BAD contrast: A blanket “50% off if you stay!” modal for all three groups — cosmetic win-back that pays completed-lifecycle users to linger, hides the week-10 rotation bug, and leaves the marketing mismatch burning CAC.

Why this works: Diagnosing which kind of churn preceded any fix, so investment went to the broken job (recipe variety) instead of a discount that treats the symptom — exactly the chapter’s warning that win-back without fixing the job is cosmetic.

Example 13 — Expansion

Definition (per this chapter): Users deepen usage or spend; in ethical products, expansion follows new jobs served well — not dark patterns that hide cancellation.

Scenario — “Vaultline,” a cloud file platform for architecture firms. A 5-seat firm has been using Vaultline for drawings storage for a year. Discovery interviews surface a new job: “When a client requests changes, I want the whole revision conversation attached to the drawing, so approvals don’t get lost in email.” Vaultline ships client-review links as a Business-tier capability and surfaces the upgrade only in the moment the job appears — a user shares a third external review link in a month and sees: “You’re sharing reviews often. Business adds client approval tracking and audit history — try it on this project free for 30 days.” Expansion revenue from this cohort grows 23% in two quarters; net revenue retention passes 115%.

  • BAD contrast: “Expansion” via auto-enrolling teams into Business after the trial with the downgrade path hidden behind a support ticket. Revenue spikes one quarter; renewal-time trust collapses, and procurement at two large accounts flags the practice in security review.

Why this works: Spend deepened because a genuinely new job was served well at the moment it appeared — the chapter’s definition of ethical expansion — rather than through dark patterns that hide the exit.

Section 4.7 — Monetization Consent

Example 14 — Monetization Consent

Definition (per this chapter): Users understand what they pay, why, what they get, and how to leave — in contrast to hidden fees, obstructed cancel flows, guilt screens, and forced continuity without clear reminders.

Scenario — “The Meridian,” a news subscription app.

  • BAD (dark-pattern stack): “$1 for 3 months!” (renews at $24.99/month, disclosed in 8-point gray text). Cancellation requires a phone call, Mon–Fri 9–5. The cancel page pleads: “Journalism dies without you. Are you SURE you want to abandon the truth?” Short-term conversion is up 0.9%; twelve months later, chargebacks triple, an FTC “click-to-cancel”-era complaint lands, and brand-trust survey scores fall 14 points.
  • GOOD (consent-aligned): The paywall states the full deal in one glance: “$4/month for 3 months, then $16/month. Renews automatically — we’ll email you 7 days before the price changes. Cancel anytime in two taps.” The reminder email actually arrives: “Your intro rate ends March 3. Keep, switch to annual ($150/yr), or cancel — one tap each.” Cancellation is self-serve: Settings → Manage subscription → “Cancel — you’ll keep access until April 2.” Price packaging maps to jobs and segments — a “Weekend reader” tier exists because discovery found a large segment hiring the app only for long-form Saturday reads — not to whichever button color converted 0.3% better in isolation from trust metrics. Result: intro-offer conversion drops 0.6 points, but 12-month retention of converts rises from 34% to 51%, and support contacts about billing fall 40%.

Why this works: Consent-aligned monetization traded a small short-term conversion trick for higher retention quality and lower regulatory risk — the chapter’s claim, demonstrated — and treated “cancel is part of the product” as a design surface, not a leak.

Section 4.8 — B2B: Buyer Versus User

Example 15 — Buyer Versus User

Definition (per this chapter): The buyer (economic decision-maker, IT, security, procurement) and the user (daily operator) diverge; winning RFPs while tormenting users creates shelfware, and delighting users while failing security review never enters the account.

Scenario — “Gatekeep,” an endpoint-security management platform.

  • BAD (buyer-only): Gatekeep wins a 4,000-seat hospital RFP on its compliance matrix and SSO checklist. But the daily operators — help-desk analysts — face a 9-click quarantine flow with alerts labeled “Event Class 4B-ANOMALOUS.” Analysts route around it with a shared spreadsheet; console weekly-active usage is 12% of licensed seats. At renewal, the CISO sees a usage dashboard full of shelfware and cuts seats by half.
  • GOOD (both surfaces as first-class products):
  • For users: Alert triage rebuilt around the analyst’s job — “Isolate this laptop” is one confirmed tap, alerts read “Ransomware-like encryption pattern on LT-2214 (Maria G., Radiology) — recommended: isolate now,” and an AI-drafted incident summary is editable before filing. Analyst task time drops from 14 to 4 minutes; these users become internal champions.
  • For buyers: Admin and compliance experiences treated as products, not afterthoughts — a SOC 2 / HIPAA evidence-export button, SCIM provisioning that IT can configure in an afternoon, and a quarterly “value recap” dashboard (“1,204 incidents contained; median response 6 min”) that gives the CISO renewal evidence for the board.

Renewal expands to 5,500 seats.

Why this works: Designing for both surfaces — champion-making user workflows and buyer-facing evidence, admin, and compliance — reflects the chapter’s point that ignoring either side is not focus, it is incomplete discovery.

Section 4.9 — PLG Versus Sales-Led

Example 16 — Product-Led Growth (PLG)

Definition (per this chapter): The product is the primary acquisition and expansion engine — self-serve signup, freemium or trial, viral loops, in-product education — demanding exceptional activation, empty states, templates, and upgrade moments that feel like help.

Scenario — “Quillbase,” a serverless database for indie developers. No sales team touches deals under $10k. The PLG machine:

  • Self-serve signup: GitHub OAuth to a live database in 40 seconds; no credit card, no “Book a demo.”
  • Empty state that teaches: “Your database is empty. Run npx quillbase seed for sample data, or import a CSV — most developers ship their first query in under 5 minutes.”
  • Templates: “Start from: SaaS starter · Chat app · Inventory tracker,” each a one-click deployed schema.
  • Viral loop: Every shared query result page footer reads “Powered by Quillbase — fork this database,” converting at 3.1% to signups.
  • Upgrade moment that feels like help: At 80% of the free row limit: “You’re at 8M of 10M free rows. Nothing breaks at the limit — reads keep working, writes queue for 48 hours so you never lose data. Upgrade to Pro ($25/mo) for 100M rows.” Note the model/recovery care: the limit’s behavior is explained before it is hit, and no data is ever destroyed.

Free-to-paid conversion runs 5.8%, with 71% of paid accounts never having spoken to a human.

Why this works: Every UX investment sits where the chapter says PLG lives — activation, empty states, templates, and upgrade moments that feel like help rather than a toll booth.

Example 17 — Sales-Led Motion (and the Hybrid Failure Mode)

Definition (per this chapter): Growth relies on demos, RFPs, and human negotiation — demanding demo credibility, configurable enterprise flows, and admin tooling that survives procurement.

Scenario — “Civica Analytics,” selling caseload-analytics software to county social-services agencies. Nothing here is self-serve: deals run 9–14 months through public RFPs. UX investment goes where the motion needs it:

  • Demo credibility: A “demo county” dataset with realistic (synthetic) case records, so the AE’s walkthrough survives the question “show me a caseworker with 40 open cases” instead of collapsing into lorem ipsum.
  • Configurable enterprise flows: County-specific intake fields, state-mandated report templates, and role-based access mapped to civil-service job classes — configured by the agency’s admin, not by an engineering ticket.
  • Admin tooling that survives procurement: An accessibility conformance report (Section 508/WCAG 2.2 AA — a hard legal requirement for this buyer), audit logs, data-residency controls, and an offline-capable field mode for caseworkers in rural dead zones, all documented well enough for the RFP’s 200-line security questionnaire.

The hybrid failure the chapter warns about, both directions: Civica’s board demands “PLG motion” and marketing ships a “Start free trial” button — onto a product that requires two weeks of county data integration before showing any value. Trial signups: 312; activated: 3. PLG copy on a product that cannot self-serve. The reverse failure appears at competitor “MeritCase,” whose sales-led team closes an 11-month county deal and then expects the product to “just be sticky” without any investment in self-serve value: a caseworker’s first login lands on an empty dashboard reading “No reports configured — contact your account executive,” the only templates live in a 60-page training PDF, and in-product education is two webinars the AE schedules. Weekly active caseworkers fall from 71% during training week to 18% by month four as workers rebuild their caseload lists in spreadsheets; at renewal the county cites “low utilization,” reopens the RFP, and Civica wins the seat.

Why this works: UX investment matched the growth motion — demo credibility, configurability, and procurement-grade admin evidence — instead of bolting PLG UX onto an enterprise backend, the mismatch the chapter names as strategy failure.

Section 4.10 — Experiment Governance, Research Ops, Instrumentation

Example 18 — Experiment Governance

Definition (per this chapter): Rules for what may be tested on whom; ethical limits; primary metrics paired with guardrails (accessibility, trust, support volume); duration and peeking policy; documented results so orphaned tests do not repeat.

Scenario — “Lendia,” a mobile lending app, wants to test a redesigned loan-offer screen. The governance charter, applied to this test:

  • What may be tested on whom: Pricing, credit limits, and repayment terms are never A/B tested — same-situation applicants must see the same offer (fairness and regulatory safety come before conversion). Only presentation and explanation may vary. Users in active hardship programs are excluded from all experiments.
  • Ethical limits: No deceptive fake charges, no countdown timers implying an offer expires when it does not.
  • Primary metric + guardrails: Primary: offer-acceptance completion. Guardrails that can kill a winning test: screen-reader task success must not drop (measured in moderated sessions with 5 assistive-tech users before ramp), “what will this cost me?” support contacts must not rise >10%, and 7-day loan-regret cancellations must not increase.
  • Duration and peeking policy: Two full weekly cycles minimum, no stopping on day-3 significance; the dashboard literally hides p-values until day 14.

  • Documentation: Result logged in the experiment registry: “EXP-2211: variant B +6% completion, guardrails green, shipped 2025-11-04” — so next year’s team doesn’t re-run the orphaned 2023 version of the same test.

  • BAD contrast: An ungoverned growth pod ships 14 overlapping tests in a quarter; two touch the same funnel step and corrupt each other’s data (metric thrash), and one variant quietly degrades contrast below WCAG ratios for three weeks. User distrust and unusable data — the chapter’s predicted cost.

Why this works: Safety, fairness, and inclusion guardrails are structurally senior to the conversion metric, and documentation plus peeking rules turn experimentation from thrash into governed learning.

Example 19 — Research Ops

Definition (per this chapter): The infrastructure that makes continuous discovery sustainable — participant recruiting, incentives, GDPR/CCPA-aware consent, knowledge repositories, insight taxonomy, and tooling so PMs and designers can research weekly without chaos.

Scenario — “Wellcove,” a European health-tracking company with six product trios.

  • BAD (heroic, chaotic research): Each PM DMs users from a personal spreadsheet of emails scraped from support tickets (a GDPR incident waiting to happen), pays incentives from a personal card, and stores recordings in a private drive folder. Insights live in slide decks nobody can search; trio #4 unknowingly re-interviews the same eight users trio #2 exhausted last month.
  • GOOD (ops as infrastructure): A research-ops lead stands up:
  • Recruiting: An opt-in research panel recruited via an in-product prompt — “Help shape Wellcove: join our research panel (30-min sessions, €40 voucher, leave anytime)” — with quota rules so no participant is contacted more than once a quarter, and deliberate recruitment of screen-reader users and participants over 65.
  • Consent, GDPR/CCPA-aware: A consent flow that states purpose, retention (“recordings deleted after 12 months”), and withdrawal rights; special-category health data flagged so sessions touching symptoms use a stricter template reviewed by the DPO.
  • Repository and taxonomy: Every session is summarized (AI-drafted, researcher-verified) and tagged against the shared taxonomy — job, lifecycle stage (activation/retention/churn/expansion), opportunity ID from the OST — so a designer can search “churn + sleep-tracking” and find nine coded interviews in 30 seconds.
  • Tooling for weekly cadence: Calendaring, incentive payouts, and templated interview guides are self-serve, so each trio sustains its weekly touchpoints without a research guild bottleneck.

Sessions per month across trios go from 11 (chaotic) to 46 (sustainable), with zero consent incidents.

Why this works: Continuous discovery survived scaling because the operational substrate — recruiting, consent, repository, taxonomy — made weekly research the easy path, freeing insights from the chapter’s “slide decks nobody can search” trap while keeping participant privacy and consent first.

Example 20 — Instrumentation

Definition (per this chapter): Connecting UX to evidence — an event taxonomy aligned to jobs and outcomes, funnels that match mental models, session replay used ethically, and dashboards where input metrics lead the north star; without it, OSTs become opinion trees.

Scenario — “Wayfarer,” a trip-planning app with an AI itinerary assistant.

  • BAD (developer-convenience events): The taxonomy is button_click_37, screen_view_home, api_call_success. The “funnel” mirrors the codebase, not the traveler: nobody can answer “do people who build an itinerary actually use it during the trip?” The OST devolves into an opinion tree — the loudest voice wins prioritization.
  • GOOD (job-aligned taxonomy): Events are named for progress in the job “plan a trip I’ll actually follow”: trip_created, itinerary_day_planned, ai_suggestion_kept vs ai_suggestion_replaced (a trust signal, mirroring the assumption on the OST), itinerary_opened_during_trip_dates, offline_map_saved. The funnel matches the traveler’s mental model — Dream → Plan → Book → Travel — not the screen graph. The dashboard shows input metrics (day-planned rate, offline-save rate) leading the north star (trips where the itinerary was opened on ≥2 travel days). Session replay is used ethically: opt-in disclosed in plain language, payment and passport fields masked at the SDK level, and replays watched only for sessions where users hit the “Something went wrong” state. When ai_suggestion_replaced runs at 68% for restaurant picks, the team pairs the quant signal with five interviews — honoring the chapter’s closing symmetry: without instrumentation, OSTs are opinion trees; without research, dashboards are cargo cult. The interviews reveal the assistant ignores stated budget and walking distance; after suggestions honor both, ai_suggestion_replaced for restaurants falls to 41% within a month, and the north star — trips where the itinerary was opened on ≥2 travel days — climbs from 46% to 58% across the next two monthly cohorts.

Why this works: Because events map to jobs and outcomes, every claim on the OST can be checked against evidence, the diagnostic signal (replacement rate) led to a fix whose effect showed up in the north star, and the qual/quant pairing keeps the dashboard from becoming cargo cult.

Section 4.11 — Competitive Teardown and Support as Product Surface

Example 21 — Competitive Teardown

Definition (per this chapter): Structured learning comparing jobs served, activation paths, pricing consent, accessibility posture, and differentiation — not screenshot galleries of UI trends.

Scenario — “Keyhaven,” a password manager, tears down two competitors before its 2026 planning cycle.

  • BAD (inspiration theater): A 40-slide deck of competitor screenshots titled “Loving their new gradient onboarding! Let’s clone the passkey animation.” No comparison of jobs; the team copies UI chrome from a product serving a different segment.
  • GOOD (structured teardown): One comparison table, filled by actually running each competitor’s flows end to end:
Dimension Competitor A Competitor B Keyhaven today
Jobs served “Never lose family logins” (shared vaults strong) “Pass the audit” (enterprise policy engine) Solo power users
Activation path Imports from browser in 2 min; first autofill < 10 min Requires IT deploy; user sees value only after admin setup Manual CSV import, 27-min median to first autofill
Pricing consent Clear tiers; cancel self-serve Renewal terms buried in MSA; users complain publicly Clear, but trial-end email missing
Accessibility posture VoiceOver-labeled autofill; WCAG statement published Keyboard traps in admin console Untested with assistive tech
Differentiation gap Weak offline access on mobile No family/prosumer story Opportunity: offline-first vault + family sharing

The strategic questions get answered in the chapter’s terms: Competitor A owns the family opportunity; Competitor B is mismatched with the prosumer users Keyhaven can serve. The teardown feeds two OST opportunities (browser import to cut activation time; offline-first family vaults) — and an inclusion action item (assistive-tech audit) that is sequenced before the differentiation bet.

Why this works: The teardown compared jobs, activation, pricing consent, and accessibility posture to find opportunities competitors own or neglect — strategic input, not the anti-pattern of cloning UI without comparing jobs.

Example 22 — Support as Product Surface

Definition (per this chapter): Tickets, chat transcripts, and help centers reveal discovery gold and design debt; reducing contact drivers by fixing the product is strategy — deflecting with unreadable FAQs is not efficiency.

Scenario — “Roomsync,” a smart-thermostat and home-energy app.

  • BAD (call-center problem): Support volume rises 30% after a firmware update; leadership responds by adding a deflection chatbot that answers “Why is my schedule not running?” with a link to a 3,000-word FAQ written for installers. Contacts per 1,000 users stay flat; CSAT drops to 61%; the product team never hears any of it.
  • GOOD (product truth, loop closed): A monthly contact-driver review pipes coded ticket themes straight into discovery:
    1. Top driver (23% of tickets): “Schedule didn’t run” — transcript mining shows users don’t realize the thermostat keeps running its last synced schedule when home Wi-Fi drops, and the app shows nothing. This becomes an OST opportunity — owner: the core-app trio — under the outcome “cut schedule-confusion contacts 50%.”
    2. The fix is in the product, not the FAQ: a status line — “Offline since 2:14 PM — running your last saved schedule. Changes will apply when it reconnects.” — plus a queued-changes state (“2 changes waiting to sync”).
    3. The help center is rewritten to match the user’s words (“thermostat ignoring schedule,” the top search phrase) instead of the firmware team’s (“scheduler daemon persistence”).

Two months post-ship: schedule-related contacts down 57%, and the support team’s coding taxonomy now shares IDs with the OST so every quarter’s top contact reasons become opportunities with owners.

Why this works: The team treated support volume as product truth — closing the loop from top contact reasons to OST opportunities with owners — and fixed the user’s mental model of the offline state (model/recovery before delight) rather than deflecting with unreadable FAQs.

End of Chapter 04 worked examples. Coverage: 22 examples spanning all eleven numbered sections and all sixteen Key Terms.

Chapter 05 Worked Examples — Design Systems and Craft at Scale

This companion document turns every teachable concept in Chapter 5 into a worked example set in a plausible modern product (2024–2026 era: mobile-first, AI-assisted, offline-capable, privacy-conscious). Each example gives a one-line definition anchored to the chapter’s usage, a concrete scenario with real UI copy, states, flows, and numbers, a BAD vs GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Examples honor the book’s priority hierarchy — safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight — throughout.
