§5.1 Why Design Systems Exist

Example 1 — Design System as Shared Language

Definition (per this chapter): A design system is not a component library with a logo; it is the shared language, constraints, and delivery mechanisms that let many teams build coherent experiences without reinventing interaction grammar on every screen.

Scenario. Brightledger, a small-business banking app, has 11 product squads. In Q1 2025 an internal audit finds the predictable craft failures the chapter lists: the “Pay now” button exists in 7 visual variants diverging by 2–4 px of padding; “secondary” means a gray outline in Billing but a blue text link in Onboarding; dark mode was painted onto only 61% of screens; the empty Invoices table shows a blank white rectangle; and the loading spinner bounces decoratively for 400 ms even when data arrives in 80 ms.

The systems team does not respond by shipping “more components.” They ship a contract:

  • One interaction grammar: every destructive action (e.g., “Cancel this transfer”) uses the same confirmation anatomy, everywhere.
  • One vocabulary: tone="critical" means the same thing in Billing and Onboarding.
  • One delivery mechanism: tokens and components ship as versioned packages with release notes, so the fix reaches all 11 squads without 11 separate rewrites.

Six months later the audit rerun shows button variants down from 7 to 1, dark-mode coverage at 98%, and every table with a designed empty state (“No invoices yet. Create your first invoice to get paid faster.”).

BAD: The systems team publishes a Figma file named “Brightledger DS v2 ✨” with 340 components and announces it in Slack. Nothing constrains the squads; divergence continues at the same rate, now with a logo.

GOOD: The team ships fewer components but with constraints (lint rules that flag raw hex values), shared language (documented meaning of critical, neutral, success), and delivery (npm package + Figma library published in lockstep).

Why this works: It makes the right choice the easy choice — the chapter’s definition of a healthy system — instead of mistaking a component inventory for a system.

Example 2 — Content as Interface

Definition (per this chapter): Labels, helper text, errors, and empty states are not afterthoughts pasted onto chrome; they are first-class parts of the interaction model, specified alongside components.

Scenario. MyBenefits, a state government benefits portal, redesigns its document-upload flow for SNAP renewals. The old flow surfaced schema names and dead-end errors. The content team now owns error anatomy as a system asset: every error must answer what / why / next, in the user’s language, at a 6th-grade reading level, translated into the state’s top 5 languages.

BAD (before):
- Field label: “Doc_Type_Cd”
- Error: “Upload failed. Error 422.”
- Empty state: a blank list.

GOOD (after):
- Field label: “What kind of document is this?” with helper text “For example: a pay stub or a letter from your employer.”
- Error: “We couldn’t read this file. The photo is too blurry to verify. Take a new photo in good light, or upload a PDF instead.” — what, why, next.
- Empty state: “You haven’t uploaded any documents yet. You’ll need 2 documents to finish your renewal: proof of income and proof of address. Start with proof of income →“
- Privacy as a system rule, not per-screen judgment: the sensitive-data display pattern masks identifiers by default (SSN renders “•••-••-6789 Show”, and “Show” auto-remasks after 30 seconds — designed for shared and over-the-shoulder devices like library kiosks), and consent copy is a specified content slot on every upload component: “We use this document only to verify your income for this renewal. We don’t share it with other agencies.”

Call-center contacts about upload failures drop 34% in the first quarter, and renewal completion on mobile rises from 58% to 71%.

Why this works: The system owns the contract between intent and presentation — content is part of the interaction model, so recovery (model/recovery in the priority hierarchy) is designed, not improvised, and plain-language multilingual copy serves inclusion before polish.

§5.2 Atomic Composition and Semantic Tokens

Example 3 — Atomic Composition (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Building UI from layered, reusable units — tokens → primitives → patterns → kits — with clear ownership, so that the blast radius of change stays small.

Scenario. Loomcart, an e-commerce platform, wants a “compact density” refresh for its merchant admin before the 2025 holiday rush: sellers reviewing hundreds of orders want more rows per screen. Because the admin was built atomically, the change is three token edits, not a rewrite:

  1. space.stack.md drops from 16px to 12px in the new density=compact context.
  2. type.body.size gains a compact variant (14px → 13px).
  3. control.height.md drops from 40px to 32px — with a documented exception: touch targets on mobile stay ≥ 44px regardless of density mode.

Every card, table row, and form built from primitives inherits the change. The team ships density mode to 100% of the admin in 9 days, touching 3 token files and 0 product screens.

BAD contrast: A competitor’s admin has spacing hard-coded per screen; their density project is a 4-month migration across 212 screens, and 31 screens ship half-compact, half-comfortable.

Why this works: Composition is not a style preference; it is how you keep change blast radius small — exactly the chapter’s argument that if spacing, color, and type are tokens, a density refresh does not require rewriting every card.

Example 4 — Semantic Token (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): A design decision named by role or meaning (color.text.critical) rather than raw value (red-600), so consumers depend on meaning that survives rebrands, theming, and dark mode.

Scenario. Carelink, a home-health nursing app, flags overdue medication doses. The mobile team originally styled the overdue badge with the palette token red.600. In the 2025 rebrand, red shifts toward the new brand coral — and suddenly the “overdue dose” badge fails contrast on the white card background (3.2:1) while marketing surfaces look great.

The systems team restructures:

Layer Token Value
Core / palette red.50 / red.300 / red.600 / red.700 / red.950 ramp #FEF3F2 / #FDA29B / #D92D20 / #B42318 / #55160C (foundation authors only)
Semantic color.text.critical maps to red.700 on light, red.300 on dark
Semantic color.bg.critical.subtle maps to red.50 light / red.950 dark

App code may reference only the semantic layer; a lint rule fails CI on any red.* import in product packages. The overdue badge becomes color.text.critical on color.bg.critical.subtle, and the contract “critical text meets 4.5:1 in every theme” is tested in CI across both themes.

The third layer — component tokens (rare; prefer semantic). The chapter’s token table includes a component layer (button.bg.primary), and Carelink’s review bar for it is explicit. One request is approved: button.bg.critical.pressed, because the critical button’s pressed state needs a darkening step that no existing semantic role names — pinning it as a component token keeps the exception documented, owned, and themeable. A second request, badge.bg.overdue, is rejected in review: it merely restates color.bg.critical.subtle under a component-specific alias, and every needless component token is one more value a rebrand must chase. The docs rule: “Reach for a component token only when a component needs a value no semantic role can name; otherwise prefer semantic.”

BAD: <Badge className="text-red-600">Dose overdue</Badge> — paint, not meaning; breaks on rebrand and in dark mode.

GOOD: <Badge tone="critical">Dose overdue</Badge> — the badge resolves critical through semantic tokens per theme.

Why this works: Semantics survive rebrands, theming, and dark mode because consumers depend on meaning — “meaning before paint” — and in a medication-safety context, the guaranteed-contrast critical role is a safety property, not a style preference.

Example 5 — Theming and Dark Mode as Token Remaps

Definition (per this chapter): Themes and dark mode are token remaps, not alternate component trees; if dark mode requires forked markup, the system has leaked presentation into structure.

Scenario. Inkwell, a reading and annotation app, supports four themes: Light, Dark, Sepia, and High Contrast (added for low-vision readers — inclusion before delight). Each theme is a single JSON remap of ~180 semantic tokens; components never branch on theme.

Before shipping the Sepia palette change in March 2025, the team runs the chapter’s pre-ship checks under every theme:

  • Contrast: automated check on all text.*/bg.* pairs — Sepia initially fails on text.subtle over bg.surface.raised (3.9:1); the ramp is adjusted to hit 4.6:1.
  • Elevation: dark mode can’t rely on shadows alone, so elevation.raised remaps to a lighter surface tint (bg.surface.raised = +6% lightness) instead of a forked “dark card” component.
  • Focus rings: border.focus remaps to a 2px #99C2FF ring on dark so keyboard focus never disappears against dark surfaces.

BAD: A <CardDark> component maintained in parallel with <Card>; six months later CardDark is missing the new “shared with team” footer, and dark-mode users see stale UI. Dark mode has become “inverted colors,” the anti-pattern the chapter names.

GOOD: One <Card>; the theme provider swaps token maps; a visual-regression suite renders 42 key screens × 4 themes on every palette PR.

Why this works: Testing contrast, elevation, and focus rings under every theme before shipping a palette change is exactly the chapter’s bar, and one component tree keeps structure free of leaked presentation.

§5.3 Layers: Foundation → Primitives → Patterns → Kits

Example 6 — Foundation Layer

Definition (per this chapter): The foundation holds motion curves, duration tokens, type, color semantics, elevation, grid, iconography rules, content voice, and accessibility baselines — motion and content included, not bolted on later.

Scenario. Slateboard, a collaborative whiteboard tool, writes its foundation as testable rules, not a mood board:

  • Motion: duration.fast = 120ms (hover/press feedback), duration.moderate = 240ms (panel open/close), duration.slow = 400ms (cross-screen continuity) — each with a documented “when to use” rule, because a duration token without a “when to use” rule is decoration. Rule excerpt: “Use duration.moderate with easing.exit when a surface leaves the screen; never animate board content while a collaborator is drawing.”
  • Content voice: “Confident, never blaming. Errors name the system as the actor: ‘We couldn’t sync your board,’ never ‘You lost connection.’”
  • Accessibility baseline: all interactive elements reachable by keyboard; focus order documented per pattern; prefers-reduced-motion swaps movement for a 120ms opacity fade — defined once at the foundation so every component above inherits it.

BAD: The v1 foundation published duration.slow = 400ms with no when-to-use rule; within a quarter a squad had chained two of them (plus a delay) into a 900ms ornamental “board loaded” flourish that ran on every open and taught nothing — a duration token without a rule is decoration, exactly as the chapter warns.

GOOD: Every duration token ships with its when-to-use rule and a named owner, so the flourish is caught at review against the rule, not by taste.

Why this works: Motion and content live in the foundation with owners and rules — the chapter’s point that they are foundations, “not ‘nice-to-haves’ bolted onto components later.”

Example 7 — Primitive (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Primitives (buttons, inputs, checkboxes, links, icons, tooltips) are intentionally boring; their job is predictable behavior, complete states, and airtight APIs.

Scenario. Deployo, a CI/CD dashboard for developers, specs its <Button> primitive with zero cleverness and total coverage:

  • States: default, hover, focus-visible (2px offset ring, visible in all themes), active/pressed, disabled, loading (spinner replaces icon slot, label stays visible, width locked so the layout doesn’t jump). The chapter’s remaining minimum states — error, empty, read-only, selected — are recorded in the state-matrix doc as not applicable for a non-toggle action button (it holds no value to be invalid or empty, and no persistent selection), so the omission is a documented decision, not a gap.
  • API: variant="primary" | "secondary" | "ghost", tone="neutral" | "critical", isLoading, iconStart, iconEnd. No className passthrough for colors.
  • Behavior guarantees: while isLoading, the button sets aria-disabled="true" and swallows duplicate clicks — so “Deploy to production” can never fire twice from a double-click.

A product engineer requests a “gradient CTA button with confetti on success” for the upgrade page. The systems team declines to add it to the primitive: gradient stays in a marketing-page kit; confetti is evaluated against the motion foundation (it delays nothing, runs 600ms, honors reduced motion) and ships as an opt-in success affordance at the pattern level.

Why this works: The primitive stays predictable and boring — the double-fire guard is model/recovery insurance on a high-stakes action — while expressiveness is pushed to higher layers where it belongs.

Example 8 — Pattern (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Patterns compose primitives and encode workflow wisdom — form layouts, filter bars, confirmation dialogs, data tables with selection, progressive disclosure.

Scenario. Loomcart’s “destructive confirmation” pattern encodes hard-won wisdom so no team relearns it in production:

  1. Trigger: any action tagged severity="destructive" (delete product, cancel order batch, revoke API key).
  2. Dialog anatomy: title states the consequence, not the action (“Delete 14 products? This can’t be undone.”), body names the scope (“14 products and their 214 photos will be removed from your store”), the confirm button carries tone="critical" and repeats the verb (“Delete 14 products”), never “OK.”
  3. High-severity variant: revoking a live API key requires typing the key’s name (“Type storefront-prod to confirm”).
  4. Focus lands on Cancel by default; Esc cancels; the confirm is never the Enter-key default.
  5. Recovery: where the backend supports it, the pattern prefers undo over confirmation — “14 products deleted. Undo (9s)” — and the docs say when to use which.

BAD: Team A ships a native confirm("Are you sure?"); Team B ships a modal whose primary button is “OK” and takes Enter-key focus — a warehouse manager deletes a product batch by hitting Enter on autopilot.

GOOD: Both teams consume <ConfirmDestructive>; the interaction is identical in Catalog and Orders.

Why this works: The pattern layer is where workflow wisdom lives once, and this one puts safety first and recovery (undo) ahead of interrogation, per the book’s priority hierarchy.

Example 9 — Kit (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Kits are domain assemblies for recurring product surfaces — “settings page shell,” “checkout summary,” “admin user row” — that accelerate teams without pretending every product is identical.

Scenario. Freightwise, a logistics SaaS, ships a “Settings Page Shell” kit after noticing 6 squads each hand-built settings pages with different nav placement, save behavior, and unsaved-changes handling. The kit assembles patterns and primitives into a domain-level starting point:

  • Left-rail section nav with the shared landmark structure (consistent <nav aria-label="Settings sections">).
  • A sticky save bar that appears on dirty state: “You have unsaved changes — Save / Discard”, with a navigation guard dialog if the user tries to leave.
  • Slots for domain content: sections, dangerZone (which auto-applies the destructive-confirmation pattern from Example 8).

Adoption is opt-in with escape valves: the Fleet team’s live vehicle-telemetry settings page doesn’t fit the shell’s form-centric model, so they compose from patterns directly — documented as a legitimate deviation, not a silent fork. New settings pages now ship in ~3 days instead of ~2 weeks.

Why this works: Kits accelerate the common case while explicitly not pretending every product is identical — the chapter’s exact framing of what the top layer is for.

Example 10 — Layer Boundaries and Ownership

Definition (per this chapter): Healthy systems make layer boundaries explicit; crossing layers carelessly — kits that fork primitives, patterns that hard-code hex values, foundations no one owns — creates zombie systems.

Scenario. Studyhall, an ed-tech platform, institutes review gates per layer after an audit finds a “Quiz Kit” containing its own forked <QuizButton> (copied from <Button> 14 months earlier, missing the focus-ring fix that shipped 9 months ago) and a card pattern with background: #F7F5FF hard-coded.

The fix is organizational as much as technical:

  • Each layer gets a named owner: foundation (2 engineers + 1 content designer), primitives (core team), patterns (core + rotating product contributors), kits (product squads with core review).
  • CI gates per layer: kits may import patterns and primitives, never fork them; patterns may reference only semantic tokens (a lint rule fails on raw hex); foundation changes require a11y sign-off.
  • The forked <QuizButton> is deleted via codemod; the hex value becomes color.bg.brand.subtle.

Why this works: Layer ownership and review gates matter as much as Figma libraries — the chapter’s warning that careless layer-crossing is how living systems start turning zombie.

§5.4 Consistency Versus Flexibility

Example 11 — Strict Consistency

Definition (per this chapter): Constrain hard where cognition is shared across the product: focus behavior, form validation timing, destructive action confirmation, navigation landmarks, error anatomy, table keyboard models.

Scenario. Brightledger discovers its two money-movement teams solved “the same user job” incompatibly: in Transfers, form validation fires on blur; in Bill Pay, it fires on every keystroke, so users see “Routing number must be 9 digits” in red after typing one digit. Same job, incompatible interaction models — by the chapter’s practical rule, the system under-specified the pattern.

The system now specifies validation timing as a strict, non-overridable rule:

  • Validate on blur for format errors; re-validate on change only after a field has been marked invalid (reward early, punish late).
  • Error anatomy is fixed: icon + color.text.critical message below the field, aria-describedby wired, focus moved to the first invalid field on submit.
  • Navigation landmarks are fixed product-wide: every page exposes exactly one <header> banner, one <nav aria-label="Main">, and one <main>; secondary navigation always renders as <nav aria-label="In this section">; the skip link is always the first focusable element and always reads “Skip to main content.” A screen-reader user who learns “jump to Main navigation” in Transfers can rely on it, verbatim, in Bill Pay.
  • Keyboard model for all data tables is one spec: arrow keys move cells, Space selects a row, Shift+Space extends, Ctrl/Cmd+A selects all in view.

Teams cannot opt out; the props to change timing simply don’t exist on <FormField>.

Why this works: Consistency reduces cognitive load exactly where users transfer habits between surfaces — and uniform validation and error anatomy is recovery design (model/recovery) applied at system scale.

Example 12 — Guided Flexibility

Definition (per this chapter): Extend where jobs differ: page composition, illustration style within brand bounds, optional pattern variants, density modes, locale-specific content length.

Scenario. MyBenefits serves both a citizen-facing portal and a caseworker console. An early mandate forced both onto the same “form page kit”: max-width 640px, one question per screen. Citizens loved it (completion +12%); caseworkers, who process 60 cases a day on 27-inch monitors, hated it — the system had over-specified the kit for teams solving different jobs.

The revised guidance:

  • Fixed for everyone: error anatomy, focus behavior, destructive confirmations, navigation landmarks (Example 11’s list).
  • Flexible within guardrails: page composition (caseworkers get a two-pane review layout; citizens keep one-question-per-screen), density (comfortable default for citizens, compact available for the console), and locale content length — Spanish labels run ~25% longer, so button and label slots must reflow rather than truncate, verified with pseudo-locale testing ("Ŝúbmít réñéwáł one two").
  • Illustration style varies by audience within brand bounds: warm spot illustrations for citizens, none in the console.

Why this works: The system constrains where cognition is shared and extends where jobs differ — “consistency where cognition is shared; flexibility where jobs differ” — so it is neither a prison nor a suggestion box.

§5.5 State Completeness and Component APIs

Example 13 — State Completeness (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Explicit design and implementation of all meaningful interactive and data states; incomplete matrices become production bugs.

Scenario. Carelink’s visit-schedule table serves nurses in rural areas with patchy connectivity — so the data-bound state list from the chapter is not academic. The team builds the full matrix before shipping:

State Designed behavior + UI copy
Skeleton/loading 6 shimmer rows matching final layout (no layout jump)
Zero results “No visits scheduled today. Your next visit is tomorrow at 9:00 AM.”
Partial failure Loaded visits render; banner: “2 of 14 visits couldn’t load. Retry“
Offline Cached data shown with badge “Offline — showing your schedule as of 7:42 AM”; edits queue with “Will sync when you’re back online”
Permission denied “You don’t have access to Ward B schedules. Ask your coordinator to add you.”
Error “We couldn’t load your schedule. Check your connection and try again.”
Selected / bulk Row checkboxes; sticky bar “3 visits selected — Reassign / Cancel visits“
Read-only Past visits lock with “Completed” chip; no edit affordances rendered

The offline row is the safety case: a nurse must never see an empty schedule (and skip a home visit) merely because the request failed — the matrix forces the distinction between “zero results,” “offline with cache,” and “error.”

BAD: The v1 table showed the zero-results illustration for any failed fetch. During a regional outage, 40+ nurses saw “No visits scheduled today” and two missed visits were reported.

GOOD: Every fetch resolves to a named state; the QA checklist enumerates all eight and the component won’t ship without designs for each.

Why this works: “Complete states or do not ship” — missing empty/error/loading distinctions here are not polish gaps but safety defects, the top of the priority hierarchy.

Example 14 — Component APIs Express Intent

Definition (per this chapter): Component APIs should express intent, not CSS trivia; API design is UX design for engineers, and breaking prop changes are treated like breaking changes to user-facing flows.

Scenario. Deployo redesigns its <TextField> API after an internal survey shows engineers averaging 25 minutes to build a compliant form field with the old primitive.

BAD (old API):

<TextField className="input-red" label={false}>
  <span class="lbl">API token</span>
  {err && <div className="err-txt">{err}</div>}
</TextField>

Undocumented children conventions, color-by-className, no a11y wiring — every consumer hand-rolls aria-describedby, and 4 of 9 audited forms had errors screen readers never announced.

GOOD (new API):

<TextField
  label="API token"
  helpText="Find this under Settings → Access. We never store it in plaintext."
  errorMessage={error}   // presence sets tone=critical + aria-invalid + aria-describedby
  isRequired
  value={token}
  onChange={setToken}     // controlled; uncontrolled via defaultValue is documented
/>

Content slots (label, helpText, errorMessage) are named and required-or-explicitly-omitted; accessibility wiring is automatic; controlled vs uncontrolled is explicit. Defaults, aria-* hooks, and composition rules (“TextField may not wrap another form control”) are documented on the docs site.

When the team later renames helpText → description, they treat it as a breaking change: major version bump, deprecation warning for two minors, and a codemod — because breaking props break products.

Why this works: The API encodes intent and accessibility by default, making the right choice the easy choice for the system’s other user group: engineers.

Example 15 — Forms and Tables Deserve Library-Level Investment

Definition (per this chapter): Forms and tables concentrate density, validation, sorting, selection, bulk actions, and keyboard complexity; a system that only ships buttons will fragment fastest where users spend the most time.

Scenario. Freightwise’s ops users spend 70%+ of session time in tables (shipments, invoices, driver rosters). Yet the v1 system shipped 42 polished primitives and zero table pattern — so the audit finds five ad-hoc table implementations: three different sort-arrow behaviors, two incompatible bulk-action bars, and one table where Ctrl+A selected the page’s entire DOM text.

The systems team reallocates a full quarter to a <DataTable> pattern:

  • Sorting, column resize/reorder, sticky headers, virtualized rows (tested to 50,000 shipments).
  • Selection + bulk actions bar (“128 shipments selected — Assign driver / Export CSV / Cancel”), with select-all-across-pages made explicit: “All 128 on this page selected. Select all 3,204 matching shipments”.
  • One keyboard model (the strict spec from Example 11) and screen-reader row/column announcements.
  • The full data-bound state matrix from Example 13, inherited by contract.

Adoption is tracked: 5 forks → 1 pattern in two quarters; table-related a11y defects drop from 19 open to 3.

Why this works: Investment lands where density, complexity, and user time concentrate — the chapter’s warning that leaving tables to tribal knowledge fragments the system fastest exactly where the outcomes are.

§5.6 Content, Motion, and Docs as Product

(Content as interface is exemplified in Example 2, which serves both §5.1 and §5.6.)

Example 16 — Motion as Foundation

Definition (per this chapter): Purposeful transitions serve continuity (shared-element navigation), feedback (press, success), and orientation (panel open); ornamental bounce that delays task completion is banned, and reduced-motion alternatives are first-class.

Scenario. Nightreel, a mobile streaming app, audits its motion against the three purposes:

  • Continuity: tapping a poster expands it into the detail page as a shared element (duration.slow, 400ms) so users track which title they opened in a dense grid.
  • Feedback: the “Download for offline” button shows a press scale (98%, 120ms) and, on completion, the download icon draws a checkmark (240ms) — confirmation without a toast.
  • Orientation: the episode drawer slides up from the bottom edge it will dismiss toward, teaching the gesture.

The audit also removes delight-first violations: a 900ms logo bounce on every app open (pure delay — cut to 0 on warm start) and a “confetti” burst that played over the Continue watching row and blocked taps for 700ms.

Reduced motion is designed, not defaulted: with prefers-reduced-motion, the shared-element expand becomes a 120ms cross-fade, the drawer appears in place with a fade, and the checkmark draws instantly — every motion spec in the foundation carries a “reduced” column, reviewed in the same PR.

Why this works: Motion earns its place through continuity, feedback, and orientation; inclusion (reduced-motion as first-class) and outcomes (no task-delaying ornament) outrank delight, per the hierarchy.

Example 17 — Docs-as-Product (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Documentation is a shipped, versioned experience with the same quality bar as components — live examples, do/don’t, accessibility notes, content guidelines, migration guides, changelogs.

Scenario. Slateboard’s system docs were “a Notion page last edited 14 months ago plus a Slack channel” — folklore, in the chapter’s word. The team rebuilds docs as a product with its own backlog, owner, and release process. Each component page now ships:

  • Live examples: editable sandboxes for every state in the matrix, including offline and partial-failure.
  • Do/Don’t: “✅ Do: use tone='critical' only for destructive or blocking situations. ❌ Don’t: use critical tone for validation warnings a user can proceed past.”
  • Accessibility notes: keyboard map, screen-reader behavior, focus order, and which aria-* wiring is automatic.
  • Content guidelines: button-label voice (“verb first: ‘Invite teammates,’ never ‘Submit’”), error anatomy (what/why/next).
  • Migration guides + versioned changelog: “Migrating Dialog v3 → v4: onClose → onOpenChange; run npx slate-codemod dialog-v4.”

Docs freshness is measured (see Example 22): any page untouched 2 releases after its component changed is flagged “stale” in the docs header, and stale-page count is on the team dashboard (currently 4 of 61 pages).

BAD: The only truth about Dialog focus-trapping lives in a 2024 Slack thread with 47 replies, three of which contradict each other.

GOOD: The Dialog docs page is the contract; the Slack channel’s pinned message says “If the docs are wrong, that’s a bug — file it.”

Why this works: If the only truth lives in a Slack thread, you have folklore, not a system — docs shipped and versioned like components are what make the system’s contract enforceable.

Example 18 — Figma↔Code Parity (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): Alignment of names, tokens, states, and APIs across design and engineering sources of truth — an operational goal you measure, not a slogan.

Scenario. Brightledger discovers drift the expensive way: a designer specs a Button size=xl that exists only in Figma; engineering “approximates” it, and three approximations ship. The systems team institutes a parity operation:

  • Source-of-truth agreement (written down): tokens and behavior live in code; exploration lives in Figma. Figma component and variant names must match code props exactly — the Figma component is Button with variant, tone, size, isLoading — same words, same casing.
  • Token export pipeline: semantic tokens export from the code repo to Figma variables nightly; designers never hand-pick hex values.
  • Parity measured quarterly: mismatched props (Figma variants with no code prop, and vice versa), missing states (Figma has hover/focus/pressed; does code? does Figma have loading and error, which code has?), divergent spacing (rendered component screenshots diffed against Figma frames). Baseline audit: 23 mismatched props, 11 missing states, 9 spacing divergences. Two quarters later: 3 / 1 / 2.

BAD: The Figma library proudly shows a Banner with a “dismissing” animation state the code never implemented — designers keep specing it, engineers keep silently dropping it (the chapter’s anti-pattern: Figma states code does not implement).

GOOD: The parity audit flags Banner.dismissing; the RFC process (Example 19) decides to implement it in code rather than delete it from Figma, and the audit’s mismatch count is the team’s north-star chart.

Why this works: Parity is treated operationally — shared naming, pipelines, and measured drift — which is precisely how the chapter says design–engineering drift is prevented.

§5.7 Contribution, RFCs, and Versioning

Example 19 — Contribution Model and RFCs

Definition (per this chapter): A system without a contribution model ossifies or forks; the typical path is proposal → RFC (problem, options, migration cost, a11y impact) → prototype → review → release notes → adoption metrics.

Scenario. A Carelink product squad needs a “medication timeline” visualization that doesn’t exist in the system. Instead of forking, they follow the contribution path:

  1. Proposal (30 min): a lightweight issue — “Nurses need to see dose history and upcoming doses on one axis; nothing in the system fits.”
  2. RFC (1 page): Problem: three squads have adjacent needs (medication, vitals, visits). Options: (a) new Timeline pattern; (b) extend DataTable with a timeline view; (c) squad-local component. Migration cost: option (a) lets Vitals squad delete 1,400 lines of custom D3. A11y impact: timelines are canvas-hostile; the RFC commits to a table-equivalent view for screen readers and full keyboard traversal of events.
  3. Prototype: built in a branch, tested with 2 nurses and 1 screen-reader user.
  4. Review: foundation owner checks token usage; a11y reviewer checks the table-equivalent; content designer reviews event labels (“Missed — 8:00 AM dose” not “MISSED_DOSE_EVT”).
  5. Release notes: ships in system v7.3 with docs, do/don’t, and a migration note for the Vitals squad.
  6. Adoption metrics: 3 squads adopted within two sprints; escape-hatch CSS in timeline surfaces drops to zero.

Median contribution latency (proposal → release) is tracked at 6 weeks; the previous ad-hoc process averaged “never” (teams just forked).

BAD: That is exactly how the Vitals squad’s 1,400 lines of custom D3 came to exist: a year earlier, with no contribution path advertised, they built squad-local — no keyboard traversal, no screen-reader equivalent, a hex-coded axis color that broke in dark mode. The chapter’s warning made concrete: a system without a contribution model ossifies or forks, and this one forked.

GOOD: The published proposal → RFC → prototype → review → release path makes contributing cheaper than forking — and retires the Vitals fork as part of the Timeline release.

Why this works: The RFC path converts a would-be fork into shared system capability — contribution and versioning treated as part of the product, exactly as the chapter and Principle 5 demand.

Example 20 — Versioning and Deprecation

Definition (per this chapter): Versioning should be semantic and honest; deprecations need timelines, codemods when possible, and dual-running guidance.

Scenario. Deployo’s system team must replace <Modal> (focus-trapping bugs, no nested support) with a new <Dialog>. The honest-versioning playbook:

  • v6.2 (minor): <Dialog> ships alongside <Modal>. <Modal> logs a dev-only deprecation warning: “Modal is deprecated and will be removed in v8 (est. May 2026). Migrate with npx deployo-codemod modal-to-dialog. See migration guide.”
  • Codemod: handles the 80% mechanical cases (prop renames, children → slots); the guide documents the 20% needing human judgment (nested modals, custom focus logic).
  • Dual-running guidance: “Both components may coexist during migration; do not nest a Modal inside a Dialog; z-index tokens guarantee correct stacking either way.”
  • Timeline honored: v7 keeps <Modal> (warning only); v8, released 11 months after the deprecation notice, removes it. Release notes list every breaking change with a before/after snippet.
  • Honesty rule: any prop removal or behavior change — including the helpText→description rename from Example 14 — is a major, never smuggled into a patch. The team’s changelog literally has a section titled “Breaking (we mean it).”

BAD: Publishing the removal as v7.4.1 “because it’s a small change,” breaking 14 product builds on a Friday.

Why this works: Breaking changes to props break products, so they are handled like breaking changes to user-facing flows — with warning, tooling, timeline, and truthful semver.

Example 21 — Gen-UI Constrained to the System

Definition (per this chapter): AI-assisted layout and generated UI must be constrained to the system — allowed components, tokenized styles, validated props, banned arbitrary CSS — or generation recreates pre-system chaos at machine speed.

Scenario. Freightwise ships “Build a view,” an AI assistant that generates internal dashboard pages from prompts like “Show me late shipments by carrier with a weekly trend.” The guardrails:

  • Allowed-component manifest: the model can emit only PageShell, StatCard, DataTable, Chart, FilterBar, EmptyState — a JSON schema of system components and their validated props. Output is schema-checked before render; invalid props are rejected, not “best-effort rendered.”
  • Tokenized styles only: the generation schema has no style or className field at all — spacing and color exist only as semantic choices (tone, density), so the model cannot emit #FF0000 or margin: 13px.
  • States by contract: because generated views compose real system components, every generated table arrives with loading, zero-results, partial-failure, and permission-denied states for free.
  • Human-visible provenance: generated pages carry a header chip “Generated view — Review before sharing” and enter the normal review flow before becoming team-wide dashboards.

In the first month, the validator rejects 8.2% of raw model outputs (mostly invented props like <StatCard color="red">); rejected outputs are regenerated against the schema rather than patched with one-off CSS.

BAD: A rival tool lets its model emit raw HTML+CSS; within weeks it has produced 5 new button styles, hex-coded “critical” reds that fail contrast in dark mode, and tables with no empty states — pre-system chaos at machine speed.

Why this works: “Constrain generation — Gen-UI must consume the system, not bypass it”: the schema makes the system the model’s only vocabulary, so scale of generation multiplies coherence instead of chaos.

§5.8 Health Metrics and Zombie Systems

Example 22 — System Health Metrics

Definition (per this chapter): Track adoption (% of surfaces on current major), contribution latency, documentation freshness, a11y defect rate on system components, theme coverage, and escape-hatch frequency — not vanity component counts.

Scenario. Studyhall’s design system team replaces its old slide (“We now have 178 components! 📈”) with a quarterly health dashboard:

Signal Q1 2025 Q3 2025 Target
Adoption: % of surfaces on current major (v9) 54% 81% ≥85%
Contribution latency (proposal → release, median) 11 wks 5 wks ≤6 wks
Docs freshness (pages stale > 2 releases) 17 4 0
A11y defect rate on system components (open, P0–P2) 12 3 0 P0/P1
Theme coverage (screens passing all 3 themes) 66% 94% 100%
Escape-hatch frequency (!important + one-off CSS + forked components, per 1k LOC) 6.1 1.9 <1.5

Escape hatches are counted by a repo-wide scanner; each hit files a tracked “escape” with a reason field. The most instructive finding: 40% of escapes clustered around date-pickers — a signal that the system was missing a needed pattern, not that teams were undisciplined. The team ships DatePicker via the RFC path, and date-related escapes drop to near zero.

BAD: Celebrating component count while adoption falls — the chapter’s named anti-pattern (“counting components as health while adoption falls”).

Why this works: “Measure health — adoption, escapes, and doc freshness beat vanity component counts,” and reading escape hatches as demand signals turns policing into product discovery.

Example 23 — Zombie System (Key Term)

Definition (per this chapter): A design system that appears alive — website, Figma library — but versions lag years, teams fork silently, docs contradict code, there is no RFC path, dark mode is broken, and nobody owns tokens; kill or revive deliberately, because neglect is the most expensive option.

Scenario. An insurance company’s “Cornerstone” design system checks every zombie box in a 2025 diagnosis:

  • The docs site is up (last deploy: 22 months ago) and shows a Select API that was rewritten twice since — docs contradict code.
  • 3 of 9 product teams are on v4; the current major is v6; one team froze on v3 in 2023.
  • A repo search finds 5 forked buttons, including ButtonNew2FinalFix.
  • Dark mode fails contrast on 30+ screens; the last token owner left the company 14 months ago; token PRs sit unreviewed for 60+ days.
  • There is no RFC path — the contribution page says “Message #design-system,” a channel archived last year.

Leadership makes the chapter’s deliberate choice rather than continuing neglect. They score two options: kill (declare v6 end-of-life, adopt an open-source base like Radix-plus-tokens, migrate over 3 quarters) versus revive (staff 4 people, re-establish token ownership, freeze new components for a quarter, fix the top-10 adoption blockers, restore the RFC path). Because 81% of product surfaces still consume some Cornerstone code, revival is cheaper; they fund it with explicit success criteria tied to Example 22’s dashboard: adoption of the current major back above 70% within 3 quarters, an owner-of-record for every token file, zero docs pages contradicting shipped APIs — or the kill plan executes.

BAD: The status quo: keep the website up, keep linking new hires to it, let every team quietly fork — paying the zombie tax forever.

GOOD: A dated decision memo: “Revive with these criteria by Q2 2026, else kill” — either outcome is deliberate.

Why this works: The chapter’s closing warning is that neglect is the most expensive option — a zombie is killed or revived deliberately, with the same health metrics used to prove which one happened.

End of Chapter 05 worked examples. Concepts covered: 23 examples spanning all eight numbered sections and all seven Key Terms (duplicates merged: content as interface serves §5.1 and §5.6; atomic composition, semantic token, primitive/pattern/kit, state completeness, docs-as-product, Figma↔code parity, and zombie system each covered once at their home section).

Chapter 05B Worked Examples — Visual Craft, Information Architecture, and Prototyping

This companion applies every concept from Chapter 5B to concrete 2024–2026 product situations: mobile-first, AI-assisted, offline-capable, privacy-conscious. Each example gives a one-line definition anchored to the chapter, a realistic scenario with actual UI copy and numbers, a BAD → GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Examples honor the book’s priority hierarchy — safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight.
