Section 6.1 — Content Is a Trust Surface

Example 1 — Content Is a Trust Surface

Definition (per this chapter): Every string is a promise — labels promise outcomes, errors promise honesty, consent copy promises control — so content is interface behavior expressed in language, not “writing for UI.”

Scenario. Drafthouse, a 2025 offline-capable collaborative notes app, lets field researchers edit while disconnected and syncs when a connection returns. On a spotty train connection, a user edits 6 blocks; 4 sync, 2 fail because an attached 40 MB video exceeds the offline upload queue limit.

BAD (the promise-breaking version). The app shows the generic success toast:

“Saved!”

Two hours later the user opens the note on her laptop and the two blocks are missing. She now distrusts every “Saved!” the app has ever shown — the vague success toast after partial failure destroyed trust faster than a clear error would have.

GOOD (the honest version). The toast reflects reality and names the state:

“4 of 6 changes synced. 2 waiting — video attachment is over the offline limit (25 MB). View pending changes“

The note header carries a persistent Pending sync (2) chip (state name: partially-synced), announced to screen readers via a polite live region so the honesty is inclusive, not visual-only. Tapping the chip lists exactly which blocks are queued and offers “Retry on Wi-Fi” or “Remove attachment.”

After shipping the honest state, Drafthouse’s “where did my edits go?” support contact rate dropped from 3.1% to 0.4% of offline sessions.

Why this works: It treats the success toast as a promise the interface must be able to keep — precision, timing, and respect are what users infer trustworthiness from, and a clear partial-failure message beats a false “Saved!” (§6.1), putting model/recovery ahead of the delight of a clean green toast.

Example 2 — Microcopy System

Definition (per this chapter): A microcopy system aligns voice, vocabulary, and patterns — how you name objects, speak about time, refer to the user, handle nulls, and announce irreversible actions — as reusable content patterns, like visual tokens.

Scenario. Relay CI, a developer-tools platform, audits its product in 2024.

BAD (the pre-audit screens, verbatim). Three screens, one object, three stories:

Dashboard card: “Workflow #211 — last run 3d“
Runs list: “job chain payments-pipeline · Jul 11“
History panel: “Pipeline updated 3 days ago — status: —”
Deletion dialog: “Are you sure? [OK] [Cancel]”

The same object is a “workflow,” a “job chain,” and a “pipeline”; the same moment is “3d,” “Jul 11,” and “3 days ago”; a null renders as a bare “—”; and a permanent deletion is confirmed with a contentless “Are you sure?” A user cannot build one mental model from four dialects.

GOOD (the shipped microcopy system). The content designer ships a microcopy system alongside the component library:

  • Object vocabulary: the runnable unit is always “pipeline”; a single execution is always “run.” A lint rule flags any other term in UI strings.
  • Time pattern: relative under 7 days (“3 days ago”), absolute after (“Jul 11, 2025”), always with a full timestamp in the tooltip.
  • Null pattern: never a bare “—”; nulls read “Not run yet” or “No owner assigned,” matching the empty-state templates.
  • Irreversible-action pattern: a confirmation slot with fixed anatomy — consequence first, object named, verb-matched button: “Deleting payments-pipeline removes its 214 run logs. This can’t be undone. [Cancel] [Delete pipeline]” — never a bare “OK.”
  • Error anatomy slot: every error component reserves fields for what / why / next plus a reference ID (see Ex. 3), so pattern reuse is structural, not aspirational.
  • Tone-by-stakes pattern (Principle 3: tone follows stakes). The system encodes the chapter’s tonal rule as two registers for the same product voice. Exploration, where warmth belongs: the first-run empty state reads “No pipelines yet — create your first and we’ll walk you through a run.” Security and loss, where clarity belongs: the deletion confirm above stays deliberately clinical — no “Oops!”, no softeners, consequence stated flat. The written rule: if a message concerns security, money, or irreversible loss, strip the warmth and state the consequence.

The system lives in the same repo as the design tokens; PRs adding UI strings get a content review checklist. Post-rollout, task-failure comprehension in usability tests rose from 61% to 89% (“I know what a failed run means now”).

Why this works: Like visual tokens, content patterns become reusable infrastructure — error anatomy, empty-state templates, confirmations — so voice and vocabulary stay aligned across the whole surface instead of being rewritten per screen (§6.1).

Section 6.2 — Error Message Craft: What / Why / Next

Example 3 — What / Why / Next (with validation vs. system errors, preserved input, and reference IDs)

Definition (per this chapter): The what / why / next pattern names the failure in user terms, gives a usable cause when known, and provides a recovery action — with a stable reference ID for supportability that is never the headline.

Scenario. Ledgerly, a small-business payments app, lets an owner send an invoice to a customer. Two distinct failures occur in testing.

BAD (the anti-pattern, both failures identical).

“Something went wrong. Error 0x4F221.”

The user’s typed line items are also cleared on reload. The internal code is the only message; the user can’t tell whether she can fix it or must wait; her input is gone.

GOOD — Failure A is a validation error (user can fix now). Inline, attached to the email field, because inline errors belong to fields:

What: “We couldn’t send your invoice.”
Why: “The customer’s email address is missing an @ — ‘mara.chen.gmail.com’.”
Next: “Edit email” (button focuses the field, input preserved).

BAD (the triple-echo variant, cut in review). An earlier build rendered this one validation failure three ways at once:

Inline, under the field: “Invalid email format.”
Toast, bottom-left: “Couldn’t send — please check your input.”
Page banner, top: “Submission failed. Correct the errors below.”

Three places, three wordings, one mistake — the user can’t tell whether there are one problem or three, and the chapter forbids duplicating the same error in three places with three wordings. The shipped GOOD version renders the inline message only, because inline errors belong to fields.

GOOD — Failure B is a system error (we must fix or retry). Page-level, because page-level errors belong to submissions and server failures:

What: “We couldn’t send your invoice.”
Why: “Our email service isn’t responding right now — this isn’t something you did.”
Next: “Your invoice is saved as a draft. Try again, or contact support with reference ID 8F2A if it keeps failing.”

The reference ID sits in the last line in smaller type — present for supportability, never the headline. The draft (all 14 line items) is preserved automatically. Ledgerly’s metric: first-contact resolution for send failures rose 34% once agents could pull logs by reference ID instead of asking users to describe the error.

Why this works: It answers all three questions — what happened, why, next — while distinguishing validation errors from system errors, never blaming the user for a system fault and never hiding a user mistake behind “Something went wrong” (§6.2).

Section 6.3 — Empty States as Teaching

Example 4 — Empty States as Teaching (four causes, four designs)

Definition (per this chapter): An empty state is onboarding for a moment of non-data — it explains what will appear and why it matters, offers a primary action, and differs by cause.

Scenario. Stallfront, an e-commerce seller dashboard, has one “Reviews” screen that can be empty for four different reasons. In 2024 all four rendered the same sad-box illustration with “Nothing here yet.” Sellers with a permissions problem filed bug reports; sellers with filters applied created duplicate listings. The redesign gives each cause its own named state:

  1. empty-never-used (new seller, zero reviews ever):

    “Customer reviews will appear here after your first delivered order. Buyers read reviews before purchasing, so your earliest ones matter most. Share your store link“
    A “How reviews work” help link sits below the action, only after the action path is clear. An earlier draft embedded a conversion statistic in the copy itself (“listings with 5+ reviews sell 2.3× more”); the content review cut it — an unsourced persuasion number inside an empty state shifts the tone from teaching the model toward growth pressure, and it is a promise Stallfront cannot keep for any individual seller.

  2. empty-filtered-to-zero (seller filtered to “1-star, last 7 days”):

    “No reviews match these filters. Clear filters · Adjust date range”
    The primary action is adjust filters, deliberately not “Share your store link” — pushing “create new” here would teach the wrong model (that no reviews exist at all).

  3. empty-no-permission (warehouse-staff role):

    “Reviews are visible to Owner and Marketing roles. Your role: Fulfillment. Request access from Dana (Owner)“
    It explains access without implying the feature is broken.

  4. error-disguised-as-empty (reviews API timed out) — the trap the chapter warns about. Instead of rendering the blank state, Stallfront shows:

    “We couldn’t load your reviews right now. Retry — or check status.stallfront.com”

After the split, “reviews are broken” tickets fell 71%, and new-seller store-link shares from the empty state rose 18%.

Why this works: Each cause gets its own teaching, action, and model — never used vs. filtered to zero vs. no permission vs. error disguised as empty — so the empty state teaches instead of apologizing for existing (§6.3, Principle 2).

Section 6.4 — Conversation Design and Auth/Recovery UX

Example 5 — Conversation Design

Definition (per this chapter): Conversation design applies when a product interacts in turns — one job per turn, confirm critical interpretations, allow repair, keep context visible — and conversational UI must surface system components for actions, not freeform traps.

Scenario. Meridian Air ships an AI-assisted rebooking assistant in its 2025 app. A passenger types: “my flight got cancelled, get me home tonight.”

BAD (the anti-pattern turn).

Bot: “Sure! What’s your booking reference, full name, date of birth, and the password on your account?”

Four jobs in one turn, and it collects a password in freeform chat — exactly the transcript trap the chapter forbids. If the bot mishears “tonight” as “tomorrow night,” there is no repair path, and when the flow stalls there is no human exit.

GOOD (the redesigned flow).

  1. Context kept visible: the assistant already knows the signed-in user and pins a context card at the top of the chat: MER-4471 · SEA → DEN · Cancelled.
  2. One job per turn: “I found 3 flights arriving in Denver tonight. Want me to show them?”
  3. Confirm critical interpretation: “Just to confirm — rebook tonight, Jul 14, not tomorrow? [Yes, tonight] [No, tomorrow]” — confirmation as buttons, a design-system component, not parsed prose.
  4. Secure input via system components: the $32 fare-difference payment opens the platform’s secure payment sheet. The bot never asks for card numbers or passwords in the chat transcript.
  5. Repair: the user types “wait, actually the 9pm one” after selecting 7pm; the assistant treats it as a correction — “Switched to the 9:05 PM departure. Confirm?” — instead of erroring.
  6. Escape to human is never buried: a persistent “Talk to an agent” button sits beside the message composer on every turn — deliberately not in an overflow menu, which would be the buried escape hatch the chapter’s anti-pattern list forbids. After two failed interpretations the assistant proactively offers it with the transcript attached (see Ex. 11).

Rebooking completion in-assistant hit 64%, and — the trust metric — zero credentials appear in stored transcripts.

The same principles outside chat (§6.4’s transfer claim). The chapter says these principles transfer to modal wizards and multi-step forms, and Meridian Air proves it in its non-conversational seat-change wizard — a four-step modal form. One job per step: flight → seat → payment → review. Confirm the critical interpretation: the review step states the consequence in words, not just a summary table — “You’re moving to seat 14C on the 9:05 PM departure, not your original 7:00 PM flight. [Confirm change] [Back].” Keep context visible: the stepper (Flight · Seat · Payment · Review) persists on every screen. Allow repair: Back never wipes entered data. A wizard is a conversation with the turns laid out as steps.

Why this works: Turn-taking discipline plus system components for confirm buttons and secure inputs keeps the conversation efficient without becoming a freeform trap that collects secrets in chat transcripts (§6.4).

Example 6 — Auth/Recovery UX and the Dead-End Exit

Definition (per this chapter): Authentication and recovery are trust crucibles: clear recovery paths with time expectations, honest MFA benefits and backup codes, work-saving timeout warnings, enumeration-safe copy — and a designed dead-end exit to human support.

Scenario. GovFile, a state tax-filing portal, redesigns sign-in and recovery before the April 2026 filing peak.

BAD (the pre-redesign screens).

Reset form: “No account found for that email.”
MFA nag: “Secure your account now!” [Set up] — no skip, no explanation.
Minute 15: silent sign-out; the half-finished return is gone.

The reset copy confirms exactly which emails are registered — account enumeration handed to attackers. The MFA nag states no benefit and offers no choice. The silent timeout destroys an hour of work. And when recovery stalls, the flow loops back to the same reset form forever — no human anywhere.

GOOD (the redesigned states).

  • Enumeration-safe reset that still feels helpful. “If an account exists for m.osei@…, you’ll get a reset link within 5 minutes. Didn’t get it? Check spam, or try another way.” The copy doesn’t leak whether the email exists, and the time expectation (“within 5 minutes”) is explicit.
  • Wrong password vs. account locked, within security policy. Because policy forbids revealing lock state to unauthenticated visitors, GovFile pairs the security constraint with a support path instead of a dead end: “That password didn’t work. If you’ve tried several times, your account may be temporarily protected — verify your identity another way or call 1-800-555-0164 (avg. wait 4 min).” One maintenance caveat the team wrote into the content system: the wait figure is injected live from the call-center queue and is suppressed whenever that feed is stale — every string is a promise, so GovFile quotes a wait time only while the system can actually keep it current.
  • Honest MFA enrollment. “Add a second step so a stolen password alone can’t reach your tax records. Takes ~2 minutes. You’ll get 10 backup codes — save them; they’re how you get in if you lose your phone. [Set up] [Not now]”
  • Session timeout that saves work. At minute 13 of a 15-minute session: “You’ll be signed out in 2 minutes for your security. Your return is saved through Step 4 of 6. [Stay signed in]” The warning is a focusable dialog announced to assistive tech, and the draft really is saved — the copy promises only what the system does.
  • The dead-end exit. When automated recovery stalls (no access to the old email and lost phone), the flow does not loop. Screen recovery-exhausted reads: “We can’t verify you automatically. A specialist can — schedule an ID-verification call (next slot: today 3:40 PM) or visit a field office. Your case number: RC-20817.” Recovery abandonment fell from 22% to 9% after the exit shipped.

Why this works: Each state pairs the security constraint with honesty and a path forward, and the flow is designed so users can always find human help after automated paths stall — the dead-end exit the chapter requires (§6.4), with safety outranking conversion.

Section 6.5 — Privacy Consent and Data Rights

Example 7 — Just-in-Time Consent

Definition (per this chapter): Just-in-time consent asks for a permission at the moment a feature needs it, with a plain-language purpose — informed choice at the moment of relevance, not a checkbox maze.

Scenario. Susurra, a 2025 respiratory-health app, offers an AI cough-analysis feature that needs the microphone.

BAD (the launch-day wall). First app open, before any feature is touched, a stacked modal: “Susurra needs Microphone, Motion, Notifications, and Location to give you the best experience. [Allow all]” No purposes, four permissions bundled, and the OS prompt fires with zero context — 68% deny microphone, and the flagship feature is dead on arrival.

GOOD (the just-in-time redesign). No permission is requested at onboarding. When the user taps “Check my cough,” a pre-permission screen appears at the exact moment of relevance:

“Use your microphone to record a 10-second cough sample. The recording is analyzed on your device; it’s uploaded only if you choose to share it with your care team. [Continue] [Not now]”

Only after “Continue” does the OS microphone prompt appear. “Not now” is a first-class equal-weight button, and the feature card remains available to try later — declining is not punished. Notifications are asked for separately, at their moment of relevance (after the first result: “Want a reminder to re-test in 7 days?”).

Microphone grant rate: 91% at the moment of need, versus 32% in the launch-wall variant of the A/B test.

Why this works: The permission arrives when the feature needs it, with a plain-language purpose the user can weigh — the chapter’s “Use your camera to scan the warranty card” pattern applied to a health context — making consent informed choice at the moment of relevance (§6.5, Key Term).

Example 8 — Data Rights, Retention in Human Terms, and Dark-Pattern Avoidance

Definition (per this chapter): Privacy UX separates necessary processing from optional analytics, makes data-rights entry points (export, delete, correct, download) findable without legal scavenger hunts, shows retention in human terms, and avoids dark patterns — because the product, not the policy page, is the ongoing ability to understand and control.

Scenario. Vireo, a video-streaming service, rebuilds its consent and privacy surfaces for a 2025 EU launch.

BAD (the dark-pattern original).

“We value your privacy! 🎉 [Accept all and enjoy]”
Pre-checked: ☑ “Personalized ads” ☑ “Partner marketing emails” — bundled with the necessary account processing. The reject path is a grey “Manage 47 options” link opening a per-vendor toggle maze. Deleting an account requires emailing legal@vireo.tv. Retention is described as “as long as necessary for legitimate business purposes.”

Every element is a named anti-pattern: pre-checked marketing consent, bundling necessary with optional, impossible-to-find reject, guilt-adjacent celebration framing.

GOOD (the redesign).

  • Unbundled, equal-weight choice: “Vireo needs your watch history to stream and resume playback — that’s required to run the service. Separately: may we use viewing patterns to improve recommendations? [Yes, help improve] [No] — both buttons identical in size and color. Nothing is pre-checked. You can change this anytime in Privacy Center.”
  • Findable data rights: Settings → Privacy Center, one tap from the profile screen, with four verbs as buttons: Download my data (“ready within 24 hours, we’ll email you”), Delete my account, Correct my details, Export watch history (CSV). No legal scavenger hunt; the policy page is linked but is not the mechanism.
  • Retention in human terms: “We keep your watch history while your account is active. Voice-search recordings are deleted after 30 days. Deleted accounts are fully erased within 28 days.”
  • No guilt language: declining recommendations analytics produces “Okay — recommendations will be based only on what’s trending,” not “Are you sure you want a worse experience?”

Post-launch: 41% opt in to analytics — lower than the dark-pattern baseline’s 88%, but complaint volume to the DPA dropped to zero and 30-day churn among decliners fell 12%, because control itself retains.

Why this works: Necessary and optional processing are never bundled, rejection costs the same effort as acceptance, and rights are product features — the ongoing ability to understand and control, not a policy wall (§6.5), trading short-term outcomes for durable trust exactly as the priority hierarchy demands.

Section 6.6 — Warning Severity Ladder

Example 9 — Severity Ladder

Definition (per this chapter): A calibrated info → success → warning → critical → emergency messaging scale, matched to irreversibility and blast radius — not to engineering log level.

Scenario. Quarry is a database-administration console for developers.

BAD (everything is red). Quarry once rendered every backend event as a red banner: a deprecation notice, a successful backup, and a pending table drop all looked identical. Users developed banner blindness and one engineer clicked through a red banner that was, that day, an actual production drop — accidental destruction caused by overused critical styling.

GOOD (mapped to the ladder). The 2025 redesign maps messages to the ladder:

Severity Quarry event Pattern and copy
Info Driver v2 deprecation timeline Quiet inline note in the connection panel: “The v1 driver retires in March 2026. Migration guide →”
Success Nightly backup completed Brief dismissible toast: “Backup complete — 4.2 GB, 02:14 AM.” Gone in 5 s.
Warning Query will scan 90M rows on the primary Clear consequence + confirm: “This query scans ~90M rows on the production primary and may slow live traffic for ~2 min. [Run anyway] [Run on replica]”
Critical DROP TABLE orders on production Blocking modal, high visibility: “You’re about to permanently delete orders (2.1M rows) on production. This can’t be undone. Type the table name to confirm.”
Emergency Credential leak detected in a public repo Not a banner at all — a dedicated flow (per §6.7): forced interstitial on next load, key auto-revoked, email + status page coordinated.

A key calibration call: a failed staging backup logs as ERROR in engineering telemetry but surfaces as a warning, not critical — small blast radius, fully recoverable. Severity follows irreversibility and blast radius, not log level. Twelve months in: accidental production drops fell from 7 to 0, and warning-banner dismissal-without-reading dropped from 83% to 31% — a drop the team reports with a caveat, since a same-quarter onboarding revamp likely contributed and the two effects were never separated.

Why this works: Reserving critical styling for irreversible or harmful outcomes keeps attention calibrated — overuse creates banner blindness, underuse creates accidental destruction (§6.6, Principle 5).

Section 6.7 — Breach Notification and Trust Repair

Example 10 — Breach Notification and Trust Repair

Definition (per this chapter): Breach notification is a moral and regulatory duty expressed as UX: state what was exposed, what you’re doing, what users should do, how to get help, and be honest about the timeline — across coordinated channels — then keep repairing trust after the notice.

Scenario. Parcelmade, a handmade-goods marketplace, discovers on March 3, 2026 that an attacker accessed a support-system database covering 210,000 buyers.

BAD (the anti-pattern email). Subject: “An important update from the Parcelmade family 💌”. Three paragraphs about the brand’s commitment to craftsmanship, then: “Out of an abundance of caution, we’re writing about a security incident involving certain data. We take your privacy seriously. Please remain calm.” No scope, no actions, a 15% discount code at the bottom — breach notice buried in marketing style, demanding calm while withholding scope, plus opportunistic upsell.

GOOD (the coordinated notification). Subject: “Security incident: what was exposed and what to do.”

  • What was exposed: names, email addresses, and order histories from support conversations (Jan 2024–Feb 2026). Not exposed: passwords, and full card numbers — we never store them.
  • What we’re doing: we closed the access within 4 hours of detection on March 3, revoked the compromised vendor credential, and hired an external forensics firm. We’re publishing findings as we confirm them.
  • What you should do: be wary of emails pretending to be Parcelmade support that reference your real orders. You don’t need to reset your password (passwords weren’t exposed) and you don’t need to freeze credit — card data wasn’t taken. (Only relevant actions — no reflexive “reset everything.”)
  • Get help: dedicated line 1-888-555-0142 and security.parcelmade.com/incident — support macros are updated so agents tell the same story.
  • Timeline honesty: “We detected this March 3 and are notifying you March 5. Investigation is ongoing; we’ll email again by March 19 either way.”

The in-app banner, the email, and agent scripts all state the same scope — omnichannel object continuity for the incident itself, the incident being the shared object. Trust repair continues after the notice: the status page gets dated updates; when forensics finds phone numbers were also exposed, a follow-up correction goes out within 48 hours (“We said phone numbers were safe. We were wrong — here’s what changed”); and marketing automation is suppressed for the notified cohort for 60 days — no opportunistic upsell. Churn in the notified cohort ran 2.1% versus 9.8% in a benchmarked competitor breach with a marketing-style notice.

Why this works: Scope in categories not jargon, only relevant protective actions, honest timelines, coordinated channels, and repair that outlasts the announcement — incidents deserve product UX, not only legal email (§6.7, Principle 7), with user safety placed above brand outcomes.

Section 6.8 — Support Handoff and Omnichannel Continuity

Example 11 — Support Handoff

Definition (per this chapter): Support handoff is the transfer of context and ownership across people or channels without forcing repetition — capture context before transfer, pass the transcript or summary, keep the case ID visible, and say what happens next.

Scenario. Northline Fiber, a home-internet provider, hands off from its AI chat assistant to a human agent, and later to a phone callback.

BAD (the restart-the-story version). After 12 minutes describing an outage to the chatbot, the user reaches a human whose first message is “Hi! How can I help you today?” The transcript is discarded; the agent asks for the account number the user is literally signed in with — support asking for information the product already has. When chat escalates to phone, a new ticket number is issued and the story restarts a third time.

GOOD (the designed handoff).

  1. Capture context before transfer. The assistant assembles a structured handoff packet: product area (home-internet / connectivity), modem model and last three diagnostic results (sync loss 4:12 PM, 4:40 PM, 5:15 PM), last error shown to the user (ERR-DSL-1102), steps already tried (modem restart ×2, line test passed), and case ID NF-88213.
  2. Pass the summary. The human agent’s console opens with a 4-line summary plus the full transcript collapsed beneath it. Their first message proves it: “Hi Maya — I can see your connection has dropped three times since 4 PM and you’ve already restarted the modem twice, so let’s not do that again. I’m checking the line to your node now.”
  3. Same case ID across channels. When the agent schedules a phone callback from engineering, the user sees: “Case NF-88213 — an engineer will call you between 9–11 AM tomorrow. Everything we’ve covered travels with the case.” The engineer’s script opens with the same packet.
  4. What happens next, and when. Every transfer ends with an explicit expectation, never a silent queue.

Repeat-explanation complaints dropped 64%; average handle time on escalated calls fell 3.5 minutes because agents stopped re-collecting known facts.

Why this works: Context and ownership move together so users never restart the story at handoff (§6.8, Principle 6, and the anti-pattern list: support must not ask for information the product already has).

Example 12 — Object Continuity (Omnichannel Object Continuity)

Definition (per this chapter): Object continuity is the stable identity of a user’s goal or object — order, ticket, claim, return — across touchpoints, so the user’s mental model of “my return” survives channel switches.

Scenario. Moss & Marrow, an e-commerce furniture brand, handles a damaged-chair return that will cross four channels over nine days.

BAD (the fragmented version). The app shows “Return #R-2291: Processing.” The confirmation email references “RMA 0058817-B.” The carrier’s pickup text mentions only a tracking code. When the customer calls, the agent asks, “Do you have your order number?” — a different ID again — and the app still says “Processing” three days after the email said “Refund issued.” Three IDs, two contradictory statuses: the customer’s mental model of “my return” has been shattered into per-channel fragments, and she calls twice “just to check,” at $11 per contact.

GOOD (one object, many windows). The return is a single service object, Return R-2291, and every channel is a window onto it:

  • App: a return card with named states — pickup-scheduled → in-transit → received-at-warehouse → refund-issued — currently “Pickup scheduled: Thu Jul 16, 12–4 PM.”
  • Email: subject “Return R-2291: pickup scheduled Thu Jul 16” — same ID, same state, same date, generated from the same status source the app reads.
  • Carrier SMS: “Moss & Marrow return R-2291: driver arriving ~1:20 PM.”
  • Phone: the IVR reads the caller’s number, matches the open return, and opens with: “Calling about your chair return, R-2291? It was received at our warehouse this morning; your refund of $412.50 is processing and lands in 3–5 business days.” No re-identification interrogation.

Backstage (see Ex. 13), this requires one canonical status field that all channel templates consume — the service-design work that makes continuity operational. “Where is my return?” contacts fell 47%.

Why this works: The user’s object keeps one name, one state, and one story everywhere, so the mental model of “my return” survives every channel switch — omnichannel object continuity made operational by service design rather than promised by copy (§6.8, Key Term).

Section 6.9 — Service Blueprints Lite

Example 13 — Service Blueprint Lite

Definition (per this chapter): A condensed five-layer map — user steps, visible staff/product actions, backstage systems, support evidence, and failure points with recovery UX — whose job is to reveal seams before customers find them.

Scenario. Hearthview, a smart-home camera company, blueprints one journey the chapter recommends mapping: consent withdrawal — a user revoking cloud video analysis (an AI feature) while keeping local recording.

BAD (the un-blueprinted service). Before anyone mapped the journey end to end, every seam in row 5 below was live in production: the control was findable only via search, the confirm screamed critical-red for a reversible choice, the email said “immediately” while the app said 30 days, the ML pipeline kept analyzing for up to 6 hours after “off,” and agents couldn’t see deletion status — so a user who withdrew consent met a contradiction at every step, and no single team owned the whole picture.

GOOD (the one-page lite blueprint). The team builds the lite blueprint in a 90-minute workshop on one page:

Layer Step 1: Find the control Step 2: Withdraw consent Step 3: Confirmation Step 4: Data deletion Step 5: Later support call
1. User steps (frontstage) Opens Privacy Center → “Cloud video analysis” Taps “Turn off,” reads consequence Sees “Analysis off. Local recording continues.” Expects old analysis clips deleted Calls: “Am I really off?”
2. Visible staff/product actions Toggle with plain-language purpose copy Warning-severity confirm (not critical — it’s reversible): “You’ll lose person alerts. Recordings stay on your hub.” Email receipt: “Cloud analysis off as of Jul 14. Stored analysis data deletes within 30 days.” Progress note in Privacy Center: “Deletion completes by Aug 13” Agent confirms, reads deletion status aloud
3. Backstage systems Consent flag in identity service Flag write → ML pipeline unsubscribe queue Email service template (same status source as app) 30-day deletion job across ML store + backups CRM shows consent-flag history
4. Support evidence (what agents see) — — Case timeline shows withdrawal event + timestamp Deletion-job status field visible to agents Agent screen shows “Analysis: OFF since Jul 14 · Deletion: 62% complete”
5. Failure points & recovery UX ⚠ F1: Control findable only via search (legal scavenger hunt) → add to Settings top level ⚠ F2: Confirm previously styled critical/red → recalibrated to warning per severity ladder ⚠ F3: Email said “immediately,” app said “30 days” — two status stories → single source ⚠ F4: Queue lag left flag ON in ML for up to 6 h → SLA + “processing” state shown honestly ⚠ F5: Agents couldn’t see deletion status → users repeated themselves; new evidence field added

The blueprint surfaced five seams — a findability failure, a severity miscalibration, an object-continuity break between channels, a backstage lag masked by dishonest copy, and a support-evidence gap — in one workshop, before a regulator or a Reddit thread found them. Three were fixed in the next sprint; F4’s honest “processing (up to 6 hours)” state shipped instead of a false instant “Done.”

Why this works: Five layers on one page are enough to mark where content, privacy, and handoff break — the lite blueprint’s job is to reveal seams before customers find them, without the weight of a full service blueprint (§6.9, Key Term).

How These Examples Honor the Priority Hierarchy

Safety leads: enumeration-safe recovery copy (Ex. 6), secure inputs instead of chat-transcript traps (Ex. 5), breach scope honesty (Ex. 10). Model and recovery come next: what / why / next with preserved input (Ex. 3), honest partial-sync states (Ex. 1), dead-end exits to humans (Ex. 6). Inclusion runs throughout: live-region announcements (Ex. 1), focusable timeout dialogs (Ex. 6), plain language over legalese (Ex. 8). Outcomes follow — grant rates, contact deflection, churn — and are reported after the trust work, never as its justification for cutting corners (Ex. 8 explicitly accepts a lower opt-in rate). Systems thinking appears as reusable patterns (Ex. 2), single status sources (Ex. 12), and blueprints (Ex. 13). Delight is last and quietest: a warm store-link nudge in an empty state (Ex. 4) — never a celebration emoji on a consent wall (Ex. 8’s anti-pattern) or a heart in a breach subject line (Ex. 10’s anti-pattern).

Chapter 07 Worked Examples — Research Methods and Evidence

This companion applies every concept in Chapter 7 — each of its ten sections (referenced by exact title, since the chapter’s sections are unnumbered) and every Key Term — to concrete product situations from the 2024–2026 era: mobile-first, AI-assisted, offline-capable, privacy-conscious. Each example follows the same format: a one-line definition anchored to the chapter’s usage, a realistic scenario with actual UI copy, states, flows, and numbers, a BAD vs GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Products vary deliberately — fintech, health, gov services, collaboration tools, e-commerce, media, developer tools — so no single scenario carries the chapter. Throughout, examples honor the book’s priority hierarchy: safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight.

Contextual Inquiry: Work Where Work Happens

Example 1 — Contextual Inquiry

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Apprenticeship-style observation and interview in the participant’s real environment — the participant demonstrates the job while you ask clarifying questions at the moment of action.

Scenario — “VistaCare,” a mobile charting app for home-health nurses. The team is redesigning wound-documentation. Instead of a lab session, researcher Dana rides along with nurse Priya for two visits in a rural county.

What Dana observes that no lab could produce:

  • Priya’s phone drops to one signal bar in the patient’s basement apartment. The app shows the state “Saving locally — will sync when you’re back online”, but Priya doesn’t trust it: she also photographs the wound with the native camera app “in case VistaCare eats it.” A workaround signaling a broken recovery model.
  • A social constraint: the patient’s son is in the room, so Priya angles the screen away before opening the “Wound stage: 3 — deteriorating” field. Privacy of the screen is part of the job.
  • An artifact within arm’s reach: a paper index card taped inside Priya’s kit lid listing supply codes, because the in-app picker takes 9 taps. Dana photographs it (with consent).
  • An interruption: mid-entry, the agency dispatcher calls; when Priya returns, the app has timed out to the login screen and discarded 4 minutes of charting — a safety-relevant data-loss failure, ranked above any workflow-speed finding in the report.

Dana asks apprentice-style questions at the moment of action (“You just took a second photo outside the app — walk me through why, right now”) rather than in a debrief when memory has smoothed over friction.

BAD version (the lab illusion): The team invites five nurses to a quiet office, hands them a fully charged phone on office Wi-Fi, and asks them to “chart a sample wound.” Everyone completes the task; the report says documentation is “largely usable.” The offline distrust, the shoulder-surfing son, the timeout data loss, and the index card never appear — the team designs for a fiction.

GOOD version: Two ride-alongs per region across urban/rural, sampling the connectivity, interruptions, and social conditions the job actually depends on; artifacts photographed; findings ranked safety first (timeout data loss), then model/recovery (sync distrust), then outcomes (9-tap picker).

Why this works: It observes the job in context before optimizing the interface, and samples the conditions — connectivity, noise, colleagues, device switching — the chapter warns you must sample or design for a fiction.

Story-Based Interviews

Example 2 — Story-Based Interview

Definition: An interview structured around specific past episodes — anchored on time, place, people, and outcome — rather than general preferences or “how you usually…” abstractions.

Scenario — “Remitly-class” cross-border money transfer app. The team suspects first-time senders abandon at identity verification. Researcher Malik interviews eight recent sign-ups.

BAD interview (abstraction harvesting):

Malik: “How do you feel about identity verification in finance apps?”
Participant: “I like it when it’s simple and secure.”

Weak evidence — an abstraction preference, exactly what the chapter says bad interviews produce.

GOOD interview (episode elicitation):

Malik: “Tell me about the last time you actually sent money to family. Where were you, what day, what happened?”
Amara: “Two Fridays ago, on my lunch break — my mother’s rent was due that Friday — standing outside because the staff room has no signal. I got to the step that said ‘Scan the front of your ID’ — but my national ID is laminated and the glare kept failing. It said ‘We couldn’t read your document. Try again.’ three times. My break ended. That night my cousin sent it from her account instead. Honestly, I was embarrassed asking her.”

The sequence maps cleanly to the chapter’s structure: trigger (“rent was due that Friday”) → attempt (lunch-break signup) → obstacle (glare on laminated ID, 3 failures) → workaround (cousin’s account — a compliance and safety concern the team escalates first) → emotional residue (“embarrassed asking her”) → next attempt (none; churned).

Malik then probes for exceptions: “What was different the time it did work?” Amara: “My cousin did it at night, indoors, and her phone let her upload a photo from the gallery instead of live-scanning.” The exception reveals the real requirement: an upload-from-gallery fallback and glare guidance, not “simpler verification.”

Across eight participants, five recount structurally similar failures (document capture in bad lighting under time pressure) — stronger evidence than any number of stated preferences.

Why this works: It prefers stories and behavior over opinions: recounted episodes with converging failure structure are strong evidence; “I like simple interfaces” is not.

Diary Studies and Cultural Probes for Time-Distributed Jobs

Example 3 — Diary Study

Definition: Longitudinal self-reporting of events as they occur (or at fixed intervals), used because the job unfolds in fragments that interviews would collapse.

Scenario — “DoseKeeper,” a medication-adherence companion for adults managing hypertension. Adherence is not a single sitting: doses happen at 7 a.m. rushes, forgotten evenings, and disrupted weekends. Interviews collapse that time; a 14-day diary preserves it.

Design of the study, per the chapter’s compliance warning:

  • Channel: one SMS prompt at each self-reported dose window plus an anytime keyword. Reply costs under 20 seconds: TAKEN, SKIPPED, or a voice note.
  • What counts as an entry (told to participants explicitly): “Any time you take, skip, delay, or almost forget a dose — the almost-forgets matter most to us.”
  • How much detail: one line on where you were and what interrupted you. No more.

BAD version (over-instrumentation): A 20-question daily Google Form covering mood, diet, sleep, and app opinions. Compliance data from a pilot: 12/14 participants complete day 1, 4/14 by day 3, 1/14 by day 7 — the exact “twenty daily questions and three days of compliance” anti-pattern the chapter names. The surviving entries are from the one hyper-organized participant, i.e., noise about the wrong user.

GOOD version results: 11/14 participants still logging on day 14 (79% compliance). The diary surfaces a timing pattern no interview found: 68% of SKIPPED entries cluster on evenings when participants were away from home (“at my daughter’s — pills are on my kitchen counter”). The team’s response respects the hierarchy: first a safety review (double-dose risk when a skipped dose is “made up”), then a recovery-friendly feature: “Away from your meds? We’ll remind you when you’re back home” (opt-in, on-device location only, never uploaded — a privacy-conscious design the consent form states plainly).

Three anomalous logs trigger follow-up calls — the diary → interview sequencing from the chapter’s “Diary vs Interview: A Decision Frame” section.

Why this works: It matches the method to the temporal shape of the job — frequency, timing, and interruption patterns were the unknowns, and diaries preserve the time that interviews collapse.

Example 4 — Probe (Cultural Probe)

Definition: A generative kit or prompt that invites participants to capture contextual artifacts — metaphors, rituals, constraints — you could not sit inside for weeks; raw material for synthesis, not finished insight.

Scenario — “ShiftBridge,” a coordination tool for families sharing elder-care across shifts. The team cannot embed in private homes for three weeks, so they mail a probe kit to nine caregiving households:

  • A disposable-style camera prompt card: “Photograph the place in the house where information about Mom’s care actually lives.”
  • A fridge-magnet map of the week with stickers: “Put a red dot wherever a handoff between caregivers felt shaky.”
  • A small notebook with one prompt per page: “Finish this sentence: handing off to my brother feels like ______.”

Returns are strange and rich, exactly as probes should be: seven of nine households photograph the refrigerator door — layered with pill schedules, a laminated “IF SHE FALLS” sheet, and Post-its in two languages. One notebook entry reads: “handing off feels like passing a sleeping baby — you don’t dare say everything out loud.” Red dots cluster on Sunday evenings, when the weekday and weekend caregivers never overlap in person.

BAD handling: The PM screenshots the fridge photos into a deck titled “Insight: users want a digital fridge door” and ships a mood-board feature. Probe returns treated as finished insights — the exact misuse the chapter forbids.

GOOD handling: The team runs two synthesis workshops treating the returns as raw material. Synthesis yields a design concept the probes only hinted at: an asynchronous “Sunday handoff note” with a mandatory safety section (“Falls, meds changes, doctor contacts”) auto-carried forward — safety information first, ritual and warmth (the sleeping-baby tenderness) expressed in tone, not features.

Why this works: Probes are generative — they surfaced the fridge-door ritual and the Sunday gap the team would never have asked about — and they were fed into synthesis rather than presented as conclusions.

Usability Testing That Earns Its Keep

Example 5 — Usability Testing

Definition: Evaluating whether people can complete representative tasks with a design under defined conditions — behavioral evidence with pre-defined success criteria, not a focus group or popularity contest.

Scenario — a state unemployment-insurance claims portal, mobile web. The team is testing a redesigned claim-status flow before release.

BAD test (leading tasks + preference theater):
- Task as narrated UI: “Tap ‘My Claims,’ then tap ‘Search,’ then enter your claim number.” Participants follow the breadcrumbs; 10/10 “succeed”; nothing is learned.
- Closing question: “Do you prefer the new design or the old one?” Eight say the new one is “cleaner.” The team ships on preference — a popularity contest, not evidence.

GOOD test:
- Task written as a goal: “You filed three weeks ago and rent is due. Find out whether your claim was paid, and if not, what’s holding it up.”
- Success criteria defined before any session: participant states payment status AND the specific pending item within 4 minutes, unassisted.
- 8 moderated sessions for diagnosis (why people fail), then 40 unmoderated remote sessions for volume and geographic spread — the moderated/unmoderated tradeoff chosen deliberately.
- Think-aloud used carefully: “Keep doing what you’d do; just tell me what you’re looking for” — so narration never becomes a second task.
- Measures: completion 9/40 (22%) against the 4-minute criterion — completers’ median time-to-success was 3m10s, while non-completers spent a median of 6m40s searching before giving up or timing out — plus severity-rated blockers. The top blocker is severity-critical: the status “Adjudication in progress” is read by 31/40 participants as “my claim was denied,” and 6 say they would stop certifying weekly — a safety-level consequence (loss of benefits), prioritized above every cosmetic finding. Rewritten copy — “We’re reviewing your claim. No action needed from you. Keep filing your weekly claim.” — was retested with a fresh 40-participant unmoderated panel recruited through the same screener, running the identical task and success criteria, and completed at 34/40 (85%) — an apples-to-apples comparison with the 22% baseline.
- Fidelity matched to the question: label comprehension was first tested on a clickable prototype; the final round runs on the production build to validate the offline/queued state — “You’re offline. Your weekly claim is saved and will submit automatically” — because edge-state recovery only shows up in production, exactly as the chapter prescribes.
- And no shortcut: the high-risk adjudication assumption was not “validated” with five agency staffers who already know the portal.

Why this works: Goal-framed tasks, pre-committed success criteria, and behavior over preference produce actionable evidence rather than preference theater — and fidelity was matched to the question being asked.

Assumption Mapping

Example 6 — Assumption Map

Definition: A prioritized inventory of the team’s beliefs about users, jobs, context, value, and feasibility, ranked by risk (how much being wrong would hurt) and ignorance (how little evidence exists).

Scenario — “ReviewPilot,” an AI code-review assistant for developer teams. Before spending any participant hours, the team writes down what it believes and scores each claim (Risk × Ignorance, each 1–5):

# Assumption Risk Ignorance Priority
A1 Developers will read AI review comments before merging, not auto-dismiss them 5 4 20 — study first
A2 Teams will allow their private repo code to be processed by our model (privacy/consent) 5 4 20 — study first
A3 A wrong AI suggestion confidently worded could be pasted into production code 5 3 15 — safety-class, high bar
A4 Junior devs benefit more than seniors 3 4 12
A5 Developers want comments in the PR, not a separate dashboard 4 2 8
A6 Dark mode matters to adoption 1 2 2 — do not research
A7 (Feasibility) The model can return review comments within 60s on PRs up to 2,000 changed lines — slower and the comments arrive after merge 4 3 12

The map deliberately spans all five claim categories from the chapter — users (A1, A4), jobs (A5), context (A2), value (A3), and feasibility (A7) — because a map of purely user/value beliefs hides the technical claims that can sink the product just as fast.

High-risk / high-ignorance items (A1, A2, A3) become the research priorities; A6 is explicitly not studied — not every belief earns fieldwork.

BAD version (research theater): The PM already wants to ship the dashboard, so the study plan is “5 interviews asking developers if they’d find AI code review useful.” Everyone says yes; the deck says “validated.” The map’s whole purpose — preventing studies that confirm what the team already wanted to ship — is defeated.

GOOD version: A1 gets a behavioral log study on a design-partner repo (do merge events follow comment-view events?); A2 gets story-based interviews with engineering managers about the last time they approved or vetoed a third-party tool touching source code; A3 gets an adversarial usability test seeding one plausible-but-wrong suggestion, with a pre-set evidence bar: “If ≥2 of 10 participants merge the wrong suggestion without edit, the confident tone ships behind a hedged-phrasing redesign.” A7, being a feasibility claim, gets engineering evidence rather than participant hours: a technical spike replaying 50 sampled design-partner PRs against the model (median 41s, p95 74s — close enough to proceed with a streaming-comments mitigation). After each study the map is revisited: A2 crosses its bar — 8 of 9 engineering managers recounted approving comparable tools once per-repo opt-in and retention terms were explicit — and is retired; A1 fails (41% of comments never viewed) and is escalated to the roadmap; A5, which no study touched this round, stays open on the map rather than being quietly assumed true.

Why this works: Ranking beliefs by risk × ignorance before fieldwork sets evidence bars in advance and forces assumptions to be retired or escalated explicitly, preventing research theater.

Triangulation: Qualitative + Quantitative

Example 7 — Triangulation

Definition: Cross-checking a claim with independent methods or data types — qualitative explaining why/how, quantitative estimating how often/how large — before making a consequential decision.

Scenario — “MeetScribe,” an AI meeting-notes tool inside a collaboration suite. Support tickets say the AI summary “misses decisions.” Is this rare grumbling or a core failure?

Three independent signals are lined up:

  1. Qualitative (story-based interviews, n=9): Seven participants recount a specific episode of re-listening to the recording because the summary omitted who committed to what. (“Last Thursday’s vendor call — the summary said ‘pricing was discussed,’ but I needed ‘Sam agreed to the 12% discount.’”)
  2. Quantitative (product analytics): 34% of sessions with a generated summary are followed within 10 minutes by the event recording_scrubbed — users going back to the source. Among sessions where users tap “Was this summary accurate?” → “Missing something”, the rate is 61%.
  3. Quantitative (support): 214 tickets in Q1 tagged summary-incomplete, 3.1× the next category.

Three independent methods, one failure mode: decision-attribution is the gap. That convergence clears the evidence bar for a roadmap change (a “Decisions & owners” extraction section, with each extracted commitment linking to its transcript timestamp so users can verify the AI rather than trust it — model/recovery before delight).

The conflict-as-information moment: A quarterly CSAT survey shows summary satisfaction at 4.2/5 — apparently contradicting everything above. The BAD move: cite the survey and ignore the inconvenient methods. The GOOD move, per the chapter: treat the conflict as information. Two deep interviews reveal what “satisfied” meant — respondents were rating transcription accuracy, because the survey question (“How satisfied are you with MeetScribe’s notes?”) never distinguished transcript from summary. Different measurement, not a real contradiction; the survey item is rewritten.

Why this works: Neither the interviews nor the analytics alone would justify a consequential roadmap decision; converging independent signals do — and the conflicting survey was interrogated as information rather than used as a vote to ignore the other methods.

Recruiting Screeners: Assistive Technology and Low Connectivity

Example 8 — Screener for Assistive Technology (AT) Participants

Definition: A screener is a filter that selects for the jobs and constraints you claim to design for; for AT participants, that means screening for actual AT use and the platform + AT combination, not merely self-identified disability.

Scenario — “NorthBank,” a mobile banking app adding an AI transaction-search feature (“Ask about your spending”). Inclusion is on the line: if screen-reader users can’t operate it, the feature ships exclusionary.

BAD screener:

“Do you have a visual impairment? ☐ Yes ☐ No”

This recruits self-identification, not constraint. It could yield participants who don’t use AT at all — and the team might then treat one Blind VoiceOver user as universal accessibility proof, the exact anti-pattern the chapter names.

GOOD screener (excerpt):

  1. “Which of the following do you use every day to operate your phone? (Select all)” — VoiceOver / TalkBack / screen magnification (specify zoom level) / voice control / switch access / captions as primary channel / none
  2. “Which phone and OS version? Which screen reader and braille display, if any?” (confirms platform + AT combination: VoiceOver + iOS 18 behaves differently from TalkBack + Android 15)
  3. “Tell us about the last time you did mobile banking with your screen reader. What happened?” (screens for the actual job under the actual constraint — and screens out professional testers whose answer sounds like a test script)
  4. Disqualifier: participated in a paid usability study in the last 6 months (authenticity matters here)
  5. Screens in an edge role: one participant who banks on behalf of a low-vision parent (a proxy user), because the job includes them.

Study logistics follow the chapter: 90-minute sessions instead of 60, compensation at 1.5× standard, and participants use their own devices and AT setups — not a lab phone with VoiceOver freshly enabled. The panel: 3 VoiceOver users, 2 TalkBack users, 2 magnification users, 1 voice-control user. The study plan names its own gaps rather than hiding them: no switch-access, captions-as-primary-channel, or braille-display participants were recruitable this round, so those constraints are logged as not yet covered and scheduled for a follow-up panel — the report never claims coverage the screener’s own option list shows is missing. The magnification cohort alone finds the release-blocking bug: the AI answer card “You spent $412 on groceries in June” renders in a fixed-height container that clips at 200% zoom.

Why this works: It recruits for the constraints that break the product — real daily AT use, specific platform combinations, longer fairly-paid sessions on the participant’s own setup — and never lets one participant stand in for all of accessibility.

Example 9 — Screener for Low-Connectivity Participants

Definition: Screening for real network conditions — prepaid data caps, shared Wi‑Fi, rural latency, intermittent offline work — so the sample includes the people whose connectivity breaks the product.

Scenario — “AgriLedger,” a field-sales and inventory app for agricultural supply reps, with offline-capable order capture and queued sync.

BAD screener:

“Ages 25–45, owns a smartphone, uses mobile apps for work.”

This recruits “people with smartphones” — urban fiber users who will never find the bug that dominates in the field.

GOOD screener (excerpt):

  1. “How do you pay for mobile data?” — prepaid bundle / capped monthly plan / unlimited (quota: ≥60% prepaid or capped)
  2. “In a typical work week, how often do you have no signal at all while trying to do your job?” — never / 1–2× / most days (quota: majority “most days”)
  3. “Tell us about the last time a work task failed because of connectivity. What were you doing, and what did you do next?” (the chapter’s “ask about last failure” — an episode, not an opinion; blank or vague answers screen out)
  4. “Do you share a Wi‑Fi connection or a device with others?” (screens in shared-device households where the job includes them)

Sessions run partly on the participants’ own networks in the field. Result: 7 of 9 participants reveal a queued-sync trust failure the office sample never hit. UI copy at fault: the badge “3 orders pending” with no timestamp. Reps can’t tell pending since 10 minutes ago from stuck since Tuesday, so they re-enter orders on paper and phone them in — duplicate orders downstream. The fix targets the users’ model and recovery before any visual polish: “3 orders waiting to send — last try 2m ago. We’ll keep retrying; nothing is lost.” plus a manual “Sync now” affordance. Duplicate-order tickets drop 44% the following quarter.

Why this works: Recruiting for the constraint that breaks the product — not a convenience sample — is what surfaced the failure mode, and screening on a recounted last failure kept the sample authentic.

Evidence Bars

Example 10 — Evidence Bar

Definition: A pre-committed standard specifying what quality and quantity of signal is required before a given class of decision is allowed.

Scenario — “Streamline,” a video-streaming app whose new VP wants to remove the “Downloads” tab from the bottom navigation (“it clutters the nav; nobody downloads anymore”). Classic HiPPO pressure.

Because the team wrote evidence bars before this fight started, the decision routes through policy instead of hierarchy. From their published decision standards:

Decision class Bar
Cut a primary navigation path ≥2 independent methods showing the same low-value / same failure mode, AND usage segmented by connectivity and region
Claim “users prefer X” Behavioral task evidence plus a segment-sized sample — never stated preference alone
Copy change on a non-critical screen One moderated round of 5, or ship-and-measure

Note the third row: bar height is mapped to decision risk — a tooltip rewrite does not need a diary study, which is how evidence bars protect against endless research as well as against HiPPO.

Applying the nav-cut bar:

  • Method 1 (analytics): Overall, only 6% of weekly actives open Downloads. But the required segmentation flips the story: among users on prepaid/capped data plans, it’s 41%, and 72% of their viewing minutes are from downloaded files.
  • Method 2 (story-based interviews, n=8 commuters and rural users): Six recount specific episodes of pre-downloading for subway commutes or data-cap end-of-month rationing (“last week of the month I only watch what I saved”).

Two independent methods show the same thing — Downloads is low-value on average and load-bearing for a connectivity-constrained segment (an inclusion consequence, weighed above the aesthetic tidiness the VP wanted). The bar is not met for removal; the decision log records: “Nav cut rejected 2026-03-11: fails Evidence Bar NB-1. Downloads retained; entry point de-emphasized for unlimited-plan segment only.”

BAD version: No pre-committed bar. The VP’s opinion ships, download-dependent users churn 9% quarter-over-quarter, and the team commissions research afterward to explain the damage.

Why this works: Setting the bar before fieldwork — and mapping bar height to decision risk — protects the team from both the highest-paid person’s opinion and from research without end.

Research Ops Repositories and Event Dictionaries

Example 11 — Research Ops Repository

Definition: A system of record for study plans, screeners, consent artifacts, access-controlled raw notes, synthesis, clips, and decision logs — tagged so future teams can find prior art instead of re-running studies.

Scenario — “Fieldnote,” the internal repository at a 300-person collaboration-tools company.

BAD state (insights die in slide decks): In 2024, research lived in a Drive folder of PDFs named Final_FINAL_research_readout_v3.pdf. A new PM planning “async video messages” research has no way to discover that a near-identical study ran 14 months earlier. The study is re-run at a cost of ~$18k and five weeks — and reaches the same conclusion. No tags, no assumption IDs, no decision links: the chapter’s anti-pattern verbatim.

GOOD state: Every study in Fieldnote gets a structured record:

  • Tags: job (async-status-update), segment (frontline-managers), platform (android, offline-first), and assumption ID (A-114: managers will record video updates on mobile).
  • Artifacts: study plan, the exact screener used, consent forms (retention: raw video auto-deletes after 12 months per the consent language participants actually saw — privacy is honored in the infrastructure, not just the form), raw notes behind access control (researchers only; PII never in the open tier), synthesis doc, and three 30-second highlight clips.
  • Decision log linked to product tickets: DEC-2091: Cut auto-transcribe-on-record; ship opt-in. Evidence: Study S-77 + support ticket cluster T-audio-privacy. Ticket: COLLAB-4410.

Eighteen months later, a different squad searches Fieldnote for assumption:A-114 before proposing the same feature, finds the failed assumption and the clips, and spends its research budget on the next unknown instead. Time-to-prior-art drops from “ask around on Slack for a week” to under an hour.

Why this works: Findings tagged by job, segment, platform, and assumption ID — and linked to decisions and tickets — keep insights alive and reusable instead of trapped in PDFs.

Example 12 — Event Dictionary

Definition: Shared definitions linking qualitative phenomena to consistently named analytics events, so qualitative and quantitative teams describe the same failure in the same words.

Scenario — “Cartwheel,” an e-commerce checkout team investigating abandonment.

BAD state (folk etymology): Interviews report participants “abandoned checkout because of a surprise fee.” Analytics has three overlapping events created by three engineers across two years: checkout_exit, payment_page_bounce, and order_dropoff, none of which distinguishes saw the fee, then left from left for any reason. In the triangulation meeting, the data scientist says abandonment is 12%, the researcher says “most participants” hit the fee problem, and nobody can connect the two — triangulation has become folk etymology, exactly as the chapter warns.

GOOD state: The researcher and analytics engineer co-author dictionary entries, each pairing the qualitative code with the instrumented event:

Qualitative code (from interviews) Event name Definition (shared)
“surprise fee shock” checkout_fee_shown First render of any fee line item not displayed on the product page (shipping, service, import duty)
“fee-driven abandonment” checkout_abandoned_after_fee Session ends or cart exits within 60s of checkout_fee_shown with no further field interaction
“fee tolerated” checkout_completed_after_fee Order placed in a session containing checkout_fee_shown

Now triangulation is arithmetic: checkout_abandoned_after_fee fires in 9.4% of mobile sessions vs 3.1% on desktop — and the diary themes from a two-week shopping study can be checked directly against these event rates. When an engineer later wants to log a new fee_displayed_v2 event, the dictionary review catches the duplicate before the vocabulary forks again.

Why this works: It instruments language — qualitative codes and quantitative events sharing one dictionary — so that a phrase spoken in an interview and a spike on a dashboard are provably about the same phenomenon.

Diary vs Interview: A Decision Frame

Example 13 — Choosing Diaries vs Interviews (and Sequencing Them)

Definition: A decision frame for matching method to the temporal shape of the job: diaries when timing/frequency/interruption patterns are the unknown or social desirability would distort live answers; interviews when you need rich causal narrative of few episodes, rapid iteration, or in-the-moment probing of contradictions.

Scenario — “LedgerPay,” a small-business fintech studying how owners handle weekly payroll approval. The research lead runs two questions through the chapter’s frame:

Question A: “Owners say they approve payroll ‘every Friday morning’ — is that true, and what interrupts it?”
Frame says diary: the unknown is timing/frequency/interruption; the job spans weeks; and social desirability is in play (no owner will admit in a live interview to approving payroll from a bar at 11 p.m. on a phone — but they’ll log it). Also: ecological validity of when things happen is the whole question.
→ 3-week diary, one-tap prompt at each approval event: “Where are you right now? What almost stopped you?” Results: only 38% of approvals happen Friday morning; 22% happen after 9 p.m.; the most common near-miss is “waiting on one employee’s missing hours.”

Question B: “Why did two owners in the pilot approve a payroll run they knew had a wrong amount?”
Frame says interview: few critical episodes, rich causal narrative needed, contradictions to probe in the moment (“You said you always double-check — walk me through that Tuesday”). A diary would never carry this weight, and these two owners “cannot or will not log reliably” anyway — one abandoned the diary in week 1, and the other logged only 2 of the roughly 9 approval events the payroll system shows for the same period. The interviews reveal the cause: the “Approve all” confirmation reads “Approve payroll for 12 employees — $14,208?” with no per-employee anomaly flag, and reversing a run takes a support call. That’s a safety-adjacent money-movement failure with a broken recovery path, escalated ahead of every timing insight from the diary.

The sequenced design (often the best design, per the chapter): diary → interview. The diary’s logged moments select the interview sample: every participant whose log contains a near-miss entry gets a 30-minute follow-up call within 48 hours, while memory is fresh. Logs identify the moments; interviews explain them.

BAD version: One method forced onto both questions — a single round of interviews asking “when do you usually approve payroll?” (collapses time, invites the flattering Friday-morning story) or a diary asked to explain the wrong-amount approvals (fragments with no causal depth).

Why this works: Method is matched to the temporal shape of the job — diaries preserve time and dodge social desirability; interviews deliver causal depth on few episodes — and sequencing them lets each do what the other cannot.

This companion document gives one worked example per teachable concept in Chapter 08. Each example anchors the chapter’s definition in a concrete 2024–2026 product scenario — with actual UI copy, named states, flows, and plausible metrics — and, where instructive, a BAD vs GOOD contrast. Examples honor the book’s priority hierarchy: safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight.
